title: How to talk with a parent about getting help at home
dek: A practical guide for adult children in New Jersey: the signs it is time, how to open the conversation, what to avoid, and the first calls to make.
keyFacts: NJ Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC): 1-877-222-3737
Free Medicare counseling (SHIP): 1-800-792-8820
Medicare open enrollment runs Oct. 15 to Dec. 7
Property Tax Relief (PAS-1) applications are due Nov. 2, 2026
Find a geriatric care manager at aginglifecare.org
body:
Most families do not plan this talk. It happens after a fall, a fender bender or a pile of unopened mail on the kitchen table. If you are reading this before a crisis, you are ahead. If you are reading it after one, you are still in time.

This guide is for the adult son or daughter who has started to worry about Mom or Dad. It walks through the signs worth noticing, how to start the conversation, the papers to find and the New Jersey offices that can help, most of them free.

How do I know it is time to talk?

There is rarely one moment. Look for a pattern of small changes over weeks or months. Holiday visits are often when families first notice them.

  • Around the house. Spoiled food in the fridge, scorched pots, piles of mail, overdue notices, a messier home than usual, or a thermostat set far too hot or cold.
  • Health. Weight loss, missed doctor visits, pill bottles that are too full or too empty, new bruises, or a fall they did not mention.
  • Getting around. New dents on the car, getting lost on familiar roads, or avoiding the stairs to the bedroom.
  • Money. Unpaid bills, unusual withdrawals, a stack of new subscriptions, or talk of a prize they "won." Scammers target older New Jerseyans, so read our guide to common scams in NJ.
  • Mood and contact. Dropping out of church, the senior center or card night. Sounding flat on the phone. Repeating the same story in one call.

One sign alone may mean little. Several together mean it is time for a conversation, and probably a visit to the doctor.

Offering a hand early keeps your parent in charge longer.

How do I start the conversation?

Your parent is an adult who has run a household for decades. The goal is to help them stay in charge of their own life, with more support. Lead with that.

  1. Pick a calm time and place. Choose a quiet afternoon at their kitchen table. Avoid holidays, birthdays and the day after a scare, when everyone is upset.
  2. Start with what they want. Ask, "What matters most to you about the next few years?" Many people say they want to stay at home. That gives you a shared goal.
  3. Share one specific thing you noticed. "I saw the stairs are getting harder" lands better than "You can't manage anymore."
  4. Ask, then listen. "What would make the day easier?" Let silences sit. Their answer may surprise you. Many parents worry about the same things you do.
  5. Offer small, concrete steps. A grab bar, a pill organizer, grocery delivery or a weekly helper is easier to accept than a big change.
  6. Agree on one next step. End with something simple, such as a doctor visit or a call to the county office on aging together.

Expect this to take several conversations. A "no" today often becomes "maybe" in a month, once the idea has had time to settle.

What should I avoid saying or doing?

  • The surprise family meeting. Five relatives in the living room feels like an ambush. Keep early talks small.
  • Ultimatums. "You have to move" usually ends the discussion. Talk about options and trade-offs instead.
  • Talking about them in front of them. Speak to your parent directly, including at doctor appointments.
  • Leading with brochures. A stack of assisted living flyers on the first visit sends the wrong message.
  • Guilt. "I can't keep driving down here every weekend" may be true, but it puts your parent on the defensive. Save your own limits for a later, honest talk about how to share the load.

If your parent has memory loss, keep sentences short and focus on one topic at a time. Their doctor can help judge what decisions they can still make. That matters for legal papers, covered below.

How do we bring brothers and sisters in?

Siblings often see the situation differently. The one who lives nearby sees the daily struggle. The one in another state hears "I'm fine" on the phone. Both views are real.

  • Talk to each other first. Hold a sibling call before anyone speaks to your parent. Share what you have each noticed.
  • Divide the work by strength. One person may handle medical appointments, another the bills and paperwork, another research and phone calls. A sibling in Arizona can still handle insurance calls and online bill pay.
  • Keep one shared record. A shared document or notebook with doctors, medications, account contacts and decisions avoids repeated arguments.
  • Respect your parent's choice of point person. They may want a particular child to be their health care representative. That is their call.
  • Plan for the local sibling. The child who lives closest often carries the most. Agree early on how others will give that person breaks. Our guide to respite and caregiver support in NJ lists programs that can help.

Which papers should we find?

You do not need to read everything. You do need to know where the important documents are, and whether key legal papers exist. Ask your parent to show you. Do this while they are well.

Health and insurance

  • Medicare card, plus any Medicare Advantage, Medigap or Part D drug plan cards
  • NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid), PAAD or Senior Gold cards, if they have them
  • A list of doctors, pharmacies and current medications with doses
  • Any long term care insurance policy

Legal

  • Durable power of attorney for finances
  • Advance directive (a proxy directive naming a health care representative, a living will, or both)
  • A POLST form, if their doctor completed one
  • Will or trust, and the name of the lawyer who drafted it

If these papers do not exist, putting them in place is one of the most useful things you can do. Read our guide to estate planning in NJ.

Money and home

  • Bank, brokerage and retirement accounts, and pension contacts
  • Social Security information and recent tax returns
  • Deed, mortgage, homeowners insurance and property tax bills
  • A list of online accounts and where passwords are kept
  • Military discharge papers (DD-214) for veterans, and any prepaid funeral contract
Check on property tax relief

New Jersey's combined Property Tax Relief application (PAS-1) covers ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ. The deadline for 2025 benefits was November 2, 2026. If your parent missed it, call the hotline at 1-888-238-1233. Our property tax relief guide explains who qualifies.

Who should I call first in New Jersey?

New Jersey has a free front door for older adults and families. Start there before you pay anyone.

  • Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC). Each county's office on aging serves as the local ADRC. Call 1-877-222-3737 to reach the office where your parent lives. Staff can screen for home care, meals, transportation, adult day, respite and Medicaid long term care. Services depend on your parent's county, so give their address.
  • State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP). Trained counselors explain Medicare options for free and have nothing to sell. Call 1-800-792-8820. Medicare open enrollment runs October 15 to December 7, so this fall is a good time to review your parent's drug plan. See Medicare Advantage vs. Medigap.
  • Prescription and bill help. PAAD and Senior Gold lower drug costs for many older residents. Call 1-800-792-9745. Our prescription and bill help guide lists the income limits.
  • NJ 211. Dial 2-1-1 or 1-877-652-1148 for help with food, utilities and housing.
  • Your parent's doctor. Ask for an appointment focused on function, memory and medications. Bring your list of concerns. With your parent's permission, ask to be listed as someone the office can speak with.

If your parent may need help with daily activities over the long term, ask the ADRC about Managed Long Term Services and Supports. Our guide to Medicaid and MLTSS in NJ explains how it works.

What does a geriatric care manager do?

A geriatric care manager, now often called an Aging Life Care Professional, is usually a nurse, social worker or similar professional who specializes in older adults. Think of them as a hired guide for the family. This is especially useful when siblings live far away or the situation is complicated.

According to the Aging Life Care Association, these professionals offer consultation, assessment, care coordination and advocacy. In practice, that can mean:

  • A home visit to assess safety, health, memory and daily needs
  • A written care plan with options and likely costs
  • Finding and screening home care agencies, adult day programs or facilities
  • Going to doctor visits and keeping long-distance family updated
  • Acting quickly during a hospital stay or discharge
  • Helping a family reach agreement when siblings disagree

You can search for a professional near your parent's town at aginglifecare.org. Most families pay privately, and Medicare does not cover it. AARP reports hourly rates of roughly $150 to $300 depending on the region, with a first assessment that often takes four to six hours. Ask about fees up front. Our guide to when to call a geriatric care manager goes deeper.

Questions to ask before you hire one

  • What is your professional background and license, and are you certified as a care manager?
  • How long have you worked with older adults in this county?
  • How do you charge (hourly, a flat fee for an assessment, or a monthly package)?
  • Who covers for you after hours or on vacation?
  • Do you receive any payment from agencies or facilities you recommend?
Start small

You do not have to solve everything this month. One honest conversation, one call to the ADRC and one folder of key papers is real progress.

You may also find our guides to getting paid as a family caregiver and things to do with a parent who has dementia helpful.

More guides that may help: when a parent refuses help.

faq.q: What if my parent refuses to talk about it?
faq.a: Give it time and try again in a few weeks. Focus on one small, practical change rather than the big picture. Some parents hear the same idea more easily from their doctor, a clergy member or a care manager.

faq.q: Who do I call in New Jersey to find local services for my parent?
faq.a: Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737. You will be connected to the county office on aging where your parent lives.

faq.q: Can I talk to my parent's doctor?
faq.a: Privacy rules usually require your parent's permission. Ask your parent to tell the office, or sign a form, so staff can speak with you.

faq.q: Who pays for a geriatric care manager?
faq.a: Most families pay a private care manager out of pocket, so ask about fees before you hire one. Your county ADRC can tell you about free care management through state and Medicaid programs if your parent qualifies.

faq.q: What papers should we find before a parent needs more help?
faq.a: Start with the Medicare and drug plan cards, a medication list, a durable power of attorney, an advance directive and the will. Knowing where these are, and whether they exist, saves time in a crisis.

title: Help for family caregivers in NJ: respite, leave and support
dek: New Jersey helps pay for breaks, adult day care and paid leave for people caring for an older relative. Here is who qualifies, what it covers and how to apply.
keyFacts: Statewide Respite Care Program: care recipient 18+, income up to $2,982 a month (single) in 2026
JACC: age 60+, income under $4,855 a month (single) in 2026
NJ Family Leave Insurance pays 85% of wages, up to $1,119 a week in 2026
Up to 12 weeks of paid family leave, or 56 separate days, in 12 months
Start with the ADRC: 1-877-222-3737
body:
If you drive your mother to dialysis, manage your father's pills or sleep with one ear open for your spouse, you are a family caregiver. You may never have used that word. New Jersey has programs built for you anyway.

This guide covers the state's main respite programs, adult day care, paid family leave and support groups. It also lists the warning signs that you need a break soon.

What is respite care, and why does it matter?

Respite means someone else takes over for a while so you can rest. It might be a home health aide for a few afternoons a week, a day program, or a short stay in a licensed facility while you travel or recover from your own surgery.

Caregivers who take regular breaks tend to keep going longer. That often helps the person they care for stay at home longer, too. Think of respite as part of the care plan.

Taking a break is part of the job.

Who qualifies for the Statewide Respite Care Program?

The Statewide Respite Care Program (SRCP) is overseen by the NJ Division of Aging Services and operates in every county. It helps unpaid caregivers of adults with chronic disabilities. Eligibility is based on the person receiving care.

Requirement (2026)SingleCouple
Monthly gross income of the care recipientUp to $2,982Up to $5,964
Liquid assetsUp to $40,000Up to $60,000
Age18 or older, living in the community in New Jersey
Cost shareSliding scale from 0% to 25% of service costs

Depending on the caregiver's assessed needs and available funding, the state's program brochure says SRCP can provide:

  • Home care and companion services
  • Adult day care
  • A short stay in a facility
  • Campership (a camp program)
  • A Caregiver Directed Option, which reimburses you for services or items that make caregiving easier

How to apply: Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737. You will be routed to the respite program in the county where your loved one lives.

Questions to ask when you call

  • How long is the wait for an assessment, and is there a waiting list for services?
  • Which agencies or adult day centers near us take part in the program?
  • How many hours of help could we expect each month?
  • Can I choose a relative or friend to provide care under the caregiver-directed option?
  • How is our share of the cost figured, and how will we be billed?

Have the care recipient's income, savings and insurance information handy before you call. It speeds up screening.

What is JACC, and how is it different?

Jersey Assistance for Community Caregiving (JACC) helps people who need a lot of care but have too much income or savings for Medicaid. It is aimed at older adults who might otherwise need to move to a nursing home.

Requirement (2026)SingleCouple
Age60 or older
Care needMeets nursing facility level of care
Countable monthly incomeUnder $4,855Under $6,582
ResourcesUnder $40,000Under $60,000

JACC services can include care management, respite, home modifications, medical equipment and supplies, chore help, a personal emergency response system, home delivered meals, adult day programs, home care and transportation. The state's JACC page lists a limit of $1,156 per participant per month, plus care management. Many participants pay a share based on income, on a sliding scale.

People enrolled in Medicaid's Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) cannot also use JACC. MLTSS has its own respite benefit. See our guide to Medicaid and MLTSS.

How to apply: Contact your county Area Agency on Aging through the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737. A care manager will do an assessment at home.

Is adult day care a good fit?

Adult day programs give a caregiver regular, predictable time off on weekdays. The person you care for gets meals, activities and company. Many programs offer transportation.

Social adult day vs. adult day health

  • Social adult day care focuses on activities, meals and supervision. It suits people who are fairly healthy but should not be alone all day.
  • Adult day health services (sometimes called medical day) add nursing, medication management and therapies. NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid) members should ask their plan whether a center near them is covered.

Help for families living with dementia

The Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program (AADSP) helps pay for adult day care for people with Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia who live with an unpaid caregiver. The Division of Aging Services' 2026 program chart still shows the 2025 limits for this program: gross income under $50,256 a year for a single person and $58,632 for a couple, with resources under $40,000 (single) or $60,000 (couple). It covers up to five days a week, with a sliding scale cost share. Ask the ADRC for the current limits.

Before you choose a center

  • Visit twice, once announced and once drop-in, around lunchtime.
  • Ask about staff to participant ratios and dementia training.
  • Ask how they handle toileting, falls and wandering.
  • Check pickup times and whether their van serves your town.

Can I get paid leave to care for a parent?

Yes, if you work in New Jersey. Family Leave Insurance (FLI) pays you while you care for a family member with a serious health condition. It is funded through payroll deductions, so most NJ workers are already covered.

Family Leave Insurance (2026)Details
Weekly benefit85% of your average weekly wage, up to $1,119
Continuous leaveUp to 12 weeks in a 12-month period
Intermittent leaveUp to 56 separate days in a 12-month period
Earnings to qualify20 weeks earning at least $310 a week, or $15,500 total in your base year

"Family" is defined broadly. It includes parents, parents-in-law, spouses, domestic partners, siblings, grandparents, grandchildren, children of any age, other blood relatives and people you consider family.

How to apply

  1. Tell your employer. For caring for a relative, give reasonable notice before a continuous block of leave, and 15 days' notice before each separate period of intermittent leave, unless there is an emergency. Too little notice can cut 14 days from your benefit.
  2. Start the claim online. Go to the state's My Leave Benefits site. You can start up to 60 days before leave begins. If you apply after leave starts, you have 30 days.
  3. Get the medical part done. Give your Online Form ID to your family member's doctor. It is your job to make sure the office submits its section.
  4. Ask questions. The Division of Temporary Disability and Family Leave Insurance answers calls at 609-292-7060, weekdays 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Will my job be protected?

FLI replaces wages. Job protection comes from separate laws. As of July 17, 2026, the New Jersey Family Leave Act covers employers with 15 or more employees. Workers qualify after 3 months on the job and 250 hours worked in the past year. It provides up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave in a 24-month period. The federal Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) also applies at employers with 50 or more employees nearby.

New Jersey's Earned Sick Leave law helps too. Most workers earn 1 hour of sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 40 hours a year, and can use it to care for a family member.

Where can I find a support group?

Talking with people who understand can make a hard week bearable. Many groups now meet by phone or video, which helps if you cannot leave home.

  • Alzheimer's Association. Free 24/7 helpline at 1-800-272-3900. The New Jersey chapter runs caregiver and early-stage support groups and free monthly education programs.
  • Alzheimer's New Jersey. Call 1-888-280-6055.
  • Care2Caregivers. A peer support line at Rutgers, staffed by people who have cared for a loved one with dementia. Call 1-800-424-2494 and ask about current hours.
  • Well Spouse Association. For people caring for a husband, wife or partner. Call 1-800-838-0879.
  • Family Caregiver Alliance. National education and support. Call 1-800-445-8106.
  • Your county office on aging and local hospitals. Many host caregiver groups and classes. Ask the ADRC what meets near you.

If loneliness is part of the strain, our guide to staying connected in NJ has more ideas.

What should I have ready when I call?

Screening goes faster when the facts are in front of you. Keep one folder, paper or digital, and bring it to every call and visit.

  • About the person receiving care. Date of birth, address, Medicare and any NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid) numbers, and a list of diagnoses and doctors.
  • Money. Recent statements showing monthly income (Social Security, pensions) and savings. SRCP, JACC and the dementia day program all have income and asset limits.
  • Daily needs. A short, honest list of what the person cannot do alone, such as bathing, dressing, medications or being left by themselves. Do not downplay it on the phone.
  • Your own schedule. Your work hours and the times you most need coverage. This helps the county match the right service.
  • Your job paperwork. If you plan to use Family Leave Insurance, have your employer's name and your recent pay records handy.

Here is a hypothetical example of how the pieces can fit together. Say you work full time in Edison and your father, who has early dementia, lives with you. You might ask the ADRC about an adult day program for weekdays, use intermittent Family Leave Insurance days for his doctor visits, and join a phone support group on a free evening. No single program does everything, so most families combine two or three.

What are the signs of caregiver burnout?

Burnout creeps up. Common signs include:

  • Feeling drained, emotionally and physically
  • Pulling away from friends and family
  • Losing interest in things you used to enjoy
  • Feeling hopeless or powerless
  • Changes in appetite, weight or sleep
  • Trouble concentrating
  • Getting sick more often
  • Irritability, frustration or anger

If several of these sound familiar, treat it as a signal to act. Call the ADRC about respite this week. Tell your own doctor what you are carrying. Ask one relative or friend for one specific, regular task, such as Tuesday dinner or Saturday visits.

If you are in crisis

If you feel overwhelmed or have thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, any time of day.

New to all of this? Our guide to talking with a parent about getting help covers the first steps.

You may also find our guides to getting paid as a family caregiver and things to do with a parent who has dementia helpful.

faq.q: Does the Statewide Respite Care Program look at my income or my parent's?
faq.a: It looks at the income and assets of the person receiving care (and their spouse). In 2026 the limit is $2,982 a month in gross income for a single person and $5,964 for a couple, with liquid assets up to $40,000 or $60,000.

faq.q: How much does NJ Family Leave Insurance pay in 2026?
faq.a: It pays 85% of your average weekly wage, up to a maximum of $1,119 a week, for up to 12 weeks of continuous leave or 56 separate days in a 12-month period.

faq.q: Can I use Family Leave Insurance to care for my mother-in-law?
faq.a: Yes. Parents-in-law are covered, along with parents, grandparents, siblings, spouses, domestic partners and others you consider family.

faq.q: Can someone use both JACC and Medicaid MLTSS?
faq.a: No. JACC is for people who are not enrolled in MLTSS. MLTSS members get respite and similar services through their Medicaid plan.

faq.q: Where do I apply for respite or JACC?
faq.a: Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737. You will be connected to the county where the person receiving care lives.

title: Aging in place in NJ: making your home safe and comfortable
dek: Room by room changes, what they cost, who can help pay and how to hire a contractor safely in New Jersey, from split-levels to shore condos.
keyFacts: Home improvement jobs over $500 need a written contract in NJ
You can cancel a home improvement contract until midnight of the third business day
Check a contractor's registration: 1-800-242-5846
VA HISA grants: up to $6,800 or $2,000 lifetime, depending on eligibility
Ask for weatherization on the LIHEAP/USF application, open Oct. 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027
body:
Most New Jerseyans over 60 want to stay in the home they know. Staying safely usually takes some changes. Some cost less than a tank of gas. Others need a contractor and a permit.

This guide walks through the home room by room, gives rough costs, explains who can help pay and shows how to hire a contractor without getting burned.

What does aging in place look like in a New Jersey home?

New Jersey's housing creates its own challenges. Think about where you live now and how you will move through it at 85.

  • Split-levels and bi-levels. These are everywhere in New Jersey's postwar suburbs. Every trip from kitchen to bedroom means a half flight of stairs. Handrails on both sides of every short flight are a priority. Some families turn a lower-level den into a bedroom near a bathroom.
  • Colonials and Cape Cods. The full bath is often upstairs. Adding a first floor half bath, or a full bath in a former laundry room or office, can make one floor living possible.
  • Raised shore homes. Many homes along the coast were elevated after Superstorm Sandy. Long outside staircases are hard on bad knees. Ask early about a ramp, an outdoor-rated stair lift or a residential elevator.
  • Condos and co-ops. One floor living is easier, but many older garden complexes have no elevator. Check the association's rules before you change anything. Boards often require approval for bathroom work, flooring or anything attached to shared walls.
  • Older homes in prewar towns. Narrow doorways, steep stairs and a single upstairs bathroom are common. Plan bigger changes before you need them.

What should I change, room by room?

Entrances and outside

  • Bright motion sensor lights at every door
  • Sturdy handrails on both sides of outside steps
  • A bench or shelf by the door for packages and groceries
  • Lever handles in place of round knobs
  • A plan for snow and ice, whether a neighbor, a paid service or a town volunteer program

Stairs and hallways

  • Handrails on both sides, running the full length
  • Light switches at the top and bottom
  • Contrasting tape on step edges if the steps are hard to see
  • No loose runners or clutter on stairs

Bathroom

Wet, hard surfaces make the bathroom a common place for falls. Start here.

  • Grab bars by the toilet and in the tub or shower, anchored into studs or with rated anchors. A towel bar will not hold your weight.
  • A comfort height toilet or a raised seat
  • A handheld shower head and a shower chair or tub transfer bench
  • Non-slip strips or mats
  • A walk-in or curbless shower, if a tub is getting hard to step over
  • A night light on the path from bed to bathroom

Kitchen

  • Move everyday dishes and food to shelves between hip and shoulder height
  • Pull-out shelves in low cabinets
  • Lever or touch faucets
  • A stove with front controls and automatic shutoff, or a countertop induction burner
  • Good task lighting over the counter and sink

Bedroom and living areas

  • A bed and chairs at a height that makes standing up easy
  • A lamp you can reach from bed
  • Clear walking paths and no throw rugs
  • Cords tucked away from walkways
  • Working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms on every level

What do these changes cost?

Prices vary by house and town. These national estimates from HomeGuide give a starting point. Always get local quotes.

ProjectTypical installed cost
Grab bar, per bar$100 to $350
Straight stair lift$2,000 to $8,500
Curved stair lift$7,500 to $15,000 or more
Walk-in shower, prefab kit$1,000 to $8,000
Walk-in shower, custom tile$3,500 to $15,000

A few ways to keep costs down:

  • Have several grab bars put in on one visit to save on labor.
  • If your stairs have a landing, ask whether two straight stair lift rails would cost less than one curved rail.
  • Ask your doctor about a referral to an occupational therapist for a home safety check. They can tell you which changes matter most for your body and your house.
The cheapest fixes, like lights, rails and clear floors, can go a long way.

Who can help pay?

Medicaid and state programs

  • Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS). New Jersey's Medicaid long term care program can cover home and vehicle modifications and a personal emergency response system for members, based on assessed need. See our guide to Medicaid and MLTSS.
  • Jersey Assistance for Community Caregiving (JACC). For people 60 and older who need nursing home level care but have too much income for Medicaid. JACC can pay for environmental accessibility adaptations, medical equipment and an emergency response system. Details are in our caregiver support guide.
  • County programs. Many county offices on aging run or fund small home repair and safety programs. Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 to ask what your county offers.

Veterans

The VA's Home Improvements and Structural Alterations (HISA) grant helps pay for medically necessary changes, such as accessible bathrooms, ramps and wider doorways. The lifetime benefit is up to $6,800 for a service-connected condition, or for any condition if the veteran has a service-connected rating of at least 50%. Other eligible veterans can get up to $2,000. Ask the Prosthetic and Sensory Aids Service at your VA medical center to confirm your balance before work starts.

Energy and weatherization

New Jersey's Weatherization Assistance Program provides a free energy audit and free efficiency work for qualifying households. You request it by checking a box on the combined LIHEAP and Universal Service Fund (USF) application. For federal fiscal year 2027, the income limit is 60% of state median income, which is $51,273 for one person. Applications are open October 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027. Call 1-800-510-3102 or apply online. Low-income utility customers may also qualify for Comfort Partners, which installs energy saving measures at no cost. Call 1-866-378-4345. The program serves households at or below 250% of the federal poverty level that heat with electricity or gas. If you heat with oil or propane, ask about weatherization instead. Our food and utility help guide has more.

Keeping the house affordable

Property taxes are often the biggest cost of staying put. ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ are all on one application (PAS-1). The deadline for 2025 benefits was November 2, 2026. Call 1-888-238-1233 or see our property tax relief guide.

How do I hire a contractor safely in New Jersey?

Home improvement contractors in New Jersey must register with the Division of Consumer Affairs and renew every year. Unregistered contractors cannot get municipal permits. The state says registration is no endorsement, so do your own checking too.

  1. Verify registration and complaints. Call the Division of Consumer Affairs at 1-800-242-5846 or check with your county consumer affairs office. For electricians and plumbers, confirm the license is active.
  2. Get three written estimates. Ask how long each company has been in business and whether it uses subcontractors.
  3. Confirm insurance. Registered contractors must carry at least $500,000 in liability coverage. Get a copy and call the insurer to make sure it is current.
  4. Insist on a written contract. Any job over $500 needs one. It must include the contractor's legal name, business address and registration number, plus start and finish dates, a description of the work and the total price.
  5. Know your right to cancel. You can cancel for any reason until midnight of the third business day after you receive your copy. Send the cancellation in writing by certified mail, return receipt requested, and keep a copy.
  6. Make sure permits are pulled. Final inspections should be done before your final payment.
  7. Pay in stages. A common schedule is one third up front, one third midway and one third at completion. Do not pay cash. Ask for a lien waiver.

Red flags

  • A knock on the door offering a "great deal" with leftover materials
  • Demands for cash or more than a third of the price up front
  • No registration number, or only a P.O. box address
  • "You don't need a contract for this"

Read more in our guide to scams targeting NJ seniors.

Can smart technology help?

Simple tech can make a home safer and help family worry less. Start with one or two tools you will really use.

  • Personal emergency response systems. A button worn on the wrist or neck, some with automatic fall detection. MLTSS and JACC can cover them for members.
  • Video doorbells. See who is there before opening the door.
  • Smart plugs and bulbs. Lights that turn on by voice or on a schedule, so you never walk into a dark room.
  • Smart speakers. Call family hands free, set reminders and check the weather.
  • Automatic pill dispensers. They sound an alarm and release the right dose at the right time.
  • Water leak and stove shutoff sensors. Useful for anyone who sometimes forgets.

For video calls and other ways to stay in touch, see staying connected in NJ.

When is it time to consider a move?

Sometimes a house cannot be adapted at a reasonable cost. That is a practical problem with practical answers. Signs it may be time to look:

  • The only bathroom is up a flight of stairs that a stair lift cannot serve
  • Upkeep, taxes and repairs are draining savings
  • You rarely leave the house because you no longer drive and transit is far
  • Your care needs are growing faster than the help available

Options range from a one floor condo or 55-plus community near family to assisted living. Moving while you are still healthy lets you choose on your own terms. If family is part of the decision, our guide to talking about care with a parent can help start that conversation.

For walkers, shower chairs, hearing devices and the programs that lend or pay for them, see our guide to adaptive equipment and assistive technology.

More guides that may help: home modification grants and medical alert systems.

faq.q: Do I need a written contract for a small home repair in NJ?
faq.a: New Jersey requires a written contract for home improvement jobs over $500. It must include the contractor's registration number, dates, a description of the work and the total price.

faq.q: How do I check whether a contractor is registered?
faq.a: Call the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs at 1-800-242-5846, or ask your county consumer affairs office. They can also tell you about complaints.

faq.q: Can I cancel a home improvement contract after I sign?
faq.a: Yes. You can cancel for any reason before midnight of the third business day after you receive a copy. Do it in writing by certified mail with a return receipt.

faq.q: How much is the VA HISA grant?
faq.a: Up to $6,800 over a lifetime for service-connected conditions, or for veterans rated at least 50% service-connected. Other eligible veterans can get up to $2,000. Your VA medical center's prosthetics office can confirm your balance.

faq.q: Will Medicaid pay for a stair lift or bathroom changes?
faq.a: New Jersey's MLTSS program can cover home modifications for members based on assessed need. Ask your MLTSS care manager, or call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 to start an assessment.

title: Estate planning basics for New Jersey seniors
dek: Wills, powers of attorney, advance directives, POLST, inheritance tax and probate, explained in plain English for New Jersey families.
keyFacts: NJ has no estate tax for deaths on or after Jan. 1, 2018
Class A heirs (spouse, children, grandchildren, parents, stepchildren) owe no NJ inheritance tax
Siblings: first $25,000 untaxed, then 11% to 16%
A NJ power of attorney must be signed and acknowledged, usually before a notary
Wills are probated through your county surrogate
body:
This is general information, not legal advice

Laws change, and every family's situation is different. Use this guide to get organized and ask good questions. Then talk with a New Jersey attorney before you sign anything.

Estate planning sounds like something for wealthy people. It is really about two simple questions. Who speaks for you if you cannot speak for yourself? And who gets what you leave behind, with as little hassle as possible?

A few documents answer both. Here is how they work in New Jersey.

What does a basic New Jersey estate plan include?

For most retirees, a solid plan has five parts:

  • A will that names who inherits and who will handle your estate (your executor)
  • A durable power of attorney for money and property
  • An advance directive naming a health care representative and stating your wishes
  • Up-to-date beneficiary designations on retirement accounts, life insurance and bank accounts
  • A POLST form, if you are seriously ill and want your treatment wishes written as doctor's orders

Some people also need a trust, for example to provide for a child with a disability or to plan for long term care costs. An elder law attorney can tell you whether that applies to you.

Do I need a will?

If you die without a will, New Jersey law decides who inherits, and a relative must apply to be appointed to manage the estate. That may not match what you would have chosen, especially in blended families.

What makes a will valid in New Jersey?

  • You must be at least 18 and of sound mind.
  • A typed will must be signed by you and by at least two witnesses.
  • A handwritten will can be valid without witnesses if the signature and the important parts are in your own handwriting. These often cause disputes, so a typed, witnessed will is safer.

Ask your lawyer to add a self-proving affidavit. Without one, a witness may have to appear at the surrogate's office after your death to confirm your signature. That can be hard to arrange years later.

Practical tips

  • Keep the original in a safe, known place. The surrogate needs the original, not a copy.
  • Tell your executor where it is.
  • Review it after a death, marriage, divorce, move or new grandchild.
The best plan is the one your family can find when they need it.

What is a durable power of attorney?

A power of attorney lets someone you trust (your agent) handle your money and property. That might mean paying bills, talking to the bank, filing taxes or selling a house.

The word "durable" matters. Under New Jersey law, a power of attorney ends if you become incapacitated unless it says otherwise. A durable power of attorney includes language saying it stays in effect if you lose capacity. That is exactly when your family will need it.

  • Signing. You must sign it and acknowledge your signature before a notary public or another officer allowed to take acknowledgments, such as a New Jersey attorney. You must also understand what you are signing.
  • Real estate. If your agent may need to sell or mortgage a house, the document should be recorded with the county clerk where the property is located.
  • Choosing an agent. Pick someone honest, organized and nearby, or at least comfortable with online banking. Name a backup.

Without one, your family may have to go to court to have a guardian appointed. That takes time and money. Signing a power of attorney while you are healthy avoids it.

What are advance directives and POLST?

Advance directives

New Jersey recognizes two kinds of advance directives. You can have one or both.

  • Proxy directive. Names a health care representative to make medical decisions if you cannot. It is sometimes called a durable power of attorney for health care.
  • Instruction directive. Often called a living will. It tells doctors and family what treatment you would or would not want in certain situations.

An advance directive takes effect only after a doctor determines you cannot understand your diagnosis and treatment choices. It must be in writing and signed by you. Your signature must be witnessed by two adults or by a notary, an attorney or another authorized official. You do not need a lawyer. The state's advance directive guide explains the rules, and many hospitals give out blank forms.

Give copies to your health care representative, your doctors and your hospital. Talk through your wishes with the person you name. A form alone cannot answer every question.

POLST

The New Jersey POLST (Practitioner Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment) is a medical order, usually for people with a serious illness or frailty. You complete it with your physician, advanced practice nurse or physician assistant, who signs it. It follows you across hospitals, nursing homes and hospice. A POLST does not replace an advance directive. Many people have both.

Will my family owe New Jersey taxes?

For most families, the answer is no. New Jersey has no estate tax for anyone who died on or after January 1, 2018. The state does still have an inheritance tax, and it depends on who inherits.

ClassWho is in itNJ inheritance tax
ASpouse, civil union or domestic partner, children (including adopted), stepchildren, grandchildren and great-grandchildren, parents, grandparentsNone
CBrothers and sisters, a son-in-law or daughter-in-law (the spouse or civil union partner of a child)First $25,000 untaxed, then 11% to 16%
DEveryone else, such as nieces, nephews, friends and step-grandchildren15% up to $700,000, 16% above
EQualified charities, religious and educational institutions, the State of NJNone

Any inheritance tax is due within eight months of death. If you plan to leave money to a niece, a nephew or a close friend, ask your attorney or tax adviser about the cost to them.

Tax waivers

Even when no tax is owed, some assets need a state tax waiver before they are released. For bank and brokerage accounts, when no tax is due, the executor can often complete a self-executing waiver (Form L-8) and give it to the institution. Real estate always requires a waiver issued by the state Division of Taxation. When everyone who inherits is exempt, the executor files Form L-9 to get it. The state's guide to being an executor explains the details.

How does probate work in New Jersey?

New Jersey's probate process is simpler than in many states. It runs through the surrogate in the county where the person lived. Most surrogate's offices work by appointment.

  1. Wait out the short waiting period. There is a brief wait after death before the surrogate can act. Passaic County, for example, says it cannot issue certificates until at least 11 days after death.
  2. Gather what you need. Bring a certified death certificate with a raised seal, the original will, names and addresses of next of kin, and photo ID.
  3. Meet with the surrogate. If the will is not self-proving, one of the witnesses may need to come too.
  4. Get Surrogate's Certificates. These prove the executor's authority to banks and others. Order several. Fees vary by county. In Passaic County, the minimum probate fee is $100, and extra certificates are $5 each.
  5. Handle the estate. The executor collects assets, pays debts and taxes, and distributes what is left.

If there is no will, a family member applies to the surrogate to be appointed administrator. That process has more steps and may require a bond.

Why do beneficiary designations matter so much?

Many of your largest assets may never pass through your will. IRAs, 401(k)s, annuities, life insurance and bank accounts with a payable-on-death beneficiary go directly to the person named on the account form. The form controls, even if your will says something else.

  • Request a copy of every beneficiary form and check the names.
  • Update forms after a divorce, a death or a new grandchild.
  • Name a backup (contingent) beneficiary.
  • Be careful naming someone who receives disability benefits. A direct inheritance could affect their eligibility. Ask an attorney about a special needs trust.

Joint accounts also pass outside the will, to the surviving owner. Adding a child to your bank account can create tax and family problems. Talk to a lawyer first.

How do I choose an elder law attorney?

A general estate lawyer can draft a will. An elder law attorney also understands Medicaid, long term care planning, guardianship and benefits for older adults. If you may need nursing home or in-home care someday, that experience matters. See our guide to Medicaid and MLTSS.

  • Where to look. The National Academy of Elder Law Attorneys (NAELA) has a directory of New Jersey members. Some lawyers are also Certified Elder Law Attorneys (CELA) through the National Elder Law Foundation.
  • Ask about fees. Many charge a flat fee for a basic plan of will, power of attorney and advance directive. Get the price in writing.
  • Ask who the client is. If your children set up the meeting, the lawyer still represents you. Expect to speak with the lawyer alone for part of the visit.
  • Bring a list. Include your assets, how each is titled, current beneficiaries, and the people you want to name.

Starting this with a parent? Our guide to the first conversation about care includes a checklist of papers to find.

You may also find our guide to what to do when a parent dies helpful.

For the details on one of these papers, see our guide to power of attorney in New Jersey, and for day-to-day help, managing a parent's money.

More guides that may help: probate in New Jersey, New Jersey inheritance tax, and advance directives.

faq.q: Does New Jersey still have an estate tax?
faq.a: No. There is no New Jersey estate tax for people who died on or after January 1, 2018. The state still has an inheritance tax, but it does not apply to Class A heirs such as spouses, children and grandchildren.

faq.q: Do my children pay inheritance tax on what I leave them?
faq.a: No. Children, stepchildren, grandchildren, spouses, domestic or civil union partners, parents and grandparents are Class A beneficiaries and owe no New Jersey inheritance tax.

faq.q: Does a New Jersey power of attorney need to be notarized?
faq.a: Yes, or acknowledged before another authorized officer such as a New Jersey attorney. Most people sign in front of a notary. To stay in effect if you become incapacitated, it must include language making it durable.

faq.q: Do I need a lawyer for an advance directive?
faq.a: No. New Jersey advance directives must be in writing, signed by you, and witnessed by two adults or by a notary, attorney or other authorized official. The state's advance directive guide on nj.gov explains the rules.

faq.q: Where do I probate a will in New Jersey?
faq.a: At the surrogate's office in the county where the person lived. Bring a certified death certificate, the original will, a list of next of kin and photo ID.

title: Things to do with a parent who has dementia
dek: Simple ways to spend good time together, adjusted for each stage of dementia, plus memory cafes and help for New Jersey families.
keyFacts: The Alzheimer's Association says activities can improve quality of life and may reduce wandering and agitation.
Everyday tasks like folding towels, stirring or setting the table make good activities.
Plan outings for the morning or early afternoon, when many people with dementia do best.
Alzheimer's Association helpline: 1-800-272-3900, free, 24 hours a day.
body:
When a parent has dementia, the days can start to feel like a list of tasks. Pills, meals, appointments, safety. It is easy to forget that your mom or dad still needs something to do, and someone to do it with.

The Alzheimer's Association says a person with dementia does not have to give up the activities they love. This guide covers why activity matters, how to adjust it as the disease changes, simple ideas for home and outings, and where New Jersey families can get help and a break.

Why do activities matter so much?

Activities give the day a shape. They let your parent feel useful, and they give the two of you time together that is not about care. The Alzheimer's Association notes that activities can improve quality of life and may reduce behaviors like wandering and agitation.

You do not need special equipment. The Association suggests sticking with activities the person has always enjoyed and adjusting them to match what they can do now. Making dinner together, gardening, music or a walk all count.

Your parent's own history is the best guide. A retired bookkeeper may like sorting or organizing. A lifelong gardener may still enjoy yard work.

How do activities change from early to late stage?

Dementia changes over time, and so does what works. Here is a rough guide based on Alzheimer's Association and National Institute on Aging (NIA) advice.

StageWhat it often looks likeActivities that tend to fit
EarlyMostly independent. May still drive, volunteer, take part in social activities or even work.Hobbies you both enjoy, walks and exercise together, outings, memory cafes, faith community, making plans together.
MiddleNeeds more structure and help starting and finishing tasks.Everyday chores broken into steps: stirring, folding towels, setting the table, sorting. Music, simple art, short walks, time with a pet.
LateExperiences the world mostly through the senses.Favorite music, hand lotion with a familiar scent, brushing hair, looking at old photos, sitting outside on a nice day.

In the early stage, the Alzheimer's Association describes your role as a care partner: offering support and companionship and helping plan for the future. Focus on your parent's strengths and on keeping them as independent as possible.

In the middle stage, routine matters more. Encourage your parent to do as much as they can, and be ready to step in. The Association suggests introducing more repetitive tasks as the disease progresses.

In the late stage, connection is still possible. The Association says you may be able to keep connecting through touch, sound, sight, taste and smell.

What can we do together at home?

These ideas come from Alzheimer's Association and NIA lists. Pick one or two to try.

  • Music and familiar songs. Play music your parent knows, talk about the song and the singer, sing along or dance. The Alzheimer's Association suggests letting the person choose the music when possible. It also notes that someone in the late stage may still tap a beat or sing lyrics from childhood.
  • Simple cooking. Your parent can mix and pour while you handle the stove. The NIA also suggests letting them tell someone else how to prepare a recipe.
  • Folding laundry. Towels are ideal. Nobody minds if the corners don't line up.
  • Sorting. Coins, mail, recycling, buttons or old greeting cards.
  • Photo albums and old stories. The Alzheimer's Association suggests using photos to remind your parent of important people and places.
  • Gardening. Water houseplants, plant flowers or vegetables in a pot, and talk about how they are growing.
  • Art. Painting, drawing or making cards for friends. Keep projects on an adult level and avoid anything that feels childlike. Use safe materials, and the project does not have to be finished in one sitting.
  • Pets. Feeding, brushing, walking or simply holding a calm pet.
  • Faith. Prayer, sacred music, holiday rituals or worship your parent has known for years. If going to services is too much, the NIA notes that online services are an option.
  • Gentle exercise. A short walk, stretching bands, or tossing a soft ball or balloon back and forth.

How do I keep an activity from turning into a struggle?

  • Keep it simple. Break the task into small steps and give one step at a time. Too many directions at once can overwhelm.
  • Follow their lead. Notice what makes your parent happy and what makes them anxious or irritable. If they would rather watch than help, that is fine. The NIA says to let them simply watch if they enjoy that more.
  • Help them get started. Many people still want to do things but have trouble beginning. Show the first step, or start the brush moving on the paper.
  • Focus on enjoyment. The Alzheimer's Association puts it plainly: "Focus on enjoyment, not achievement."
  • Skip the memory tests. Questions like "Who is this in the picture?" can feel like a test your parent might fail. The Alzheimer's Association advises against criticizing or correcting, and both it and the NIA suggest simple yes or no questions. Try "That looks like your sister Rose, doesn't it?" instead.
  • Know when to stop. If attention fades or frustration builds, end the activity or switch to something easier.

Does the time of day matter?

Yes. Many people with dementia have more confusion and agitation in the late afternoon or early evening, which is called sundowning. The Alzheimer's Association suggests scheduling outings, appointments and bathing for the morning or early afternoon. It also suggests time outside in daylight and less stimulation in the evening, such as less TV and loud music.

Keep the setting calm while you do things together. The NIA recommends reducing noise and clutter and keeping a regular routine for meals, bathing and dressing. For music, the Alzheimer's Association suggests turning off the TV, closing windows to cut outside noise and choosing music without commercials.

What do NJ care managers and therapists say?

In October 2026 we talked with more than 30 private instructors and about 50 older adults, adult children, care managers and home care professionals around North Jersey. Here is what came up most often about activities and dementia.

  • Music often lands best. Care professionals we spoke with said music is often the activity that reaches someone with dementia when other things don't.
  • Change it up within the hour. A therapy practice that serves families at home told us an hour on one thing is hard for many people with dementia, so they switch between music, art and conversation.
  • Bring back an old favorite. A care manager described a client who stopped playing bridge after his diagnosis and would welcome a partner who came to play with him.
  • Price. Recreation, art and music therapists who visit the home charge roughly $160 to $200 a visit in North Jersey, and other activity instructors often less. Ask about dementia experience.
  • The caregiver usually arranges it. Families said a spouse or adult child almost always sets it up, and a regular visit also gives the caregiver a break.
Before anyone teaches in the home

Trust came up in almost every conversation we had. Ask about a background check, insurance and a reference, have family there for the first visit, and pay per session. Our guide to vetting someone who comes into the home walks through each step.

Where can we go in New Jersey?

The NIA suggests you keep going out as long as you are both comfortable. Good choices include a favorite restaurant during quieter hours, a park or nature trail, a zoo or aquarium, or a short museum visit. Plan outings for the time of day your parent is at their best, and keep them short enough that they don't get worn out.

Memory cafes are relaxed social gatherings for people with memory loss and the people who care for them. In New Jersey, many meet at libraries. In Montclair, Lifelong Montclair and the Montclair Public Library run a free monthly Memory Cafe for adults with early memory loss and their caregivers. Registration is required (call 973-744-3278). The Somerset County Library System's Manville branch hosts a memory cafe for adults with early-stage dementia and their caregivers. Registration is required, and the contact number is 908-458-8425. To find others, search the Dementia Friendly America memory cafe directory or ask your local library.

Museums. The Zimmerli Art Museum at Rutgers in New Brunswick runs Art Heals: Creative Connections, a free creative arts program for people with memory loss and their care partners. Its website says the program is postponed until spring 2027, so check back or call the museum's access coordinator at 848-932-6178.

Adult day programs offer a structured day with activities, meals and company, and they give you regular time off. Through the state's Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program, contracted centers offer at least a five-hour day, a meal, activities adapted to abilities and staff trained in dementia care. The program can cover part of the cost for families who qualify. See our list of adult day programs in New Jersey.

Can someone come to the house to lead activities?

Some services send a teacher or activity host to the home to lead music, art or games. That can give a caregiver a break. Home Happenings, a service from this site's publisher, is launching soon to bring local teachers to homes in Essex County and nearby towns for music, art, yoga and games. Respite programs, described below, may also help pay for in-home help.

Who can help New Jersey families?

WhoPhoneWhat they do
Alzheimer's New Jersey helpline1-888-280-6055Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Information, care planning and local referrals, with translation in over 200 languages.
Alzheimer's Association helpline1-800-272-3900Free, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. Information, local resources, crisis help and emotional support.
Aging and Disability Resource Connection1-877-222-3737Reaches your county office on aging, including the county's Statewide Respite Care Program.

The Statewide Respite Care Program helps unpaid caregivers take short breaks, with a sliding-scale cost share. Alzheimer's New Jersey also runs a Respite Care and Wellness Program that offers a $1,000 reimbursement toward respite care (call 973-586-4300). Read our guides to respite and help for family caregivers and dementia support in New Jersey for eligibility and next steps.

faq.q: What activities are good for someone with dementia?
faq.a: Familiar ones. The Alzheimer's Association and the National Institute on Aging suggest music, simple cooking, folding laundry, sorting, gardening, art, short walks, time with pets and faith activities the person has known for years.

faq.q: What activities work in late-stage dementia?
faq.a: Focus on the senses. The Alzheimer's Association suggests favorite music, rubbing scented lotion into the hands, brushing hair, looking at old photos and sitting outside together on a nice day.

faq.q: What is the best time of day for activities with a parent who has dementia?
faq.a: Usually the morning or early afternoon. The Alzheimer's Association suggests scheduling outings and appointments then, and keeping evenings quieter to help with sundowning.

faq.q: Where can we find a memory cafe near us in NJ?
faq.a: Yes. Many meet at public libraries, including the Montclair Memory Cafe and a memory cafe at the Somerset County Library System's Manville branch. Search the Dementia Friendly America directory or ask your library for one near you.

faq.q: Can someone come to the house to do activities with my parent who has dementia?
faq.a: Yes. Music therapists, art and recreation therapists and some private instructors visit homes in New Jersey. Look for dementia experience, ask how they adapt when attention fades, and plan for the same time each week.

title: Can I get paid to care for my parent in New Jersey?
dek: NJ FamilyCare's Personal Preference Program, VA programs, insurance and private agreements can pay a son or daughter for care. Here is who qualifies and where to start.
keyFacts: NJ FamilyCare's Personal Preference Program lets members hire relatives
PPP state helpline: 609-631-2481
VA Veteran Directed Care can pay a family member as an aide
Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC): 1-877-222-3737
body:
If you are already driving Mom to appointments, helping Dad shower and sorting the pills on Sunday night, you may be wondering whether any of that time can be paid. In New Jersey the answer is often yes, but only through a few specific doors. Which one fits depends on your parent's income, health, veteran status and insurance. This guide walks through each path, who can be paid and where to start.

Can a family member be paid through NJ FamilyCare?

Yes. NJ FamilyCare (New Jersey's Medicaid program) runs the Personal Preference Program, usually called PPP. It lets a member who qualifies for personal care assistant (PCA) services take a monthly budget instead of an agency aide, and use it to hire people they know and trust. The state's PPP materials say members can hire relatives, friends and neighbors, including their children and grandchildren.

PPP is part of the regular NJ FamilyCare benefit, so your parent does not have to be in Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) to use it. Many people who use it are in MLTSS, though, and our guide to Medicaid MLTSS in New Jersey explains that program's medical and financial rules. If your parent is not on NJ FamilyCare yet, start with NJ FamilyCare for seniors.

Who qualifies for PPP? According to the state's PPP guidance, your parent must:

  • Be enrolled in NJ FamilyCare Plan A.
  • Need help with activities of daily living, such as bathing, dressing or getting around.
  • Receive or qualify for Medicaid PCA services.
  • Be able to direct their own care, or name an authorized representative to do it for them. A parent with memory problems can still take part with a representative.

The health plan assesses your parent and sets the number of PCA hours. Those hours become the budget.

Who can be the paid worker, and who can't?

A PPP worker must be at least 18, legally allowed to work in the United States (with an I-9 form) and able to do the tasks on the schedule your parent needs. The state's PPP FAQ says a participant may hire a husband, wife or legal guardian, as well as children, grandchildren, siblings, nieces, nephews and other relatives. Rules can change, so confirm with your health plan before you count on it.

A few limits matter for families:

  • The worker can't also be the authorized representative. The representative manages the plan, is not paid for it and must live within 30 miles or one hour of your parent. So if you want to be the paid caregiver, a sibling or another trusted person may need to be the representative.
  • A guardian or power of attorney can be the worker only if they appoint someone else as the authorized representative.
  • No pay during a hospital, rehab or nursing home stay, and one worker can't be paid for more than 40 hours a week. If the budget covers more hours than that, your parent hires a second worker.
  • Benefits for the worker. The FAQ warns that wages earned by a family worker count as income if that person gets benefits such as SSI or SNAP.

How does PPP pay, and how do we apply?

The authorized hours are turned into a monthly cash management plan. The state's 2026 PPP presentation says the plan is 87.5% of the monthly amount, with 12.5% covering employer costs such as payroll taxes and workers' compensation. Workers must be paid at least New Jersey minimum wage ($15.92 in 2026) and no more than $25 an hour. Unspent money does not carry over to the next month.

A fiscal intermediary, either Public Partnerships (PPL) or PALCO, handles payroll and tax withholding. Your parent becomes the employer on paper, but the intermediary does the paperwork.

To apply, your parent (or you, with permission) calls their NJ FamilyCare health plan, asks for a PCA assessment and says they want the Personal Preference Program. The plan sends the enrollment to the fiscal intermediary, a consultant helps build the budget, and services start on the first of the following month. The state PPP helpline is 609-631-2481.

Does JACC let you pay a relative?

Jersey Assistance for Community Caregiving (JACC) is a state-funded program for people 60 and older who need nursing home level care but want to stay home and are not on NJ FamilyCare or MLTSS. Its income and asset limits are higher than Medicaid's, but services are capped at a set monthly amount. Our JACC guide covers it in full.

JACC rule (2026)What the state says
Age60 or older, living in the community
Monthly incomeUp to $4,855 single or $6,582 married (365% of the federal poverty level)
Countable assets$40,000 or less single, $60,000 or less for a couple
Service cap$1,156 a month, plus care management
Cost shareSliding scale co-pay based on income

JACC does have a self-directed option. Participants can hire their own "participant-employed providers," who are paid through a fiscal intermediary, never directly. The state's JACC pages do not say whether a relative can be one of those providers, so ask the county office when you apply. Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737.

What if my parent is a veteran?

Veteran Directed Care. This VA program gives a veteran a flexible budget to hire their own personal care aides, which the VA says may include a family member or neighbor. A veteran enrolled in VA health care can qualify if they are also eligible for VA community care, meet the clinical need and the program is offered in their area. Ask a VA social worker whether it is available near your parent.

Aid and Attendance. This is a monthly amount added to a VA pension for a veteran or surviving spouse who needs another person's help with daily activities, is largely bedbound, lives in a nursing home or has very limited eyesight. It is paid to the veteran or survivor, not to a caregiver, but the extra income can help a family cover care. Your parent must qualify for VA pension first. Apply online, at a VA regional office or by mail with VA Form 21-2680.

Family caregiver stipend. If the veteran has a VA disability rating of 70% or higher and needs at least six months of continuous personal care, the Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers can pay a monthly stipend to a primary family caregiver, including a son or daughter. The veteran and caregiver apply together on VA Form 10-10CG.

Will long-term care insurance pay me?

It depends entirely on the policy. Long-term care policies cover home health care and help with daily activities, but each contract decides who counts as a qualified caregiver. Find the policy, read the home care section and call the insurer before you start, so you know whether a relative can be paid and what paperwork they need. Tax-qualified policies usually start paying when a person can't do at least two daily activities for 90 days or more. If you hit a wall, the New Jersey Insurance Ombudsman takes calls at 1-800-446-7467.

Can my parent just pay me directly?

Yes, with their own money. Put it in writing first. A caregiver agreement lists the tasks, the hours, the hourly rate and how you will log your time. Keep it signed and dated, and keep the time sheets.

The paperwork matters if your parent may ever need Medicaid. When someone applies for long-term care Medicaid, the county reviews five years of financial history. New Jersey's rules presume that care a relative gave in the past was meant to be free. In a 2023 state fair hearing decision, payments to adult children for earlier care counted against the parent because there was no written agreement made in advance to pay a fair market rate. An elder law attorney can draft the agreement. See estate planning in New Jersey, and check what care costs in New Jersey to set a fair rate.

What about taxes?

When your parent pays you privately, your parent is generally a household employer. IRS Publication 926 says that for 2026, a household worker paid $3,000 or more in cash wages owes Social Security and Medicare tax through the employer, reported on Schedule H. The exceptions cover a spouse, a child under 21 and, in some cases, a parent. An adult child caring for a parent does not fall under them. The pay is generally taxable income to you.

Medicaid program pay can be different. Under IRS Notice 2014-7, some Medicaid home care payments can be left out of your income if you live in the same home as your parent and provide care there. The IRS rule is written for Medicaid waiver programs, so ask a tax preparer whether your PPP pay qualifies. Payments made directly from your parent's own money do not qualify. A tax preparer can confirm what applies to you.

If none of these paths fits right now, unpaid help still counts, and you need breaks too. Our guide to respite care in New Jersey covers free and low cost relief, and how to talk with a parent about getting help can make the money conversation easier. For any of these programs, the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 is the right first call.

faq.q: Can I get paid by Medicaid to take care of my mother in New Jersey?
faq.a: Yes, if she is on NJ FamilyCare and qualifies for personal care assistant services. Through the Personal Preference Program she can use a monthly budget to hire you. Ask her health plan for a PCA assessment and say she wants PPP.

faq.q: Can a spouse be paid as a caregiver under New Jersey's PPP?
faq.a: The state's PPP FAQ says a participant may hire a husband, wife or legal guardian. Confirm with your health plan, since rules can change. The worker cannot also serve as the authorized representative who manages the plan.

faq.q: How much does the Personal Preference Program pay family caregivers?
faq.a: Pay depends on the hours the health plan approves. For 2026 the state says workers must earn at least New Jersey minimum wage of $15.92 an hour and no more than $25 an hour.

faq.q: Do I need a written agreement if my parent pays me privately?
faq.a: It is strongly recommended. New Jersey Medicaid presumes past care by a relative was free, so payments without an advance written agreement at a fair market rate can be treated as gifts if your parent later applies for long-term care Medicaid.
