title: Adult day care in NJ: medical vs. social, costs and how to pay
dek: Adult day programs give a parent a safe, social day and give caregivers a break. Here is how medical and social day differ in New Jersey, what they cost, who helps pay and how to choose one.
keyFacts: Medical day centers (adult day health services) are licensed by the NJ Department of Health and provide care by a registered nurse.
CareScout's 2025 NJ median for adult day health care: $100 a day.
The Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program pays 20% to 100% of adult day costs, up to five days a week.
Medicare does not pay for adult day care. Medicaid, MLTSS, JACC, VA and respite programs may.
Start with your county ADRC: 1-877-222-3737.
body:
Adult day programs give an older adult a safe, social place to spend the day, often with meals, activities, health checks and a ride to and from home. Families use them so a parent with memory loss or frailty isn't alone, and so the caregiver can work or rest. New Jersey has two main kinds: social adult day centers and adult day health services, also called medical day care.

Several programs can help pay. NJ FamilyCare and MLTSS, the state's Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program, JACC, VA benefits, the Statewide Respite Care Program and long-term care insurance can all help, depending on the center. This guide explains the difference between the two types, what a day looks like, what it costs and how to choose a program for your mom or dad.

What is the difference between social and medical adult day care?

Medical day care, which New Jersey calls adult day health services, is for people with nursing or medical needs and has a registered nurse on staff. Social day is for people who don't need medical attention during the day but do need supervision and company.

Adult day health services (medical day)Social adult day
Who it suitsAdults with medical or nursing care needsAdults who need supervision for safety but not medical care
Health careCare by a registered nurse, help with walking and toiletingSome health monitoring and limited personal care
MealsAt least one full mealAt least one full meal
RidesTransportation to and from homeVaries by center
OversightLicensed by the NJ Department of HealthAsk each center who oversees it and what funding it accepts

The New Jersey Division of Aging Services describes both kinds this way in its 2026 program guide. Both can serve people living with Alzheimer's disease or another dementia. Both give family caregivers time to work or take a break.

Not sure which fits? If your dad needs his medications given, his blood sugar watched, a wound checked or help using the bathroom, start with medical day. If he is steady on his feet and mostly lonely or forgetful, social day may be enough.

Who is adult day care good for?

It suits older adults who shouldn't be alone all day but still live at home, and families who need daytime coverage. It is often a good step before, or instead of, a move to assisted living.

Think about adult day if:

  • Your parent has memory loss and is not safe home alone, or has started wandering.
  • They are isolated since a spouse died or since giving up driving, and the days feel long.
  • You work, and paying an aide for a full day five days a week is out of reach.
  • You are worn out and need regular, predictable time off.
  • Your parent needs health checks or therapy a few times a week but doesn't need a nursing home.

Adult day does not have to be every day. Two or three days a week is a reasonable place to start. Your parent can also attend adult day and still qualify for Medicare home health, because Medicare says going to adult day care does not end a person's homebound status. See our guide to Medicare home health care.

Your parent can start with a couple of days a week and add more later if it goes well.

What does a typical day look like?

Most programs pick your parent up in the morning, serve breakfast or a snack and a full lunch, run group activities through the day and bring them home in the afternoon. Medical day centers add nursing care and help with personal care.

Schedules vary by center. Here is what a weekday often includes:

  • Morning. Pickup by van, a light breakfast, a blood pressure or health check at medical day centers, and medications given by the nurse.
  • Late morning. Exercise, often seated, plus news discussion, trivia, crafts or music.
  • Midday. A full hot lunch. Ask whether the center handles special diets.
  • Afternoon. Games, art, music, entertainment or a quiet rest area, then the ride home.

Centers in the state's Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program must offer at least a five-hour program day, at least one full meal, activities adapted to each person's cognitive and physical abilities, help with transportation, support for families and staff training in dementia care. For ideas on what works for people with memory loss, see things to do with a parent who has dementia.

How much does adult day care cost in New Jersey?

CareScout's 2025 Cost of Care Survey put New Jersey's median cost for adult day health care at $100 a day. At five days a week, that is about $26,000 a year. Many families pay much less through public programs.

Prices vary by center, by the type of program and by how many days your parent attends. Ask every center for its daily rate in writing, and ask what is included. Some charge separately for transportation, a half day or a late pickup. For how adult day compares with home care, assisted living and nursing homes, see what senior care costs in New Jersey.

Medicare does not pay for adult day care. Medicare.gov lists adult day health care as long-term care, which Medicare doesn't cover.

How can we pay for adult day care?

The New Jersey Division of Aging Services says each center takes part in different funding programs, so ask each one directly. The main options are below.

  • NJ FamilyCare and MLTSS. NJ FamilyCare can pay for medical day care, and MLTSS can also pay for social adult day care, for members who qualify. For MLTSS, your parent must need nursing-home-level care, and the 2026 income limit is $2,982 a month for the applicant. If your parent is in MLTSS, contact the MLTSS care manager. See our MLTSS guide.
  • Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program. For people with a doctor-documented diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia who are 18 or older, live in the community and have an unpaid caregiver. The subsidy covers 20% to 100% of the cost of adult day for up to five days a week, on a sliding scale. The state lists income limits of $50,256 a year for a single person and $58,632 for a married couple, with liquid assets up to $40,000 single or $60,000 married (the state's 2025 figures). The home and car are not counted. You apply at a participating center, and your parent is not limited to centers in their own county. Questions go to the Division of Aging Services at 609-438-4733.
  • JACC. For people 60 and older who need nursing-home-level care and are not on Medicaid. It can pay for adult day health services and social adult day care, within a monthly cap. In 2026 the income limit is $4,855 a month for one person, and countable assets must be $40,000 or less. See our JACC guide.
  • Statewide Respite Care Program. Gives unpaid caregivers a break, and can pay for adult day health or social adult day care. In 2026 the care recipient's income must be under $2,982 a month (single) with liquid assets up to $40,000. See help for family caregivers in NJ.
  • VA Adult Day Health Care. Enrolled veterans who meet clinical criteria can attend adult day at a VA medical center, a state veterans home or a community program, if available. A copay may apply. Ask the VA social worker about VA Form 10-10EC. See our guide to benefits for older veterans.
  • Long-term care insurance and private pay. Some policies cover adult day. Call the insurer before your parent starts.

For social day centers, funding through the county Area Agency on Aging may also be available. You can't combine every program. A person on Medicaid or MLTSS can't also use JACC, the Alzheimer's program or Statewide Respite, and those three state programs generally can't be used at the same time. The county Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737 can screen your parent and tell you which one fits.

How do I find and choose a good program for my mom or dad?

Start with our adult day listings by county, the state's licensed facility search or your county ADRC at 1-877-222-3737. Then visit at least two centers, ideally on a normal weekday while the program is running.

The state's licensed facility search at healthapps.state.nj.us lists medical day centers. The Division of Aging Services notes that day center service areas are set by travel time, not county lines, so a center just over the border may serve your parent. For social day centers, call the ADRC.

  1. Call first. Ask about openings, the daily rate, which funding programs they accept, hours and whether they serve your parent's town.
  2. Visit during program hours. Watch the participants. Are they engaged, or parked in front of a TV? Are staff speaking to people warmly and by name?
  3. Ask about staff. Who is the nurse, and is one on site all day? How many staff work with each group? What dementia training do they have? How long have most aides been there?
  4. Ask about safety. How do they handle a fall, a medical emergency or someone who tries to leave? Are doors secured? Who gives medications?
  5. Taste the food. Ask to see a week's menu and how they handle diabetic, low-salt or soft diets.
  6. Ask about a trial day. Ask how the center helps a new participant settle in during the first few weeks.

To check on a licensed medical day center or report a problem, call the Department of Health's 24-hour complaint hotline at 1-800-792-9770. It takes complaints about adult medical day care centers.

If your parent says "I'm not going to a day care"

Some older adults bristle at the words "day care." Try calling it a club, a class or "the center." Ask the staff for tips, and start with a short trial.

How does my parent get to and from the center?

Medical day centers provide transportation to and from home. Social day centers vary, and many counties run paratransit vans that serve adult day sites.

Ask the center how long the ride usually takes, whether the driver helps your parent from the door to the van, and whether the vans have wheelchair lifts. A long route can tire someone with dementia, so ask about pickup order. If the center doesn't provide rides, check your county's senior transportation through our county pages.

For a family facing a new dementia diagnosis, adult day is often one piece of a larger plan that includes respite, support groups and legal paperwork. Our guide to dementia support in New Jersey pulls those together.

faq.q: How do I find an adult day program for my mom in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call your county Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737, search the state's licensed facility list for medical day centers, or browse our adult day listings by county. Then visit two or more centers on a normal weekday.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for adult day care?
faq.a: No. Medicare treats adult day health care as long-term care, which it does not cover. NJ FamilyCare and MLTSS, the Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program, JACC, VA benefits, the Statewide Respite Care Program and long-term care insurance may help.

faq.q: How much does adult day care cost in NJ?
faq.a: CareScout's 2025 Cost of Care Survey put the New Jersey median for adult day health care at $100 a day, about $26,000 a year at five days a week. Prices vary, so ask each center for its rate in writing.

faq.q: Can my dad with dementia get help paying for adult day?
faq.a: Yes, if he qualifies. The state's Alzheimer's Adult Day Services Program covers 20% to 100% of the cost for up to five days a week for people with a doctor-documented dementia diagnosis, an unpaid caregiver and income and assets under the state's limits. You apply at a participating center.

faq.q: What is the difference between medical day care and social day care?
faq.a: Medical day care, called adult day health services in New Jersey, is licensed by the Department of Health and includes care by a registered nurse, at least one full meal, activities, personal care and transportation. Social day is for people who need supervision but not medical care during the day.

faq.q: Can my parent get Medicare home health care and go to adult day?
faq.a: Yes. Medicare says attending adult day care does not, by itself, end a person's homebound status for home health care.

title: Rides to medical appointments for seniors in NJ
dek: How to get a parent to the doctor once they stop driving, from NJ FamilyCare rides through Modivcare and county paratransit to Access Link, volunteer drivers, Medicare plan benefits, VA travel pay and rideshare.
keyFacts: NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid) covers non-emergency rides to covered medical care through Modivcare. Book at 1-866-527-9933, at least two business days ahead.
Each of New Jersey's 21 counties runs a paratransit service for older residents and people with disabilities. Rules and fees vary by county.
NJ Transit Access Link serves people whose disability keeps them off the local bus. Start with an eligibility interview: 973-491-4224, option 1.
Original Medicare pays for an ambulance only when any other vehicle could endanger your health. Some Medicare Advantage plans cover rides to doctor visits.
Not sure where to start? The ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 connects you with your county office on aging.
body:
If your mom or dad can't drive to the doctor anymore, New Jersey has several ways to get them there. If they have NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid), rides to covered medical care are free through the state's broker, Modivcare. Everyone else can use county paratransit, which every county offers to older residents, plus NJ Transit's Access Link for people with disabilities, local senior buses and volunteer driver programs.

The right choice depends on your parent's insurance, how much help they need getting in and out of a car, and how far away the appointment is. Most families end up using two or three of these. Almost all of them need several days' notice, so book early.

Does NJ FamilyCare pay for rides to the doctor?

Yes. NJ FamilyCare covers non-emergency medical transportation to medically necessary, covered services, and Modivcare arranges the rides anywhere in the state. Call 1-866-527-9933 at least two business days before the appointment.

Modivcare takes phone reservations on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. The state says you can book by phone up to a month ahead, and online at Modivcare's TripCare site with no limit on how far ahead. A relative, caregiver or medical facility staff member can call for your parent. Have these ready:

  • Your parent's NJ FamilyCare ID number
  • Pickup address and ZIP code
  • The doctor's name, phone number and address
  • The appointment date and time
  • Any special needs, such as a wheelchair

Modivcare's New Jersey member brochure says the ride may be a car, van, taxi, rideshare, wheelchair lift van or, when needed, an ambulance. It is curb-to-curb. Drivers are not allowed to come into the home or the doctor's office, and they wait at most 15 minutes past the scheduled pickup. Your parent must bring their own wheelchair. Some plans limit the number of trips a year or the miles per trip, and a round trip counts as two trips. Call the number on the back of the plan card to ask.

Modivcare lineUse it for
1-866-527-9933Booking a ride
1-866-527-9934Late ride, or a return trip
1-866-527-9945Facilities: standing orders, discharges
1-866-333-1735Formal complaint

If your parent might qualify for NJ FamilyCare but hasn't applied, see our guide to NJ FamilyCare for seniors.

How does county paratransit work for medical trips?

Every New Jersey county runs a paratransit service for older residents and people with disabilities, and doctor visits are usually a top priority. Call your county to register, then book each trip ahead.

These are the county numbers listed by the state Division of Disability Services and the county governments. Hours, reservation rules, fees and how far the vans travel all vary, so ask before you count on a ride.

Many towns also run their own dial-a-ride vans. Morris County's list shows how much they differ. One town asks for 48 hours' notice for medical trips, another asks for a week, and most only travel within 3 to 15 miles of town. Some have wheelchair lifts and some don't. Your county page lists senior centers and local contacts, and the senior center is often the fastest way to learn about the town van.

Book the ride the same day you book the appointment. Most services fill up days ahead.

Can my parent use NJ Transit Access Link to get to the doctor?

Yes, if a disability keeps them from using the local bus or light rail. Access Link goes anywhere in its service area, for any purpose, but it is shared-ride and your parent must be approved first.

Call 973-491-4224 and choose option 1 to start. NJ Transit requires a phone or in-person interview and current medical verification. Once approved:

  • Booking. Option 2 on the same number. Reservations are taken every day from 7:30 a.m., until 4 p.m. for next-day rides and 3 p.m. for later dates.
  • Where and when. Access Link runs in the same areas and hours as local bus and light rail service. No bus nearby means no Access Link.
  • Timing. The pickup can come up to an hour before or after the requested time, and the driver waits only five minutes. A pilot program lets riders ask for a drop-off time instead, so ask about it on option 5.
  • Cost. It is not free. The fare is based on the local bus fare and zones, and the reduced fare card can't be used. An approved personal care attendant rides free.
  • Help. Service is curb-to-curb. Drivers help with boarding and securing a wheelchair. If your parent needs more help, ask on option 5 well ahead of time. Reviews can take three business days or more.

If your parent can still ride a regular bus with some coaching, the New Jersey Travel Independence Program (NJTIP) at Rutgers teaches older adults how. The only cost during training is the rider's own fares. Call 848-932-4499. Our guide to NJ Transit reduced fares explains the discount for riders 62 and older.

Are there volunteer drivers for older adults in New Jersey?

Yes, in some areas. Volunteer programs are usually free and more personal than a van, but drivers are limited, so call weeks ahead. Two examples:

  • Hunterdon County Volunteer Driver Program. For county residents with few other options who need a specialist appointment that isn't available in Hunterdon. There is no fee, but the rider pays tolls and parking. Weekdays only, for appointments between 9:30 a.m. and 2:30 p.m. Call 908-788-1368 at least two weeks ahead.
  • Caregiver Volunteers of Central Jersey. Free medical rides for people over 60 who no longer drive, in many Ocean and Monmouth County towns. Volunteers usually stay through the appointment. They can't take wheelchairs or large oxygen tanks, and they don't drive to dialysis. Toms River office 732-505-2273, Freehold office 732-876-3900.

Elsewhere, ask your county office on aging, the senior center, your parent's house of worship and local family service agencies. The Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737 can connect you with your county. You can also dial 2-1-1 and search for transportation.

Does Medicare cover rides to medical appointments?

Original Medicare does not pay for routine rides. It covers an ambulance when riding in any other vehicle could endanger your parent's health. The Medicare and You 2027 handbook says some Medicare Advantage plans cover rides to doctor visits.

Ambulance. Medicare Part B covers ground ambulance transport to the nearest appropriate facility when it's medically necessary. In some cases it pays for a scheduled non-emergency ambulance with a written order from a doctor, for example for dialysis. Your parent pays 20% of the approved amount after the Part B deductible. If the ambulance company thinks Medicare may not pay, it must give your parent an Advance Beneficiary Notice first.

Medicare Advantage. Ride benefits vary a lot by plan and change every year. Call the member services number on the card and ask:

  • Does the plan cover rides to medical appointments this year?
  • How many one-way trips, and how far?
  • Who provides the rides, and how far ahead must we book?
  • Can a family member book for my parent?

Open enrollment runs October 15 to December 7 each year, so if rides matter, compare plans then. Our guide to Medicare Advantage or Medigap covers the tradeoffs.

Veterans. VA travel pay can reimburse mileage, parking and tolls for eligible veterans going to VA care or VA-approved community care. Bus, taxi or rideshare costs need approval from the VA facility first. File within 30 days, since later claims are usually denied. Ask the Beneficiary Travel contact at your parent's VA facility. Our veterans benefits guide has more.

Is rideshare safe for my mom or dad?

It can be, especially when a family member sets it up and follows along. Rideshare works best for a parent who walks well, can get in and out of a car alone and has a phone they use.

Uber lets a family organizer add an older adult to a Family profile, book and pay for their rides, and track the trip live. Uber also takes ride requests by phone at 1-833-873-8237 and offers wheelchair-accessible vehicles (Uber WAV). Lyft says its drivers pass a criminal background check and a driving record check, and that it keeps monitoring active drivers' records.

Before the first ride

Save the doctor's address in the app so no one types it in a hurry. Show your parent how to check the license plate, car and driver's photo before getting in. Agree they will text you when they arrive. Keep a taxi or family backup number handy for the ride home, since appointments run late.

Home care staff we spoke with told us most aides don't drive clients, so don't assume a home care agency will cover appointments. Ask directly. If anyone new will drive your parent, our guide to vetting someone coming into the home explains what to check.

How do I set up a ride plan for my parent?

Write down every recurring appointment, match each one to a ride service, and post the booking numbers by the phone. Then plan a backup for the trip home.

  1. List the trips. Primary doctor, specialists, dialysis, physical therapy, labs, pharmacy. Note which repeat weekly.
  2. Check eligibility. NJ FamilyCare, county paratransit registration, Access Link, a Medicare Advantage ride benefit, VA travel pay.
  3. Book standing rides. For regular treatments, ask about standing orders. Modivcare has a line for facilities to set them up.
  4. Ask the doctor's office. Schedulers often know local ride options, and some practices and hospitals run shuttles. Morning slots leave more room for slow return rides.
  5. Plan the return. Shared rides can mean a long wait after the visit. Pack water, snacks and medications, and ask whether the office has a place to sit.
  6. Write it down. One page by the phone with each service's number, how far ahead to book and your parent's member ID numbers.

After a hospital stay, ask the discharge planner to arrange the first follow-up rides before your parent leaves. See our hospital discharge guide. For the bigger picture of life after the car keys, read when a parent stops driving and driving later in life.

For door-to-door public transit, see our guide to Access Link and county paratransit.

faq.q: How do I get my mom to the doctor if I work full time?
faq.a: Register her with your county paratransit service and book rides as soon as appointments are made. If she has NJ FamilyCare, call Modivcare at 1-866-527-9933 at least two business days ahead. A relative can book for her. An Uber Family profile lets you book and track her ride from work.

faq.q: Can I book a Medicaid ride for my dad?
faq.a: Yes. Modivcare says a relative, caregiver or medical facility staff member can arrange the ride. Have his NJ FamilyCare ID, pickup address, the doctor's name, address and phone, and the appointment time ready.

faq.q: Is county paratransit free for seniors in NJ?
faq.a: It depends on the county. Each of New Jersey's 21 counties runs its own service with its own fees, hours and booking rules. Call your county's number to ask.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for a ride to dialysis?
faq.a: Original Medicare may pay for a non-emergency ambulance with a doctor's written order saying it is medically necessary, for example for someone with end-stage renal disease going to dialysis. Regular car rides are not covered. Some Medicare Advantage plans and NJ FamilyCare cover routine rides.

faq.q: What if the Modivcare ride doesn't show up?
faq.a: Call the Ride Assist line at 1-866-527-9934. Use the same line to arrange a return trip if you didn't know when the appointment would end. To file a formal complaint, call 1-866-333-1735.

faq.q: Will an aide drive my parent to appointments?
faq.a: Often not. Home care staff told us most aides don't drive clients. Ask the agency directly, and ask whose car and insurance would be used if they do.

title: Senior living placement services in NJ: how free advisors work
dek: Placement advisors help families find assisted living and memory care at no charge because communities pay them. Here is what that means for your parent's options, what to ask and how to check a residence yourself.
keyFacts: Big placement companies say communities pay them when a referred family moves in, so families pay nothing.
A free advisor's list may include only communities that have a contract with that agency.
The NJ Department of Health licenses assisted living residences. Check a license in its long-term care facility search.
Complaints about assisted living go to the NJ Department of Health hotline, 1-800-792-9770, 24 hours a day.
Your county's Aging and Disability Resource Connection gives free help at 1-877-222-3737.
body:
A senior living placement service helps a family find an assisted living residence, memory care or independent living community for a parent. An advisor asks about your mom or dad's care needs, budget and preferred towns, sends a short list of places, sets up tours and often comes along. Families usually pay nothing. The communities pay the agency a fee when a family it referred moves in.

That arrangement can save you weeks of phone calls, especially after a hospital stay. It also means the list you get may include only communities that have a contract with the agency. New Jersey's Department of Health licenses the residences themselves, so you can and should check any place on the list on your own. Your county's Aging and Disability Resource Connection gives free, unpaid guidance at 1-877-222-3737.

What does a senior living placement service do?

It matches your parent with senior housing that has room, fits the budget and can handle their care needs. The advisor does the legwork of calling around, comparing prices and setting up visits.

You will also see these businesses called senior living advisors, placement agencies or referral agencies. Some are national companies that work mostly by phone. A Place for Mom, for example, says it has a team of more than 400 advisors and refers families to communities and home care agencies in its network. Others are franchises with a local owner who tours with you in person. CarePatrol, Assisted Living Locators, Oasis Senior Advisors and Senior Care Authority all have franchise offices that serve parts of New Jersey. There are also small independent advisors.

The steps are similar from company to company:

  1. A first conversation. The advisor asks about health, memory, mobility, help with bathing or medications, budget, insurance, veterans status and the towns you want to stay near.
  2. A short list. You get a handful of residences that the advisor says have openings and can meet those needs.
  3. Tours. The advisor schedules visits. Many local franchise owners say they go on the tours with you.
  4. Move-in help. Some advisors help with paperwork, the move date and check-ins after your parent settles in.

Placement advisors mainly cover assisted living, memory care and independent living. Some also refer families to home care agencies. If you are still deciding between staying home and moving, read our guide to assisted living vs. home care in New Jersey before you call.

How are placement agencies paid if they are free?

The community pays them. In most cases the agency earns a referral fee when a family it introduced signs a lease or admission agreement. The companies say this openly.

A Place for Mom states that it is "paid by our senior living network communities when a family we refer chooses to move into a community" and is "paid by home care agencies each time we refer a family to them." It also says that, under their contracts, communities "cannot charge families referred by A Place for Mom more than those who don't use a referral service." CarePatrol says its services are at no cost to families "as we are paid for by over 20,000 preferred senior care providers across the nation."

That model has real benefits. You get a knowledgeable person's time without a bill. But it shapes what you see.

  • The list may be partial. A residence that does not pay referral fees may never come up, even if it is ten minutes from your house and a good fit.
  • The fee depends on a move. In the usual setup, the agency is paid only if your parent moves into a place it referred.
  • Your details may travel. Ask before you give your parent's name and number which communities will receive it. A Place for Mom notes that filling out its form or calling authorizes it to contact you by phone, text or email, and that you can opt out at any time.
Free to you means the community pays. Ask which communities are on the agency's list, and which are not.

Does New Jersey license senior placement agencies?

The New Jersey Department of Health licenses the places your parent might move to. Placement agencies do not appear on its list of licensed facility types, so ask each agency directly whether it holds any license and who oversees it.

The department's list includes assisted living residences, comprehensive personal care homes, assisted living programs and nursing homes. Each has its own definition. An assisted living residence, for example, must offer apartment units with at least one unfurnished room, a private bathroom, a kitchenette and a lockable door.

At least one state has written rules for referral agencies. Texas passed a law in 2025 that requires them to give families a written disclosure saying who pays the referral fee, that the family can stop using the agency at any time, and that the list may not include every community that fits. The Texas law also bars agencies from referring families to communities they own or have a financial interest in, and from holding a power of attorney for, or the property of, the person they are helping. That law does not apply in New Jersey. It is still a handy checklist for questions to ask here.

Some advisors list private credentials such as Certified Senior Advisor or Certified Dementia Practitioner. Ask which organization issues the credential and what it required.

Where can I find a placement advisor in New Jersey?

These local advisors say on their own websites that their help is free to families. Most are paid by the communities, so ask each one how it is paid before you start. We list them by the area they say they serve. A listing here is not an endorsement, and New Jersey does not license placement advisors, so check any community they suggest yourself.

North Jersey

  • Assisted Living Locators Essex County and Northwest New Jersey, 973-413-1158. Serves Essex, Sussex and Passaic counties, northern Warren and Morris, and parts of Union and Hudson.
  • Oasis Senior Advisors Bergen County, 862-477-6591. Serves Bergen County.
  • Senior Care Authority Northern and Central New Jersey, 551-350-7566. Serves much of North and Central Jersey, from Bergen to Ocean.

Central Jersey and the Shore

  • Oasis Senior Advisors Central Jersey, 732-524-8864. Serves the Piscataway area.
  • Assisted Living Locators Princeton, 609-937-7760. Serves Princeton and nearby towns.
  • Assisted Living Locators of Monmouth County, 732-749-2610. Serves Monmouth County.
  • CarePatrol of North Shore, 732-455-2424. Serves Monmouth, Ocean and parts of Middlesex.
  • Adult Care Advisors, 908-812-9158. Based in Aberdeen.

South Jersey

  • Next Haven Senior Living Advisors, 856-588-3074. Serves Burlington, Camden and Mercer counties. Led by a registered nurse.
  • CarePatrol of Philadelphia, Mercer & Burlington, 267-449-7785. Serves Mercer and Burlington counties.
  • CarePatrol of South Jersey, 856-985-0084. Based in Marlton.
  • Senior Care Authority Southern New Jersey, 856-535-9053. Serves South Jersey, based in Marlton.
  • Assisted Living Locators Greater Cherry Hill, 856-302-4440. Serves Cherry Hill and nearby towns.
  • Oasis Senior Advisors Cherry Hill, 856-576-8983. Serves the Cherry Hill area.

Our senior living advisors list has the same advisors with short descriptions, and we add new ones once we confirm them.

What other kinds of senior living help are there?

  • Geriatric care managers are usually nurses or social workers you pay by the hour. They take no fees from communities, so they work only for your family. See when to call a geriatric care manager.
  • Senior move managers handle the move itself: sorting, packing, selling or donating, and setting up the new apartment. See senior move managers in NJ.
  • Elder law attorneys help with contracts, Medicaid planning and paying for care. See how to find an elder law attorney.
  • Your county office on aging gives free, unbiased options counseling at 1-877-222-3737.

For a plain overview of every type of community, start with senior living options in NJ.

What should I ask a placement advisor before we start?

Ask how they are paid, which communities they work with and what happens if you find a place on your own. A good advisor answers all of it plainly and puts it in writing.

  • Who pays you, and how much does a community pay when my parent moves in?
  • How many communities in our area do you work with? Are there licensed places nearby you do not work with?
  • Will you send my parent's information to communities before I say yes to each one?
  • Do you visit the residences yourself? When did you last tour the ones on our list?
  • Do you check state licenses and complaint records before you recommend a place?
  • Do you work with residences that accept Medicaid, or only private pay?
  • Will you come on tours, or do we go alone?
  • Do you have any ownership or financial interest in a community you recommend?
  • Is there anything you want me to sign? Can I read it first?
  • If we stop working with you, will you tell the communities?

The Medicaid question matters for many New Jersey families. Medicaid's Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) program can pay for assisted living for people who qualify, but not every residence takes it. If savings may run low, ask each residence whether your parent can stay after switching to Medicaid. Our MLTSS guide explains the rules, and our guide to what senior care costs in New Jersey helps you set a budget.

What are the red flags with a placement agency?

Pressure, vague answers about money and anything you are asked to pay or sign without time to read it. Walk away from any of these.

  • Rushing you. "This room will be gone by Friday" may be true. It can also be a sales line. Ask the residence directly.
  • Won't explain the fee. If an advisor will not say who pays them, treat everything else with caution.
  • Asks the family for money after describing the service as free.
  • Asks for a power of attorney, bank access or control of your parent's property. A placement advisor has no reason to hold any of these.
  • Only one option. A single recommendation leaves you nothing to compare.
  • Talks you out of checking. Any honest advisor will be fine with you looking up a license or calling the ombudsman.

If you are asked to sign an agreement with the agency, read it before you sign, and ask an elder law attorney if anything is unclear. This is general information, not legal advice. Our guide to scams targeting New Jersey seniors covers broader warning signs.

How do I check an assisted living residence myself?

Confirm the license with the New Jersey Department of Health, visit more than once and read the admission agreement and fee sheet before you sign. These checks take a few hours and work for any residence, whoever suggested it.

  1. Look up the license. Use the Department of Health's long-term care facility search to confirm the residence is licensed and see which license type it holds.
  2. Ask about state inspections. Ask the residence to show you its most recent inspection results and what it did to fix any problems.
  3. Call the ombudsman. The New Jersey Long-Term Care Ombudsman is an independent advocate for older adults in long-term care, including assisted living. Call 1-877-582-6995 with questions or concerns.
  4. Visit twice. Go once on the scheduled tour and once at a mealtime or in the evening.
  5. Get the money in writing. Ask for the full fee sheet, how the price rises as care needs grow and what happens if savings run out.

The Department of Health takes complaints about assisted living facilities on its 24-hour hotline at 1-800-792-9770. If a nursing home is on your list, our guide to nursing home ratings in New Jersey shows how to read Medicare's star ratings and state inspection data. If your parent has dementia, read nursing home vs. memory care before you tour.

Who helpsWho pays
Placement agencyThe community, after a move
Care managerYour family, usually by the hour
County ADRCPublic office, free to call

When is a geriatric care manager or the county a better fit?

Choose a geriatric care manager when you want someone paid only by your family to assess your parent and weigh every option, including staying home. Call your county first when money is tight or you want to know about public programs.

A geriatric care manager, usually a nurse or social worker, visits your parent, writes a care plan and can help compare residences. You pay for their time, so ask whether they take referral fees from any place they recommend. The answer should be no. This route makes sense when siblings disagree, when memory or medical needs are complicated, or when you live far away and need someone to oversee care after the move.

Your county's Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC), reached at 1-877-222-3737, is a public office. The state describes it as a one-stop shop that can help you figure out which government programs your parent might qualify for and connect you with county and local services. If cost is the main worry, our guide to affordable senior apartments in New Jersey covers subsidized senior buildings and how to apply.

Many families use more than one kind of help. Say your dad is finishing rehab in Morristown and the discharge planner says he cannot go home alone. You might call the county about Medicaid, ask a placement advisor for three residences with openings near your sister in Parsippany, and pay a care manager for an hour to look over the admission agreements. Our guide to leaving the hospital walks through those first days.

For care managers, social service agencies and other help by county, browse our Find care help directory.

faq.q: How do I find assisted living for my mom in New Jersey without being pushed toward one place?
faq.a: Use more than one source. Ask a placement advisor which communities it works with, look up nearby licensed residences yourself in the NJ Department of Health's long-term care facility search, and call your county's Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737. Tour at least two or three places, once at a mealtime.

faq.q: Is A Place for Mom really free?
faq.a: For families, yes. A Place for Mom says it is paid by senior living communities when a family it refers moves in, and by home care agencies when it refers a family to them. It also says its contracts bar communities from charging referred families more than other families. Because communities pay the fee, its list includes communities in its network.

faq.q: Does New Jersey license senior placement agencies?
faq.a: The NJ Department of Health licenses assisted living residences, nursing homes and other care facilities. Placement agencies are not on its list of licensed facility types. Ask any agency directly whether it holds a license or certification and who oversees it.

faq.q: My dad is being discharged from rehab and can't go home alone. Should I call a placement service?
faq.a: A placement advisor can help you find residences with openings quickly. At the same time, ask the hospital or rehab discharge planner for a list of options, call your county ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 about Medicaid and other programs, and confirm any residence's license with the NJ Department of Health before your dad moves in.

faq.q: What's the difference between a placement advisor and a geriatric care manager?
faq.a: A placement advisor is usually paid by the community your parent moves into, and the service is free to your family. A geriatric care manager, usually a nurse or social worker, is paid by your family, typically by the hour. A care manager can assess your parent and weigh every option, including staying home.

faq.q: Can I stop working with a placement agency after we start?
faq.a: You can stop calling any agency you have not signed an agreement with. If you did sign something, read it first and ask a lawyer if anything is unclear. Ask the agency to tell the communities it contacted that you are no longer working with it. This is general information, not legal advice.

title: Senior move managers in NJ: downsizing and moving a parent
dek: What a senior move manager does, what it costs, how to check credentials and mover licenses in New Jersey, and the rare cases when Medicaid helps pay.
keyFacts: Only NASMM members may use the title Senior Move Manager, a service mark the association owns.
Movers working within NJ must be licensed by the Division of Consumer Affairs. Check at 973-504-6442.
A licensed NJ mover must give you the Order for Service at least 24 hours before the move.
The minimum NJ mover liability is $1.00 per pound, per article, unless you buy more coverage.
Medicaid MLTSS can pay up to $10,000 in one-time costs to move from a nursing home to a home of one's own.
body:
A senior move manager is a hired professional who runs a later-life move from start to finish. They help your mom or dad decide what to keep, draw a floor plan of the new place, arrange the sale or donation of the rest, book and supervise the movers, and unpack so the new home works on the first night.

In New Jersey, you can find them through the national trade group, the National Association of Senior and Specialty Move Managers (NASMM). Fees are hourly or by the project, so get a written estimate. If the company will also carry furniture within the state, it must hold a public mover license from the New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs. This page is general information, not legal advice.

What does a senior move manager actually do?

They plan the move, manage the people doing the work, and handle the parts families find hardest, such as sorting decades of belongings. Most offer a menu, so you can hire them for one piece or the whole job.

NASMM lists the services most of its members offer:

  • A move plan, or a plan to stay put and make the house safer ("aging in place")
  • Sorting, organizing and downsizing
  • Custom floor plans for the new home
  • Selling or giving away what is left, through auction, estate sale, buyout, consignment or donation
  • Interviewing, scheduling and overseeing movers
  • Arranging shipping and storage, and supervising packing
  • Unpacking and setting up the new home
  • Related help, such as cleaning, junk removal and getting the house ready to sell

Some move managers do the hands-on work themselves. Others act more like a general contractor and bring in movers, cleaners and estate sale firms. Ask which kind you are talking to.

Our downsizing guide covers sorting the house yourself and the New Jersey tax rules on a sale. This page is about hiring help and checking it.

A good move manager gives your parent time to say goodbye to things, and still gets the truck loaded on schedule.

How much does a senior move manager cost in NJ?

There is no standard price. NASMM says fees vary by region and by the services you choose. Some members bill by the hour and others quote one price for the whole job.

NASMM also says its members put the cost in a written estimate before you are asked to pay. Few New Jersey firms post prices online. One that does, MY Preferred Organizer in Elmwood Park, lists senior downsizing packages that start at $600 when the client sorts alongside the team and $780 when the team does the work, with the final price depending on the house and its contents.

When we read New Jersey move managers' own websites in November 2026, a common pattern showed up. Many start with a free consultation, then send a written estimate. At least one asks for a signed agreement and a deposit to hold your dates, then bills the actual hours worked, so the final invoice can differ from its non-binding estimate.

The move manager's fee is usually separate from what you pay the moving company, the estate sale company and any junk hauler. Ask for each piece in writing so you can add up the real total.

Ways to keep the bill down

Hire the move manager for the hardest parts only, such as the floor plan and moving day, and let family handle packing books and linens. NASMM says most of its members will do part of a job if you ask.

What do NASMM membership and certification mean?

"Senior Move Manager" is a service mark owned by NASMM, and only its members may use it. Members must take required courses in safety and ethics, and NASMM screens them for insurance.

The association's find a move manager directory lists members by state. When we checked in November 2026, it showed 21 members with New Jersey offices, plus a few New York firms that list New Jersey in their service area. You can also see New Jersey members on our Find care help pages.

Two extra credentials show up in listings:

CredentialWhat it means
MemberFour core courses: safety, ethics, the moving industry, contracts and liability
SMM-CAn individual who passed nine more courses and showed 40 paid move jobs
A+ AccreditedThe whole company passed a peer review of its practices

Both the SMM-C and A+ accreditation must be renewed every three years, and NASMM's directory shows the dates. A credential is a good sign. It does not replace references and an insurance certificate.

Does a move manager need a New Jersey mover's license?

Only the company that carries your parent's belongings for a move within New Jersey must be licensed as a public mover. That may be the move manager, or a moving company the move manager hires.

The New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs licenses intrastate movers. Some move managers hold their own license. Others say plainly that they are not movers and work with licensed moving companies. Licensed movers often show a number beginning with 39PM or 39PC on their websites.

To check a license and any complaint history, use the state's license verification search or call the Division at 973-504-6442.

Under state rules, a licensed mover has to do these things:

  1. Survey the goods. An on-site or virtual walk-through before the estimate.
  2. Give a written estimate. It lists the license number, rates, an inventory by room and the coverage you chose.
  3. Hand over the state brochure. It is called "Important Notice to Consumers Using Public Movers and Warehousemen," in print or as a link.
  4. Give the Order for Service 24 hours ahead. It is the contract, and it is not valid until you and the mover both sign.
  5. Give a Bill of Lading after the move. It records every service and fee charged.

Know the coverage rules before moving day. A New Jersey mover can limit its liability to as little as $1.00 per pound, per article. A six-pound lamp that breaks is worth $6 under that minimum. You can buy increased valuation or insurance, or check your homeowner's or renter's policy. If the family packs boxes itself, the state says the family is responsible for the condition of those goods on arrival.

A mover who skips the 24-hour Order for Service or the brochure loses that liability limit under state rules. Keep jewelry, cash and important papers with you, since movers are not responsible for items of extraordinary value. A mover may give a binding, fixed-price estimate but does not have to. No mover can demand a tip.

Moves to another state fall under the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration. Self-storage units and portable storage containers are not regulated by New Jersey, so read those contracts closely.

How do I vet a move manager for my mom or dad?

Treat it like hiring anyone who will spend days inside your parent's home. Check insurance, references and the contract before anyone opens a closet.

Questions to ask, many drawn from NASMM's own list:

  • How long have you done this work, and are you a NASMM member?
  • Are you insured for liability and workers' compensation? Can I see the certificate?
  • How do you charge, and will you put fees in writing before work starts?
  • Will I get a written contract? What is the deposit, and what is the cancellation policy?
  • Who will actually be in the house? Your employees or subcontractors? Have they had background checks?
  • Which moving company do you use, and what is its New Jersey license number?
  • Do you earn a commission or fee from the estate sale company, buyer or mover you recommend?
  • Can I call three recent clients, ideally families whose parent moved to a similar place?

Our guide to vetting someone who comes into the home walks through background checks and references in more detail.

Red flags

Pressure to sign the same day. A large cash deposit. No written estimate. A "mover" with no New Jersey license number. Anyone who wants your parent's checkbook, bank passwords or a signed blank check. Someone who offers to buy valuables cheaply before anything is appraised. Our scams guide lists other tricks aimed at older adults.

Stay in the loop even if you live far away. Ask for a short update after each work day and photos of the floor plan. Keep your parent's medications, glasses, hearing aids and phone charger in a bag that travels in your car or theirs.

What about estate sales, buyouts and cleanouts?

These are separate businesses that empty a house after the keepers have been chosen. Many move managers coordinate them for you, and a few run them in-house.

  • Estate sale companies price and sell the contents, usually on site, and keep a share of the sales.
  • Auction houses and consignment shops take selected items and pay you after they sell.
  • Buyouts mean one company pays a single price for the remaining contents. It is fast, but you trade speed for price.
  • Cleanouts haul away what no one wants, ideally donating what they can. You pay them.

Get every arrangement in writing. Ask the commission, who pays for cleanup, when you will be paid, and what happens to unsold items. Have anything that might be valuable, such as jewelry, art or a coin collection, looked at by an independent appraiser before a buyout. If a move manager earns a fee from a liquidator, you should know that before you choose one.

If the move follows a death, the executor usually decides what is sold. Read what to do when a parent dies before signing anything.

Can Medicaid or the county help pay for a move?

In one common case, yes. New Jersey's Medicaid long-term care program can pay one-time costs when someone leaves a nursing home for their own place in the community. Ordinary downsizing moves are not covered.

The program is called Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS). Its "Community Transition Services" can cover moving expenses, security deposits, basic furniture and household items, and utility set-up fees, up to $10,000 over a lifetime, according to the state's MLTSS services dictionary. Ask the care manager at your parent's Medicaid health plan. Our MLTSS guide explains how to qualify.

A related state program, I Choose Home NJ, helps people who are eligible for Medicaid and have lived in a nursing home for more than 60 days move back to the community with services. Call 1-855-466-3005.

For anything else, start with your county's Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737. Staff can point you to local help with chores, transportation on moving day or a senior housing waiting list. If your parent is choosing where to live, compare assisted living and home care and our senior housing guide. A placement service or a geriatric care manager can help with the choice itself.

If you have a complaint about any business involved in the move, the Division of Consumer Affairs' Consumer Service Center takes calls at 973-504-6200.

faq.q: How do I find a senior move manager for my mom in New Jersey?
faq.a: Search the NASMM directory by state at nasmm.org, or see the move managers on our Find care help pages. Call two or three, ask for an in-home consultation and a written estimate, and check references and insurance before you sign.

faq.q: What is the difference between a senior move manager and a moving company?
faq.a: A moving company packs and carries belongings. A move manager plans the whole move, helps sort and downsize, makes a floor plan, oversees the movers and sets up the new home. Some move managers are also licensed movers, and others hire one.

faq.q: How much does it cost to hire a senior move manager in NJ?
faq.a: Prices vary by region and by services. NASMM says some members bill hourly and others quote a project price, and members give a written estimate before payment. Movers, estate sale companies and junk haulers usually charge separately.

faq.q: How do I check if a New Jersey mover is licensed?
faq.a: Use the state license verification site at newjersey.mylicense.com or call the Division of Consumer Affairs at 973-504-6442. Movers that work within New Jersey must be licensed, and the search also shows complaint history.

faq.q: My dad is moving into assisted living and I live out of state. Can a move manager handle it without me there?
faq.a: Many do. Ask for a written plan, a daily update with photos, and a single contact person. Agree in writing on what will be sold, donated or sent to family, and keep important papers and valuables out of the shipment.

faq.q: Will Medicaid pay for my parent's move?
faq.a: Generally only when your parent is leaving a nursing home or similar setting for a home in the community. New Jersey's MLTSS program can cover one-time costs such as moving expenses and security deposits, up to $10,000 over a lifetime.

title: Assisted living in New Jersey: costs, rules and how to choose
dek: What New Jersey requires of assisted living, what it costs, when Medicaid helps, and how to check a residence before your parent moves in.
keyFacts: NJ median for assisted living: $8,710 a month for a private one-bedroom (CareScout 2025).
The NJ Department of Health licenses all assisted living under N.J.A.C. 8:36.
A registered nurse must be available at all times.
A discharge notice must name the Long-Term Care Ombudsman and usually comes 30 days ahead.
Complaints: NJ Department of Health hotline 1-800-792-9770, 24 hours.
body:
Assisted living in New Jersey is a state-licensed home where your mom or dad has their own room or apartment, eats meals with others, and gets help with bathing, dressing and medications from staff who are there around the clock. The NJ Department of Health licenses every residence under one set of rules, N.J.A.C. 8:36, and those rules spell out what residents are owed.

It is expensive. CareScout's Cost of Care Survey 2025 puts the New Jersey median at $8,710 a month for a private one-bedroom unit, or $104,520 a year. Medicare does not pay for it. NJ FamilyCare, the state's Medicaid program, can pay for the care part at residences that accept it, and many residences must keep some room for Medicaid residents. This guide covers the license types, the costs, the money rules, when a residence can ask your parent to leave, and how to check a place before you sign.

What counts as assisted living in New Jersey?

New Jersey licenses three kinds of assisted living. All three follow the same resident rights and care rules, but the housing is different.

License typeWhat it looks like
Assisted living residenceApartment-style units with at least one room, a private bathroom, a kitchenette and a lockable door. Meals in a shared dining room.
Comprehensive personal care homeRoom and board. No more than two residents per unit, with a lockable door. Bathrooms may be shared.
Assisted living programMeals and assisted living services brought to tenants of publicly subsidized senior housing that cannot be licensed as a residence.

The state defines assisted living as personal and health services available 24 hours a day, including for people who need a nursing home level of care. That last part surprises families. A residence is expected to keep many residents as their needs grow, within limits the admission agreement must spell out.

If you are still weighing whether your parent can stay home with aides instead, start with our comparison of assisted living and home care. If you want help finding a residence, our guide to senior living placement services explains how referral services are paid and what to watch for.

What must an assisted living residence provide?

Every residence must be able to provide personal care, nursing, pharmacy, dining, activities, recreation and social work services. It must have a registered nurse available at all times.

Here is what the state rules require in practice.

  • A nurse assessment at move-in. A registered nurse assesses your parent on admission. If they need help, a written service plan follows within 14 days.
  • Help with medications. Trained staff supervise residents who take their own pills and give medications to those who need it.
  • Trained aides. Personal care assistants must be certified, pass a criminal background check, and complete 20 hours of continuing education every two years, including dementia care.
  • Daily activities. A planned program of activities every day, plus the right to form a resident council.
  • Enough room. A single unit must have at least 150 square feet of usable floor space, not counting the bathroom, closets or kitchenette. No unit may house more than two people.
  • A written statement of rights. The state lists 42 resident rights, including privacy, choosing their own doctor and pharmacy, managing their own money, refusing treatment, hiring a private companion at their own cost, and complaining without fear of punishment.

The rules set minimums. They do not set a fixed staff-to-resident ratio. Each residence must staff according to how much help its residents need, which is why your questions on a tour matter so much.

The rules set a floor. How many aides are on the floor at 2 a.m. is something you have to ask.

How much does assisted living cost in New Jersey?

The New Jersey median is $8,710 a month for a private one-bedroom unit, according to CareScout's Cost of Care Survey 2025. The national median is $6,200.

CareScout 2025 medianMonthlyYearly
New Jersey$8,710$104,520
United States$6,200$74,400

CareScout surveyed providers from July to November 2025. Half of residences charge more than the median and half charge less, so treat it as a planning number. Our guide to what senior care costs in New Jersey compares it with home care and nursing homes.

What the state says about fees

  • The residence must give your parent, in writing, every fee for services and routine supplies, at admission and whenever charges change.
  • It cannot add a charge for a higher level of care unless a registered nurse has reassessed your parent and documented the need.
  • Your parent has the right to a written explanation of any increase that is not tied to more care.
  • A security deposit must be held in trust in an interest-bearing account. Your parent gets the interest, minus a servicing fee of no more than 1 percent a year, plus quarterly statements. The deposit comes back at discharge or death, less anything owed.

Ask for the full rate sheet, including the care levels, and ask how often prices have gone up in the last few years.

Does Medicaid pay for assisted living in NJ?

Yes, for the care, through NJ FamilyCare's Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) program. Your parent pays the room and board part from their own income.

To qualify, your parent must meet NJ FamilyCare's financial rules and need a nursing home level of care. The details, including the five-year look-back on gifts, are in our MLTSS guide. Once enrolled in assisted living services, your parent does not also get MLTSS home services such as home-delivered meals or adult day care, because the residence provides that help.

The Medicaid bed rule

Many residences must make room for Medicaid. Under N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1, a residence or personal care home licensed on or after September 1, 2001, must reach at least 10 percent Medicaid occupancy within three years of licensure and keep it there. That includes residents who moved in paying privately and later became eligible. Older residences that added beds after that date must fill at least 10 percent of the new beds with Medicaid residents.

There are exceptions. The state can waive or reduce the requirement, and residences run by continuing care retirement communities are exempt. So the rule does not guarantee your parent a Medicaid bed.

Before move-in, ask each residence two direct questions and get the answers in writing. Do you accept MLTSS? If my mother pays privately and later qualifies for Medicaid, can she stay in her apartment?

Medicare does not pay for assisted living. Long-term care insurance and some veterans benefits may help. See our long-term care insurance guide.

When can an assisted living residence ask my parent to leave?

Only for reasons in its written policies, which your parent must be told about in advance. In most cases the residence must give at least 30 days' written notice.

The notice must state the reason and your parent's right to appeal. It must include the name, address and phone number of the Long-Term Care Ombudsman. With your parent's consent, the family gets a copy 30 days ahead too. In an emergency that threatens your parent's or others' safety, the residence can transfer them sooner and must notify the Department of Health.

The state lists situations where a residence may, but does not have to, move a resident to a higher level of care. They include needing 24-hour nursing supervision, being bedridden for more than 14 days in a row, being totally dependent in four or more daily activities, a stage three or four pressure sore, needing more than two staff to transfer, being a danger to self or others, or cognitive decline so severe that your parent cannot make simple choices or follow cues.

One section of the rules, N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.14, says the 30-day notice does not apply when the move is for one of these higher-care reasons. Ask each residence how much notice it gives in that case, and get the answer in writing.

The admission agreement must say clearly which of these conditions the residence will handle, to what extent, and at what extra cost. Read that section closely. It tells you whether your parent can stay as they decline, or will face another move.

If your parent insists on doing something staff see as risky, the residence may propose a written "managed risk agreement" that records the concern, your parent's wishes and the compromise. Your parent or their guardian must be part of that negotiation.

This is general information, not legal advice. For a discharge dispute, call the Ombudsman or an elder law attorney.

How do I check an assisted living residence before signing?

Confirm the license, ask for the latest state inspection, call the Ombudsman, and visit more than once.

  1. Confirm the license. Search the residence on the NJ Department of Health long-term care facility search. Check the license type and the number of beds.
  2. Ask for the latest inspection report. The Department of Health inspects licensed residences. Ask to see the most recent survey and the plan of correction. A residence that will not show you is telling you something.
  3. Call the Ombudsman. The Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-877-582-6995 advocates for assisted living residents and can tell you how to raise concerns.
  4. Visit twice. Go once on a scheduled tour and once at a mealtime or in the evening. Watch how staff talk to residents.
  5. Take the agreement home. Read the admission agreement, fee schedule and retention policy before anyone signs. The residence must give your parent this agreement before or at admission.

Questions to ask on a tour

  • How many aides and nurses are on duty on each shift, including overnight and weekends?
  • Who gives medications, and how are errors caught?
  • What are your care levels, what does each cost, and who decides when my dad moves up a level?
  • Which of the state's higher-care conditions will you keep a resident through?
  • Can hospice come here? (Medicare says hospice can usually be provided in an assisted living facility, though room and board is not covered.)
  • How do you handle a fall at night? Who calls the family?
  • Do you have a dementia program? If so, see our memory care guide for what New Jersey requires of it.
  • What did your last state inspection find, and what did you change?

If your parent is coming out of rehab, our guide to nursing home ratings explains the federal star system, which covers nursing homes but not assisted living.

Who do I call if something goes wrong?

Call the NJ Department of Health's 24-hour complaint hotline, or the Long-Term Care Ombudsman. You can complain to both, and your parent cannot be punished for it.

Key numbers for assisted living in New Jersey

NJ Department of Health complaint hotline, 24 hours, 7 days: 1-800-792-9770. You can also file online or by mail. Long-Term Care Ombudsman: 1-877-582-6995. Aging and Disability Resource Connection, for help with MLTSS and other programs: 1-877-222-3737. In an emergency, call 911.

The Department of Health hotline takes complaints about suspected abuse, neglect, exploitation and serious injuries in licensed assisted living residences and personal care homes. You may file anonymously by phone.

In Essex County, see our list of licensed assisted living residences in Essex. In Bergen, see memory care in Bergen County.

faq.q: How do I find out if an assisted living residence near my mom is licensed?
faq.a: Search its name on the NJ Department of Health long-term care facility search at healthapps.nj.gov. It shows whether it is licensed as an assisted living residence, a comprehensive personal care home or an assisted living program. Then ask the residence for its latest state inspection report.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for assisted living in New Jersey?
faq.a: No. Medicare does not pay for assisted living. NJ FamilyCare's MLTSS program can pay for the care services for people who qualify, while the resident pays room and board. Long-term care insurance may also help.

faq.q: Can my dad stay in assisted living if he runs out of money?
faq.a: Only if the residence accepts NJ FamilyCare (MLTSS) and agrees to keep residents who switch from private pay. Many residences licensed since September 2001 must keep at least 10 percent of their beds filled by Medicaid residents, but there are waivers and exemptions. Ask before move-in and get the answer in writing.

faq.q: How much notice does assisted living have to give before discharging a resident in NJ?
faq.a: In most cases at least 30 days' written notice, stating the reason, the right to appeal and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman's contact details. A residence can act sooner in an emergency that threatens safety, and it must then notify the Department of Health. The rules also allow shorter notice when the move is for one of the higher-care needs the state lists, so ask about this before move-in.

faq.q: Can an assisted living residence raise my mom's fee because she needs more help?
faq.a: Only after a registered nurse reassesses her and documents the need. The residence must give fees in writing at admission and whenever they change, and your mom can ask for a written explanation of any increase not tied to more care.

faq.q: What is the difference between assisted living and a comprehensive personal care home?
faq.a: Both are licensed by the NJ Department of Health and follow the same care and rights rules. An assisted living residence has apartment-style units with a private bathroom and kitchenette. A comprehensive personal care home offers room and board, with no more than two residents per unit.

NJ Division of Aging Services: County Offices on Aging and ADRC (1-877-222-3737)
NJ DMAHS: Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS)
