title: Memory care in New Jersey: costs, safety and choosing a place
dek: What New Jersey requires of dementia programs, what memory care costs, how Medicaid fits in, and the questions that help you choose well for your parent.
keyFacts: NJ has no separate memory care license. Dementia programs in assisted living follow N.J.A.C. 8:36-19.
Programs must train all direct care staff in dementia care and keep shift staffing records you can request.
You are entitled to a written list of dementia activities, how often they run, and safety policies.
NJ assisted living median: $8,710 a month (CareScout 2025). Memory care is usually more.
Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline: 1-800-272-3900.
body:
Memory care in New Jersey usually means a secure dementia unit or program inside a licensed assisted living residence. There is no separate memory care license. A residence that advertises an Alzheimer's or dementia program must follow extra state rules in N.J.A.C. 8:36-19, including written program policies, dementia training for every direct care worker, and staffing records you can ask to see.

Memory care costs at least as much as regular assisted living, whose New Jersey median is $8,710 a month (CareScout 2025), and often more. Medicare does not pay for it. NJ FamilyCare's MLTSS program can pay for the care at residences that accept it. This guide explains what to look for, what to ask, and how to make the move easier on your mom or dad.

If you are still deciding between memory care and a nursing home, read our comparison of nursing homes and memory care first. This page goes deeper on choosing and living with memory care.

What does New Jersey require of a memory care program?

Any assisted living facility that advertises an Alzheimer's or dementia program must meet four extra rules on top of the regular assisted living standards.

RuleWhat it means for you
Written policiesProgram policies must be available to staff and to the public. Ask for a copy.
Clear criteriaAdmission and discharge criteria, based on a registered nurse's assessment of thinking and function.
Dementia trainingTraining in dementia care for all licensed and unlicensed staff who give direct care.
Shift recordsDaily records of direct care staff on each shift, shared with the public on request.

The residence must also give anyone seeking a placement a written list of its dementia activities, how often they happen, and its safety policies and any security monitoring for residents with dementia. That list is the single most useful document you can collect. Compare it across places.

All assisted living staff must get at least yearly training on dementia care. Certified personal care assistants must complete 20 hours of continuing education every two years that covers cognitive impairment and dementia. A registered nurse must be available at all times.

Ask for the activity list and the shift staffing records. The state says you can have both.

What does memory care cost in New Jersey?

There is no official New Jersey median for memory care. CareScout's survey reports assisted living, at $8,710 a month for a private one-bedroom in 2025, but does not break out memory care. Use that figure as a floor.

Residences price memory care in different ways. Some charge one all-inclusive monthly rate. Others charge a base rate plus a care level that rises as needs grow. Ask for the memory care rate in writing, what it includes, and how many times it has gone up in recent years.

New Jersey's fee rules apply here too. A residence cannot raise charges for more care unless a registered nurse has reassessed your parent and documented the need. Fees must be given in writing at admission and whenever they change. Our guide to assisted living in New Jersey covers deposits, fee increases and discharge notice in detail.

Will Medicaid pay for memory care in NJ?

It can pay for the care, but only at a residence that accepts NJ FamilyCare's MLTSS program. Your parent pays room and board from their own income.

MLTSS covers assisted living services for people who meet the financial rules and need a nursing home level of care. The state's clinical test counts people whose memory problems mean they need supervision and cueing with three or more daily activities, such as bathing, dressing or eating. See our MLTSS guide for the 2026 income and asset limits and the five-year look-back.

Many assisted living residences licensed since September 1, 2001, must keep at least 10 percent of their beds filled by Medicaid residents. That rule applies to the residence as a whole, not to its memory care unit, and it can be waived. Ask directly whether the memory care unit takes MLTSS, and whether your parent can stay there if they start out paying privately and later qualify.

Medicare does not pay for memory care. It does pay for hospice, which Medicare says can usually be provided in an assisted living facility, though room and board is not covered.

How do we know it is time for memory care?

Usually when safety at home depends on someone watching your parent all the time, and that someone is wearing out.

Families often describe a few turning points:

  • Your parent has gone out alone and gotten lost, or tries to leave at night.
  • The stove, car keys or medications have become dangerous.
  • Evenings bring confusion and agitation that no one at home can calm. Our guide to sundowning has ideas that help.
  • Your parent is losing weight, missing doses or not bathing, even with aides.
  • The family caregiver is not sleeping, is getting sick, or is close to quitting work.

If you are not sure what stage your parent is in, ask the doctor. If there has been no diagnosis yet, start with our guide to free memory screening. Our guide on where families can turn after a diagnosis lists adult day and respite programs that can buy time at home.

What should I ask on a memory care tour?

Ask about staffing, wandering, medications, activities and what happens as the disease progresses. Get the important answers in writing.

Staffing and training

  • How many direct care staff are on the unit on each shift, including nights and weekends? Can I see the shift records?
  • What dementia training do aides get, and how often?
  • Are the same aides assigned to the same residents most days?

Wandering and safety

  • How are exits secured, and what happens when a resident tries to leave?
  • How do you handle agitation without medication or restraints? (New Jersey rules bar restraints except briefly on a clinician's order to prevent injury, and never confining a resident in a locked room for punishment or staff convenience.)
  • How do you prevent and report falls?

Medications

  • Who gives medications, and how do you check that doses are taken?
  • How often does a doctor or nurse practitioner review antipsychotic or sleep medications?
  • Can we use our own pharmacy? (Residents have that right if the pharmacy works with the residence's medication system.)

Daily life

  • May I have your written list of dementia activities and how often they run?
  • What does a typical afternoon look like? Is there music, time outdoors, small-group activity?
  • Can family visit any time and join meals?

Our guide to things to do with a parent who has dementia explains why music and short, varied activities often work best.

As needs grow

  • What are your written discharge criteria for the dementia program?
  • If my mom stops walking or needs two people to move her, can she stay?
  • Can hospice care for her here, so she does not have to move at the end of life?

New Jersey lets a residence move a resident whose cognitive decline is so severe they cannot make simple choices or respond to cues, or who is a danger to self or others. A resident with severe combative or aggressive behavior must move to a facility licensed for that specialized care. The admission agreement must say which conditions the residence will keep a resident through. Read it closely, because a second move is hard on someone with dementia.

How can we make the move to memory care easier?

Plan it, keep the room familiar, and share who your parent is with staff before day one.

  1. Talk with staff first. Ask how they usually handle the first day, and whether they suggest a time of day for the move.
  2. Bring the familiar. A favorite chair, a quilt, framed photos, a radio with the music they love. Label drawers if it helps.
  3. Write a one-page life story. Their job, hometown, children's names, favorite foods, what calms them and what upsets them. Give it to every aide.
  4. Set up the paperwork. Bring copies of the health care proxy, power of attorney and, if your parent has one, a POLST form.
  5. Plan visits. Some families visit often from the start. Others are asked to give a few days. Follow the team's advice, and keep in touch by phone.
  6. Book a care meeting. After the first few weeks, sit down with the nurse to review the service plan and how your parent is settling in.

Expect some hard days. If your parent keeps asking to go home, tell the staff. They can share what has helped other residents settle in.

When the end of life comes closer, our guide to hospice care in New Jersey explains how hospice works alongside the residence.

Who can help us decide?

Two dementia helplines and the state's long-term care advocates can talk you through it, free.

Dementia and memory care help in New Jersey

Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline: 1-800-272-3900. Alzheimer's New Jersey Helpline, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.: 1-888-280-6055. Long-Term Care Ombudsman: 1-877-582-6995. NJ Department of Health complaint hotline, 24 hours: 1-800-792-9770.

Before you sign, confirm the residence's license on the NJ Department of Health long-term care facility search and ask for its most recent state inspection report. This is general information, not legal advice. An elder law attorney can review an admission agreement and explain Medicaid planning.

Looking in Bergen County? See memory care in Bergen County.

If you want help narrowing the list, a senior living placement advisor can suggest memory care communities and set up tours, usually at no cost to your family. Ask how they are paid first.

faq.q: How do I find memory care for my mom in New Jersey?
faq.a: Start with licensed assisted living residences that advertise an Alzheimer's or dementia program. Confirm each license on the NJ Department of Health long-term care facility search, ask for the written activity list and safety policies the state requires, and visit at least twice. The Alzheimer's helplines can help you think it through.

faq.q: Is memory care licensed separately in New Jersey?
faq.a: No. Memory care is usually a program or unit inside a licensed assisted living residence or personal care home. If it advertises an Alzheimer's or dementia program, it must follow the extra rules in N.J.A.C. 8:36-19. Nursing homes may also have dementia units under their own license.

faq.q: How much does memory care cost in NJ?
faq.a: There is no official New Jersey median for memory care. Regular assisted living has a median of $8,710 a month for a private one-bedroom (CareScout 2025), and memory care usually costs that much or more. Ask each residence for its memory care rate in writing.

faq.q: Does Medicaid pay for memory care in New Jersey?
faq.a: NJ FamilyCare's MLTSS program can pay for the care in assisted living, including dementia units, at residences that accept it. Your parent must meet the financial rules and need a nursing home level of care, and pays room and board from their income. Medicare does not pay for memory care.

faq.q: Can memory care ask my dad to leave if his dementia gets worse?
faq.a: It can, for reasons listed in its written policies and admission agreement. New Jersey allows a move when, for example, a resident cannot make simple choices or respond to cues, or is a danger to self or others. A move for these reasons can come with less than the usual 30 days' notice. Ask before move-in which conditions the residence will handle.

faq.q: What staffing information can I ask a memory care unit for?
faq.a: A residence with a dementia program must keep daily records of how many licensed and unlicensed staff give direct care on each shift and share that information with the public on request. Ask for nights and weekends, not just weekday daytime.

title: Long-distance caregiving for a parent in New Jersey
dek: Your mom or dad lives in New Jersey and you don't, or you live at the other end of the state. How to build a local team, get the paperwork in place and take time off work when you need to.
seoDesc: Caring for a parent in New Jersey from far away: county help, privacy forms, telehealth, paying bills, NJ family leave rules and an emergency plan.
keyFacts: Start with New Jersey's ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 to reach your parent's county office on aging
Medicare's 1-800-MEDICARE line needs written permission (Form CMS-10106) to talk to you
Medicare covers telehealth at home through December 31, 2027
NJ Family Leave Insurance pays 85% of weekly wages, up to $1,119 a week in 2026
Since July 17, 2026, NJ job protected family leave covers employers with 15 or more workers
body:
You can be a real help to a parent in New Jersey from hundreds of miles away. The work changes, though. Instead of doing every task yourself, you become the organizer. You build a local team, get the legal and medical permissions in place, keep the money running and plan for the call that comes at 2 a.m.

As NIH's MedlinePlus Magazine notes, you can't do it all alone, especially from far away. This guide covers where to start in New Jersey, which forms let doctors and Medicare talk to you, how New Jersey's leave laws can protect your job, and how to plan for an emergency. Parts of it touch legal and money matters, so treat it as general information, not legal advice.

Where do I start if I don't live near my parent?

Call New Jersey's Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737. It connects you with the Area Agency on Aging in your parent's county, which can screen for services and explain what is available locally.

Every county has an office on aging, and they know the local programs best: home delivered meals, adult day care, transportation, respite and help applying for benefits. Ask the office what it offers, what the wait lists look like and whether someone can visit your parent at home. Our county pages list each office, and you can call NJ 211 (dial 2-1-1) for other local services.

Before you call, find out what your parent actually needs. If you can't see it for yourself, a short visit from someone you trust or a professional assessment helps. Our guide to whether a parent is safe living alone lists the warning signs to look for and the questions to ask.

Who should be on my parent's local team?

Think of three circles: people who can check in, people who can be paid to help, and one person who can coordinate. Write down a phone number for each.

  • Neighbors and friends. One person nearby with a key and your phone number is worth more than any app. Ask who would notice if the newspaper piled up.
  • Faith community and senior center. Regulars notice when someone stops coming. Ask the county office about telephone reassurance and friendly visiting programs.
  • The pharmacist and the doctor's office. Introduce yourself by phone. Ask the office to note that you are a family contact once your parent gives permission.
  • Paid help. A home care agency can send aides for bathing, meals and errands. Our guides to choosing a home care agency and vetting in-home help explain what to check.
  • A coordinator. A geriatric care manager can be your eyes and ears, go to appointments and step in during a crisis.

If you have siblings, divide the work by strength, not by distance. The sibling who lives nearby often ends up with everything. The one far away can take the bills, the insurance calls and the research. Our find care help page lists local resources.

From far away, your job is less doing and more organizing.

How do I get doctors and Medicare to talk to me?

Ask your parent for written permission now, while things are calm. Doctors may share some information with involved family, but Medicare's phone line will not talk to you without a signed form.

Under the federal privacy rule known as HIPAA, a provider can share information with family who are involved in a patient's care when the patient agrees or does not object. A provider is not required to, though, unless you are the patient's personal representative. In practice, a signed authorization on file at each doctor's office saves many frustrating calls.

WhoWhat to set up
Each doctorSigned release naming you
1-800-MEDICAREForm CMS-10106
Patient portalProxy access, if offered
HospitalAdvance directive on file
Social SecurityAdvance designation of payee

Form CMS-10106 lets 1-800-MEDICARE share your parent's information with up to two named people, or more if listed on the back. Your parent can choose any information or limited items such as claims or plan enrollment, and can cancel it at any time. It can be submitted through your parent's Medicare.gov account or mailed to the address on the form.

Join visits by video

Through December 31, 2027, Medicare covers telehealth services your parent can get from anywhere in the country, including home. With your parent's permission you can join a video visit from your own kitchen table. After the Part B deductible, your parent pays 20% of the Medicare approved amount, the same as for most in-person visits. If your parent needs a hand with the tablet, our tech help guide lists free classes.

How can I handle bills and paperwork from far away?

Start with a durable power of attorney and online access your parent agrees to. Then automate what you can and watch the rest.

A durable power of attorney lets you act on your parent's accounts if they can't. Many families also set up automatic bill payments, direct deposit and alerts for large withdrawals. Our guide to managing a parent's money walks through bill paying, records and warning signs of exploitation.

Social Security has its own system. Your parent can name up to three people in advance who could serve as their representative payee if they ever can't manage benefits. This is called advance designation. It is not an appointment and not a power of attorney, and SSA still checks the person's suitability when the time comes. Your parent can set it up through a my Social Security account or by calling 1-800-772-1213.

Keep copies of the key papers where you can reach them. Our important papers checklist lists what to gather.

Can I take time off work to help my parent?

If you work in New Jersey, likely yes. New Jersey pays partial wages through Family Leave Insurance, and since July 17, 2026 far more workers have job protection while they use it.

Three laws can apply. They overlap, and many workers qualify for more than one.

LawWhat you get
NJ Family Leave Insurance85% of weekly wage, max $1,119 a week in 2026
NJ Family Leave Act12 weeks job protected in 24 months
Federal FMLA12 weeks unpaid, job protected in 12 months

New Jersey Family Leave Insurance (FLI)

FLI pays up to 12 consecutive weeks, or up to 56 individual days, in a 12 month period. Intermittent days suit long-distance caregivers well, since you can claim the days you travel for an appointment or a move. Caregiving includes physical care, emotional support, transportation, arranging a change in care and help with bathing or dressing. A health care provider must certify that your parent has a serious health condition and needs your care. You apply online, and your parent's provider completes their section online too. For claims starting in 2026 you need to have worked 20 weeks earning at least $310 a week, or earned $15,500 in the base year.

FLI covers more than parents. Parents-in-law, grandparents, siblings and chosen family also count.

Job protection got broader in 2026

Starting July 17, 2026, the New Jersey Family Leave Act applies to employers with 15 or more employees worldwide, down from 30. Workers need 3 months with the employer and 250 hours in the past year, down from 12 months and 1,000 hours. Workers who receive FLI benefits and are not covered by that law now also have job protection under the FLI law itself, with no minimum employer size. The state notes that formal rules may still change some procedures.

The federal Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) covers care for a parent with a serious health condition. It applies at employers with 50 or more employees within 75 miles, after 12 months and 1,250 hours of work. It does not list parents-in-law. If you work in another state, check that state's leave program, since New Jersey's covers people who work here.

Key numbers

ADRC, for your parent's county office on aging: 1-877-222-3737. 1-800-MEDICARE: 1-800-633-4227. Social Security: 1-800-772-1213. NJ SHIP Medicare counseling: 1-800-792-8820. Register Ready help: dial 2-1-1.

How do I make visits count?

Plan visits around what you can only do in person: seeing the house, meeting the team and going to appointments. Then save time for being a son or daughter.

The NIH suggests asking your parent ahead of time what they want to do during the visit, scheduling doctor appointments while you are in town (with permission) and meeting other caregivers who live nearby. On each visit, look at the refrigerator, the mail, the medicine bottles and the car. Check smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. Ask the neighbor with the key how things seem. And leave room for a meal out or a drive, so the visit is not all chores.

Visits can be hard on the person who lives nearby. If a sibling is the main caregiver, time your visit so they get a real break. Our guide to caregiver burnout covers the signs.

What is our plan for an emergency?

Decide now who goes first, who has a key and where the papers are. When the call comes, you will not have time to work it out.

  1. Make an emergency sheet. List medicines, doctors, allergies and contacts. Put it on the refrigerator. Our free emergency info sheet has a printable form.
  2. Name a first responder. Pick a neighbor or friend who can get there in minutes and agree to call them first.
  3. Share keys. Make sure at least two nearby people can get inside.
  4. Sign up for Register Ready. New Jersey's confidential registry helps emergency planners serve people with disabilities or access and functional needs in a disaster. Family members can register. Dial 2-1-1 for help.
  5. Keep a travel fund and bag. Know your fastest route home and have a bag ready.
  6. Plan for the hospital discharge. The hard part often comes after the ER. Our hospital discharge guide explains what to ask before your parent leaves.

More guides that may help: a printable caregiver log and what to look for on a visit.

faq.q: How do I take care of my mom in New Jersey when I live out of state?
faq.a: Start by calling New Jersey's ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 to reach her county office on aging. Then build a local team: a neighbor with a key, paid help if needed and possibly a geriatric care manager. Get a signed privacy release at each doctor, Form CMS-10106 for Medicare, and a durable power of attorney.

faq.q: How do I get Medicare to talk to me about my dad's coverage?
faq.a: Your dad needs to give written permission using Form CMS-10106, the Authorization to Disclose Personal Health Information. He can submit it through his Medicare.gov account or by mail. He can limit what is shared and cancel it at any time.

faq.q: Can I get paid leave in New Jersey to care for a parent?
faq.a: If you work in New Jersey, Family Leave Insurance can pay 85% of your average weekly wage, up to $1,119 a week in 2026, for up to 12 weeks or 56 separate days in a year. A health care provider must certify your parent's condition. Parents-in-law and grandparents are also covered.

faq.q: Is my job protected while I take family leave in New Jersey?
faq.a: Since July 17, 2026, the NJ Family Leave Act covers employers with 15 or more employees and workers with 3 months and 250 hours on the job. If that law does not cover you, receiving Family Leave Insurance benefits now carries its own job protection, with no minimum employer size.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for video visits at home?
faq.a: Yes. Through December 31, 2027, Medicare covers telehealth services from anywhere in the U.S., including home. After the Part B deductible your parent pays 20% of the Medicare approved amount. You can join the visit with your parent's permission.

title: Aging alone in New Jersey: planning with no family nearby
dek: No spouse, no children close by, or family you can't count on. How to choose the people who will speak for you, protect your money, and keep you safe and connected in New Jersey.
seoDesc: Aging alone in New Jersey? How to name a health care agent and money manager, avoid guardianship, plan for emergencies and stay connected.
keyFacts: A NJ advance directive needs two adult witnesses or a notary, attorney or other official
Your chosen health care representative cannot witness your advance directive
Social Security lets you name up to three possible payees in advance
NJ's Office of the Public Guardian serves adults 60+ found incapacitated by a court: 609-588-6500
Statewide ADRC for county help: 1-877-222-3737
body:
If you are getting older without a spouse, children or close family nearby, you can still plan well. The key is to choose your helpers yourself, in writing, while you can. People sometimes call this aging solo, or being an elder orphan. In New Jersey that means four things: an advance directive naming who makes medical decisions, a durable power of attorney for money, a plan for emergencies, and people who check on you.

Without those papers, a court may have to appoint a guardian if you can no longer decide for yourself. That takes court time and fees, and the judge decides who serves. This guide covers each step, who you can ask when family is not an option, and the paid professionals who fill the gaps. It is general information, not legal advice. An elder law attorney can tailor it to you.

Why does planning matter more when you live alone?

Because no one is assumed to step in. When a married person is hurt, a spouse is usually there to talk with doctors. When you live alone, the hospital may not know who to call.

Planning also protects your choices. You decide who speaks for you, what treatment you want and where you hope to live. The best time to do it is before a health scare, when nobody can question whether you understood what you signed.

Make a short list of people you trust. It can include a niece or nephew, a younger friend, a neighbor, someone from your faith community or a former colleague. They do not need to live nearby for every role. A health care agent can talk with doctors by phone. A money agent can pay bills online. The person with your spare key does need to be close.

Choose your helpers yourself, in writing, while you can. Otherwise a judge may choose for you.

Who will make medical decisions if I can't?

The person you name in a proxy directive, also called a health care representative. You can pair it with written instructions about the care you want.

New Jersey recognizes two kinds of advance directive. A proxy directive names your health care representative. An instruction directive, often called a living will, describes treatments you would or would not want, such as a ventilator or a feeding tube. Many people complete both in one document.

How to sign it so it counts

Under New Jersey law, you sign and date the directive in front of two adult witnesses who attest that you are of sound mind and free of pressure. Instead of witnesses, you can sign it before a notary public, an attorney or another person authorized to give oaths. The person you name as your representative cannot be a witness.

  • Name at least one alternate. If your first choice is traveling, ill or has died, the alternate can act.
  • Talk it through. Your representative needs to know your values, not just the form. Say out loud what a good day looks like to you.
  • Hand out copies. Give one to your representative, your doctor and your hospital. Keep one where emergency crews can find it.
  • Consider a POLST. If you are seriously ill, a Practitioner Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment form turns your wishes into medical orders. See our POLST guide.

Also sign a privacy release at each doctor's office naming your representative, and Medicare's Form CMS-10106 if you want 1-800-MEDICARE to talk with them. Our estate planning guide covers how these papers fit with your will.

Who can handle my money if I can't?

An agent you name in a durable power of attorney. If no friend or relative is a good fit, you can name a professional, such as a trust company or an attorney, and some daily money managers also take on this role.

A durable power of attorney lets someone pay your bills, deal with your bank and handle your property if you can't. Choose someone honest and organized, and name a backup. You can ask your agent to send a yearly accounting to a second person, such as your accountant or a trusted friend. That second set of eyes is valuable when there is no family watching.

Paid help with everyday money

A daily money manager handles routine tasks: paying bills, balancing accounts, organizing tax papers and checking medical bills. According to the American Association of Daily Money Managers, most charge by the hour, and some also serve as power of attorney agents, trustees or representative payees. The association offers a Certified Daily Money Manager credential.

Check anyone you hire. Ask for references, proof of bonding or insurance, and how they keep your money separate from theirs. Never give anyone signing power over your accounts without a written agreement. Our guide to managing an older adult's money lists warning signs of financial abuse.

Social Security has its own system

A power of attorney does not let someone manage your Social Security checks. Social Security uses representative payees instead. You can name up to three people in advance through advance designation. It is not an appointment, and Social Security still checks the person's suitability if the need ever comes. Set it up in your my Social Security account or by calling 1-800-772-1213.

What you needDocument or step
Medical decisionsProxy directive
Treatment wishesInstruction directive, POLST if ill
Bills and propertyDurable power of attorney
Social Security checksAdvance designation of payee
After deathWill and funeral wishes

What happens if I have no one and can no longer decide?

A court may appoint a guardian. If no friend or relative can serve, New Jersey's Office of the Public Guardian for Elderly Adults may be appointed for people 60 and older.

The Office of the Public Guardian sits within the state Division of Aging Services. It acts as decision maker for residents 60 and older whom the Superior Court has found incapacitated. It does not file guardianship cases itself. It accepts court appointments on a case by case basis. You can reach it at 609-588-6500, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Guardianship is a last resort. A guardian may make choices you would not have made, because you never put your wishes on paper. Our guardianship guide explains the court process and the less restrictive options. The surest way to avoid it is to sign an advance directive and power of attorney now.

Who can coordinate my care if family isn't nearby?

Start free with your county office on aging, through the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737. If you can pay privately, a geriatric care manager can act much like a nearby relative would.

The county office can screen you for programs such as home delivered meals, transportation, homemaker help and adult day care. It can also explain benefits that pay for care at home if your income is limited.

A geriatric care manager, usually a nurse or social worker, does an assessment, writes a care plan, hires and checks on aides, goes to appointments and steps in during a crisis. Many people who live alone hire one before they need much help. That way the manager already knows them when something goes wrong. Ask the person you name as health care agent to meet the care manager too.

If you are thinking about where to live next, read our guide to senior housing choices. Some people who live alone choose a community with staff on site, partly for the built in daily contact.

How do I prepare for an emergency when I live alone?

Make it easy for someone to know you need help and get to you fast. That means a check-in routine, a way to call for help and papers responders can find.

  1. Set up a daily check-in. Agree with a friend or neighbor on a morning text or call. If you miss it, they call, then come by.
  2. Keep a way to call for help on you. A cell phone in your pocket or a medical alert button you wear all day, including in the shower.
  3. Post an emergency sheet. List medicines, doctors and contacts on the refrigerator. Our free emergency info sheet has a printable form.
  4. Give a key to two people. Responders may otherwise have to force the door.
  5. Join Register Ready. New Jersey's confidential special needs registry helps emergency planners reach residents with disabilities or access and functional needs in a disaster. Dial 2-1-1 for help signing up.
  6. Plan for your pet. Name someone who will take your pet if you go to the hospital.
  7. Gather your papers. Use our important papers checklist and tell your agents where everything is.

Plan for the end of life as well. A will, plus written funeral wishes, spares friends from guessing. New Jersey lets you name someone to control your funeral arrangements. Our funeral planning guide explains how.

Numbers to keep by the phone

ADRC, for your county office on aging: 1-877-222-3737. Office of the Public Guardian for Elderly Adults: 609-588-6500. Social Security: 1-800-772-1213. Long Term Care Ombudsman, for concerns in a licensed facility: 1-877-582-6995. NJ 211: dial 2-1-1.

How do I stay connected and avoid isolation?

Build a weekly routine that puts you around people, and let at least one program know you live alone. Regular contact is also your best early warning system.

Senior centers, libraries, houses of worship and volunteer groups give you people who will notice if you stop showing up. Many county offices on aging run or know of friendly visiting and telephone reassurance programs, where a trained volunteer calls or visits on a schedule. Our guide to staying connected lists New Jersey programs, and volunteering is a good way to meet people with a purpose.

In some places, neighbors form membership groups often called villages. Volunteers and a small staff help members with rides, errands and social events so they can stay at home. Ask your town's senior services office or county office on aging whether one operates near you.

Finally, watch for anyone who moves too fast to become your new best friend, especially if they ask about money. People who live alone are frequent targets. If something feels wrong, our guide to reporting elder abuse explains who to call.

faq.q: Who makes medical decisions in New Jersey if I have no family?
faq.a: The person you name in a proxy directive, which can be a friend, neighbor or other trusted adult. If you never name anyone and can no longer decide, a court may have to appoint a guardian. For people 60 and older with no one able to serve, that can be the state's Office of the Public Guardian.

faq.q: How do I sign an advance directive in New Jersey?
faq.a: Sign and date it in front of two adult witnesses, or acknowledge it before a notary public, attorney or another person authorized to give oaths. The person you name as your health care representative cannot be a witness. Give copies to your representative, doctor and hospital.

faq.q: My aunt has no children. How do I help her plan?
faq.a: Help her list people she trusts, then book an elder law attorney to prepare a proxy directive, instruction directive and durable power of attorney. Help her name alternates, set up a daily check-in with a neighbor, and call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 to learn what her county offers.

faq.q: Can a stranger be my power of attorney?
faq.a: You can name any adult or a professional, such as an attorney or trust company. Some daily money managers also serve as agents. Check references, insurance or bonding and fees, sign a written agreement, and consider asking for a yearly accounting sent to someone else you trust.

faq.q: What does New Jersey's Office of the Public Guardian do?
faq.a: It acts as guardian for New Jersey residents 60 and older whom the Superior Court has found incapacitated, when it accepts the court's appointment. It does not file cases itself. Call 609-588-6500, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.

faq.q: How do I make sure someone checks on my dad who lives alone?
faq.a: Set up a daily call or text with a neighbor or friend, give a key to two nearby people and consider a wearable medical alert button. Ask his county office on aging about friendly visiting or telephone reassurance programs, and sign him up for Register Ready by dialing 2-1-1.

title: Certified home health aides in NJ: what they do and how to check
dek: What a New Jersey CHHA is trained to do, the rules on medications and money, how to look up an aide's certification, and who pays.
keyFacts: CHHAs are certified by the NJ Board of Nursing
Training is at least 76 hours: 60 classroom, 16 clinical
Certification must be renewed every two years
Aides may not hold a client's power of attorney or take loans
Board of Nursing aide unit: 973-504-6430
body:
A Certified Homemaker-Home Health Aide, or CHHA, is the hands-on helper most New Jersey families mean when they say "home health aide." The aide is certified by the New Jersey Board of Nursing after at least 76 hours of approved training, a competency exam and a criminal background check. The certification must be renewed every two years, and you can look it up online in a few minutes.

A CHHA can help your mom or dad bathe, dress, use the toilet, move around and eat, and can shop, cook and do laundry. An aide works for an agency and under a registered nurse. An aide may give medications only when a nurse has formally delegated that specific medication and written instructions for it. This guide explains what that means at home, how to check an aide and who pays.

What is a certified home health aide in New Jersey?

A CHHA is a certified worker who gives personal care at home under the supervision of a registered nurse. In New Jersey the aide must be employed by a home care services agency to work as a CHHA.

The Board of Nursing's rules define a CHHA as an aide "employed by a home care services agency" who follows a nursing plan or does tasks a registered nurse has delegated. Home care services agencies include home health agencies licensed by the Department of Health, assisted living residences and programs, nonprofit homemaker agencies, and health care service firms registered with the Division of Consumer Affairs.

In practice, the aide is licensed separately from the company that sends them. The company has its own registration or license. Our guide to choosing a home care agency covers the company side. This page is about the aide.

Check the aide as well as the company. The aide has a certification of their own.

What training and checks does a CHHA need?

At least 76 hours of Board-approved training, a passing score on a competency exam, and a criminal history background check before starting work. After that, the certification is renewed every two years.

RequirementNew Jersey rule
Training76 hours: 60 classroom, 16 clinical
ExamCompetency exam; oral option in English or Spanish
BackgroundCriminal history check before employment
RenewalEvery two years
ID tagPhoto, name and "homemaker-home health aide"

The training covers more than bathing and lifting. The state curriculum includes the aide's role, working with people, keeping the home safe, the main body systems such as skin, digestion, heart and lungs, and the nervous system, rest and sleep, and death and dying. Community colleges, vocational schools and home health agencies offer the training, and graduates then sit for the Board's competency exam.

On background checks, the Board of Nursing announced in 2018 that it had ended conditional and temporary work certification, so all applicants must clear a criminal background check before beginning work as a CHHA. Our guide to vetting someone coming into the home explains which offenses disqualify an aide and how often checks are repeated.

Renewal matters too. If an aide does not renew within 30 days after the certification expires, it is suspended without a hearing. Working as a CHHA on a suspended certification counts as uncertified practice. So check the expiration date as well as the name.

How do I check an aide's certification?

Use the free License Verification System run by the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs. Search the aide's name and confirm the certification is active and current.

  1. Ask for the full legal name. Ask the agency for the aide's name and certification number before the first shift.
  2. Search online. Go to newjersey.mylicense.com and run a person search for the aide's name.
  3. Read the status and date. Look for an active status and an expiration date in the future.
  4. Match the ID tag. State rules require every CHHA to wear a visible photo ID tag with first name or initial, full surname and the words "homemaker-home health aide." Aides working for a registered health care service firm cannot opt out of the tag.
  5. Call if anything is off. The Board of Nursing's homemaker-home health aide unit is at 973-504-6430.

Also look up the agency. Most private-pay companies are health care service firms, and the Division of Consumer Affairs Regulated Business Section answers questions about them at 973-504-6370.

What can a home health aide do, and what can't they do?

A CHHA can help with daily living tasks and housekeeping that supports your parent's care. Anything more medical has to be set up and supervised by a registered nurse.

Usually part of the job

  • Bathing, grooming, dressing and toileting
  • Help moving from bed to chair, walking and repositioning
  • Feeding and help with meals, including special diets
  • Shopping, errands, laundry and light housekeeping tied to care
  • Watching for changes and reporting them to the nurse

State rules call the household tasks "home-making activities." Your parent, your family or the supervising nurse can ask the aide to do them. Personal care follows a written plan from the registered nurse. The nurse reviews that plan with the aide and must teach the aide face to face if they are not ready for a delegated task.

Rules that protect your parent's money

New Jersey has firm rules here, and families rarely hear about them.

  • An aide may not hold power of attorney for a client or a former client.
  • An aide may not accept a loan from a client or a former client.
  • Any cash or gift worth more than $50 from the client or family must be documented, signed by the aide and the agency, and kept on file by the agency.

Breaking these rules counts as professional misconduct. If an aide offers to "help with the bills," say no and call the agency. Our guide to managing a parent's money covers safer ways to set up bill paying.

Can a home health aide give my parent's medications?

Only under strict conditions. A CHHA may administer a medication only when a registered nurse has delegated that specific medication and written detailed instructions into the care plan.

Under the Board of Nursing rule, the nurse must document the medication, the dose, route and frequency, how long the delegation lasts, side effects to watch for, when to call the nurse and how to prepare the medicine. The aide must record every dose. The aide must report right away if a dose is late, missed, wrong, refused or causes a reaction.

So ask the agency plainly: "Will a nurse delegate medications, or will the aide give reminders only?" If the agency uses delegation, ask to see the written instructions. If it does not, you need another plan. That might be a weekly pill organizer you fill, pharmacy blister packs, or a visiting nurse.

Before the first shift

Ask for the aide's name and certification number, look it up at newjersey.mylicense.com, and confirm who the supervising registered nurse is. Questions about an aide's certification go to the Board of Nursing at 973-504-6430.

Should we use an agency or hire an aide directly?

To work as a CHHA in New Jersey, an aide must be employed by a home care services agency. If you hire someone on your own, they are working as a private caregiver, and the state's nurse supervision and delegation system is not there.

That does not make private hire wrong. Many families hire a trusted companion directly. But know what you give up. Without an agency, there is no registered nurse writing a care plan, no one to delegate medications and no agency file for gift records. Your family may also become a household employer, with tax and insurance duties. Our hiring checklist walks through the questions either way.

Questions worth asking any agency:

  • Is every aide who gives hands-on care a certified CHHA?
  • Who is the supervising registered nurse, and how often will they visit?
  • Will a nurse delegate medications, or are aides limited to reminders?
  • How do you verify certification and renewal dates?
  • What is your policy on gifts, and how do you document them?
  • What happens if the aide is sick or my parent wants someone else?

Who pays for a home health aide in New Jersey?

Medicare pays for aide visits only alongside skilled care for a homebound person. NJ FamilyCare (Medicaid) can pay for ongoing personal care. Most other families pay privately or use long-term care insurance.

Medicare

Medicare covers part-time or intermittent home health aide care only if your parent is also getting skilled nursing or therapy at the same time, is homebound, and a doctor or other provider has ordered it from a Medicare-certified agency. In most cases that means up to 8 hours a day of combined nursing and aide services, with a maximum of 28 hours a week. Medicare does not pay for 24-hour care, or for personal care like bathing and dressing when that is the only help needed. Our guide to Medicare home health care has the details.

NJ FamilyCare

NJ FamilyCare covers Personal Care Assistant (PCA) services for members who need hands-on help. Your parent needs a doctor's order, and a nursing assessment sets the number of hours. Members enrolled in a managed care plan ask the plan directly. See NJ FamilyCare for seniors and Medicaid and MLTSS.

Other help

For people with too much income for Medicaid, the state's JACC program can help pay for home care. The Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737 connects you to your county office on aging for a screening.

This is general information, not legal advice. If you suspect an aide of abuse, neglect or taking money, call the agency supervisor, report it to your county Adult Protective Services office (the state's line is 1-855-835-5277, 855-TELL-APS), and call 911 in an emergency. Our guide to reporting elder abuse lists the steps.

faq.q: How do I check if my mom's home health aide is certified in New Jersey?
faq.a: Ask the agency for the aide's full name and certification number, then search it at newjersey.mylicense.com under the Board of Nursing. Make sure the status is active and the expiration date has not passed. Questions go to the Board of Nursing at 973-504-6430.

faq.q: Can a home health aide give my dad his pills?
faq.a: Only if a registered nurse has delegated that specific medication and written instructions into the care plan, and the aide documents every dose. Ask the agency how it handles medications before care starts.

faq.q: How much training does a CHHA have in NJ?
faq.a: At least 76 hours in a Board-approved program, 60 hours in the classroom and 16 hours of clinical practice, plus a competency exam and a criminal background check.

faq.q: Can we hire a certified aide privately instead of through an agency?
faq.a: You can hire a private caregiver, but under Board of Nursing rules a CHHA works for a home care services agency under a registered nurse. Hiring privately means no nurse care plan, no medication delegation and possible household employer duties for your family.

faq.q: Is it OK for my parent to give the aide a gift?
faq.a: Small thanks are common, but state rules require any cash or gift worth more than $50 from a client or family to be documented and signed by the aide and the agency. Aides may never accept loans or hold power of attorney for a client.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for a home health aide?
faq.a: Only part time, when your parent is homebound and also needs skilled nursing or therapy ordered by a provider from a Medicare-certified agency. Medicare does not pay for personal care alone or 24-hour care.

title: Assisted living in Essex County, NJ: licensed residences
dek: The state-licensed assisted living residences in West Orange, Livingston, Roseland and the rest of Essex County, which offer memory care, how to check inspection records, and what to ask on a tour.
keyFacts: We confirmed 14 licensed assisted living residences in Essex County with the NJ Department of Health and on their own websites (November 2026).
Twelve say on their websites that they offer memory care.
NJ median for assisted living: $8,710 a month for a private one-bedroom (CareScout 2025).
Complaints: NJ Department of Health hotline 1-800-792-9770, 24 hours.
body:
Essex County has more than a dozen licensed assisted living residences, and most of them sit in the western suburbs: West Orange, Livingston, Roseland, Fairfield, West Caldwell, Maplewood and Bloomfield. We confirmed 14 of them in the New Jersey Department of Health's licensed facility database and on each residence's own website. Twelve say they offer memory care, either on site or on a shared campus.

Before your mom or dad tours anywhere, look the residence up in the state's long-term care facility search. It shows the license type, when the license expires, how many beds are licensed and a five-year summary of inspections and complaint findings. Assisted living is expensive. CareScout's Cost of Care Survey 2025 puts the New Jersey median at $8,710 a month for a private one-bedroom unit, and Medicare does not pay for it. For the statewide rules on care, fees and discharge, see our guide to assisted living in New Jersey.

Which assisted living residences are in Essex County?

The 14 residences below hold a current New Jersey Department of Health license and appear on their own websites at Essex County addresses. They are in alphabetical order. We checked these listings in November 2026. This is not an endorsement or a ranking.

We looked up each residence in the state database, confirmed its license had not expired, and then checked its own website. Phone numbers come from each residence's own site. Thirteen are licensed as assisted living residences. Green Hill (marked *) is licensed as a comprehensive personal care home, which follows the same care rules but may have shared bathrooms.

ResidenceTownPhone

A few notes on the names. Crane's Mill appears in the state database under Lutheran Social Ministries, which runs it. Job Haines Home calls its assisted living Hearthside Commons. Brighton Gardens of West Orange is operated by Sunrise Senior Living. Crane's Mill, Green Hill and Winchester Gardens are larger campuses that also offer independent living and nursing care.

This is not every licensed residence in the county. We left out places we could not confirm on both the state database and their own website, and the state also licenses smaller assisted living programs inside subsidized senior housing. To see the full current list, open the state search, choose "Search by County," pick Essex and tick Assisted Living Residences and Comprehensive Personal Care Homes.

Look up the license before the tour. It takes two minutes and shows you the complaint history.

Which Essex County residences offer memory care?

Twelve of the 14 say on their websites that they offer memory care. Arden Courts of West Orange offers memory care only. The others have a separate memory care area alongside regular assisted living.

  • Memory care only: Arden Courts of West Orange, which describes four separate "houses" and enclosed courtyards.
  • Assisted living plus memory care on site: Benchmark at Roseland, Brandywine Living at Livingston, Brighton Gardens of West Orange, Brookdale West Orange, Crane's Mill (its site says 22 apartments are dedicated to memory care), Spring Hills Livingston, Sunrise at West Essex, Sunrise of Livingston and Winchester Gardens.
  • On a shared campus: CareOne at Livingston Assisted Living says its campus includes a Harmony Village memory care community. Ask whether that is part of the assisted living license or the nursing center next door.
  • Green Hill: its site describes CaringWay, a dementia program with secure units limited to 10 residents. Green Hill also offers nursing care, so ask which part of the campus and which license the program falls under.

We could not confirm a memory care program on the websites of The Cliffs at Eagle Rock or Job Haines Home. Call and ask. New Jersey has no separate memory care license, so any residence that advertises a dementia program must meet extra state rules, including dementia training for direct care staff and a written list of dementia activities and safety policies for families. Our guide to memory care in New Jersey explains those rules, and nursing home vs. memory care helps if you are torn between the two.

Does any Essex County assisted living accept Medicaid?

Possibly, but none of the 14 websites we checked said plainly that it accepts NJ FamilyCare, New Jersey's Medicaid program. That does not mean they never do. Ask each one directly.

NJ FamilyCare pays for assisted living care through its Managed Long Term Services and Supports program (MLTSS). It covers the care part. Your parent pays room and board from their own income. To qualify, your parent must meet NJ FamilyCare's financial rules and need a nursing home level of care. State rules also require many residences to set aside some room for Medicaid residents. Our guide to NJ FamilyCare and MLTSS covers the application and the five-year look-back.

When you call, ask these questions and write down the answers:

  • Do you accept NJ FamilyCare MLTSS? From move-in, or only after a period of private pay?
  • If my mom runs out of money here, can she stay? Is that promise in the admission agreement?
  • Which MLTSS health plans do you work with?
  • Is there a waiting list for a Medicaid room?

This is general information, not legal or financial advice. An elder law attorney can help if a Medicaid plan is part of the picture.

How do I check a residence's license and inspection record?

Use the New Jersey Department of Health's free facility search. Every residence on our list has a page there with its license details and inspection summary.

  1. Open the search. Go to the NJ long-term care facility search and search by name, or by county and facility type.
  2. Check the license. Confirm the license type and that the expiration date has not passed. Note the licensed name, which can differ from the sign out front.
  3. Read the inspection summary. The page counts routine inspections, complaint inspections and deficiencies cited over the past five years. Several complaint inspections with deficiencies is a reason to ask questions. It is not a verdict on its own.
  4. Ask for the latest survey. Ask the residence to show you its most recent inspection report and its plan of correction. A residence that won't show you is telling you something.
  5. Call the Ombudsman. The Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-877-582-6995 advocates for assisted living residents and can explain your parent's rights.

What should we ask on a tour?

Ask the same questions everywhere so you can compare answers. Go once on a scheduled tour and once at a mealtime or in the evening, when you will see how staff and residents really get along.

  • Price. What is the base rent, and how is the care level priced? Is medication help a separate charge? How much did fees rise in each of the last three years?
  • Nursing. A registered nurse must be available at all times under state rules. Who is in the building at night, and how many aides are on each shift?
  • The move-in assessment. A registered nurse assesses each new resident. What would make them say no to your dad, or ask him to move out later?
  • Memory care. If your mom's memory is slipping, can she move to memory care in the same building? What does that cost, and who decides when?
  • Short stays. Several Essex residences advertise respite or trial stays, including Crane's Mill (14-day respite stays), Arden Courts, Benchmark at Roseland and Brighton Gardens of West Orange. A short stay lets your parent try it before signing.
  • Getting out. Is there transportation to doctors in Livingston, Montclair or Newark? How often do residents go on outings?

Bring your parent if you can, and let them ask their own questions. If you want help finding residences, our guide to senior living placement services explains how free referral advisors are paid. If you are not sure your parent needs to move at all, compare assisted living and home care first.

What does assisted living cost in Essex County?

Expect to pay at or above the state median of $8,710 a month for a private one-bedroom, from CareScout's Cost of Care Survey 2025. That survey reports a statewide figure. Prices at individual residences vary with unit size and care needs.

Most residences charge rent for the apartment plus a care fee set after the nurse's assessment. State rules require residences to give you all fees in writing at admission and whenever they change. A residence cannot raise your parent's charges for extra care unless a registered nurse has reassessed them and documented the need. Read the admission agreement for the deposit, what happens to it if your parent leaves, and how much notice you must give.

Essex County phone numbers to keep

Essex County ADRC (Aging and Disability Resource Connection): 973-395-8375 or 1-877-222-3737. Long-Term Care Ombudsman: 1-877-582-6995. NJ Department of Health complaint hotline, 24 hours: 1-800-792-9770.

Who can help Essex County families decide?

Start with the Essex County ADRC, run by the county's Division of Senior Services, at 973-395-8375 or 1-877-222-3737. Staff can talk through options and county caregiver programs.

If your parent wants to stay home a while longer, the ADRC also takes applications for the county's respite program for family caregivers. Our Essex County senior centers guide lists lunch programs and activities, and the Essex County page has transportation and local resources. If a parent's health is declining, our guide to hospice care in Essex County explains how hospice can come into an assisted living residence.

For a professional to help you sort out care, see our list of care help in New Jersey. If you have a complaint about care in a residence, raise it with the director first, then call the Ombudsman or the Department of Health hotline.

faq.q: How do I find assisted living for my mom in Essex County?
faq.a: Start with the licensed residences on this page, then confirm each one in the NJ Department of Health long-term care facility search. Call two or three, tour at a mealtime, and call the Essex County ADRC at 973-395-8375 if you want help weighing options.

faq.q: Which assisted living residences in Essex County have memory care?
faq.a: In November 2026, Arden Courts of West Orange (memory care only), Benchmark at Roseland, Brandywine Living at Livingston, Brighton Gardens of West Orange, Brookdale West Orange, Crane's Mill, Spring Hills Livingston, Sunrise at West Essex, Sunrise of Livingston and Winchester Gardens said on their websites that they offer memory care. CareOne at Livingston says its campus includes a Harmony Village memory care community, and Green Hill describes a CaringWay dementia program.

faq.q: Does Medicaid pay for assisted living in Essex County?
faq.a: NJ FamilyCare's MLTSS program can pay for the care part at residences that accept it, while your parent pays room and board. None of the Essex residence websites we checked said plainly that they accept it, so ask each one directly.

faq.q: How can I check if an assisted living in NJ is licensed?
faq.a: Search the residence by name in the NJ Department of Health long-term care facility search at healthapps.nj.gov. The page shows the license type, expiration date, licensed beds and a five-year inspection summary.

faq.q: What is a comprehensive personal care home?
faq.a: It is a type of assisted living license in New Jersey. It follows the same care and resident rights rules as an assisted living residence, but units hold no more than two residents and bathrooms may be shared. Green Hill in West Orange holds this license.

faq.q: Who do I call with a complaint about my dad's assisted living?
faq.a: Talk to the residence director first. Then call the Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-877-582-6995 or the NJ Department of Health 24-hour complaint hotline at 1-800-792-9770.

dek: The state-licensed residences in Bergen County that run dedicated memory care programs, from Paramus to Woodcliff Lake, how to check them, and where families can get dementia help.
keyFacts: We confirmed 11 Bergen County residences with a current NJ Department of Health license and a dedicated memory care program on their own websites (November 2026).
NJ has no separate memory care license. Dementia programs in assisted living follow N.J.A.C. 8:36-19.
You can ask for a written list of dementia activities and for shift staffing records.
Bergen County Division of Senior Services: 201-336-7400 or 1-877-222-3737.
Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline: 1-800-272-3900.
body:
Memory care in Bergen County usually means a secure dementia neighborhood inside a state-licensed assisted living residence. A few small homes hold a separate state license as residential dementia care homes. We found 11 residences in Paramus, Woodcliff Lake, Tenafly, Saddle River, Emerson, Edgewater and Wyckoff that appear in the New Jersey Department of Health's licensed facility database and describe a dedicated memory care or dementia program on their own websites.

New Jersey has no separate memory care license for assisted living. Any residence that advertises an Alzheimer's or dementia program must follow extra state rules, including written program policies, dementia training for every direct care worker, and shift staffing records the public can request. This page lists the Bergen programs we confirmed and the local help available. For costs and the statewide rules in full, see our guide to memory care in New Jersey.

Which Bergen County residences have memory care programs?

The 11 residences below are listed in alphabetical order. Each holds a current license from the New Jersey Department of Health and says on its own website that it offers dedicated memory care. We checked these listings in November 2026. This is not an endorsement or a ranking.

We confirmed each license in the state's facility database, then read each residence's own website for its memory care program. Phone numbers come from each residence's own site. Ten are licensed as assisted living residences. Fox Trail (marked *) is licensed as a residential dementia care home; its website lists the number as 1-855-5MEMORY.

Brightview ParamusParamus201-561-7221
Brightview TenaflyTenafly201-775-4667
Brookdale EmersonEmerson201-986-9009
CareOne at The CupolaParamus201-444-8200
Christian Health (Longview and Courtyard)Wyckoff201-848-4303
Fox Trail Memory Care Living *Woodcliff Lake1-855-563-6679
Harmony Village at CareOne ParamusParamus551-276-7200
Juniper Village at ParamusParamus201-251-9600
Sunrise of EdgewaterEdgewater201-941-6111
Sunrise of Woodcliff LakeWoodcliff Lake201-782-1888

This is not every option. We left out residences whose websites did not describe a dedicated memory care program, and any we could not confirm on both the state database and their own site. To see every current license, open the state facility search, choose "Search by County," pick Bergen and tick Assisted Living Residences, Comprehensive Personal Care Homes and Residential Dementia Care Homes.

One more residence describes a dedicated memory care neighborhood on its website: The Bristal at Woodcliff Lake, which calls it Reflections. We did not add it to the table because its state license showed an expiration date of October 31, 2026 when we checked, with no renewal posted yet. Look it up in the state search to see whether the renewal has been recorded.

Ask every residence for its written list of dementia activities. New Jersey says you can have it.

What are the memory care programs called?

Most Bergen residences give their memory care area its own name. Knowing it helps when you call, because the staff, pricing and admission rules often differ from regular assisted living.

  • Brightview Paramus and Brightview Tenafly. Brightview Paramus calls its dementia care program Wellspring Village and also offers independent and assisted living. Brightview Tenafly describes itself as a memory care and assisted living community.
  • Brighton Gardens of Saddle River. Its site says it offers memory care for mild memory loss, plus a Reminiscence Neighborhood for moderate to advanced Alzheimer's and other dementias.
  • Brookdale Emerson. Brookdale's memory care program is called Clare Bridge.
  • CareOne at The Cupola and Harmony Village at CareOne Paramus. CareOne's memory care service is called Harmony Village. The Cupola offers it alongside assisted living. Harmony Village at CareOne Paramus, on Paramus Road, is a separately licensed memory care assisted living.
  • Christian Health in Wyckoff. Courtyard is a residence connected to the Longview assisted living, designed for people in the early stages of dementia.
  • Fox Trail Memory Care Living at Woodcliff Lake. A small home serving only people with memory loss. The state licenses it for 15 residents.
  • Juniper Village at Paramus. Assisted living plus what it calls Wellspring Memory Care.
  • Sunrise of Edgewater and Sunrise of Woodcliff Lake. Both list assisted living and memory care. Sunrise calls its memory care program Reminiscence.

Which program fits my parent's stage of dementia?

Ask each residence which stages it serves and when it would ask your parent to move. Programs differ. Christian Health's Courtyard is built for early stages. Brighton Gardens of Saddle River separates mild memory loss from moderate to advanced care.

State rules require every dementia program to have written admission and discharge criteria based on a registered nurse's assessment of thinking and daily function. Ask for that document. It tells you more than the brochure.

Say your mom has started wandering at night but still dresses herself and enjoys a crowd. A large secure neighborhood with a busy activity calendar may suit her now. If your dad gets overwhelmed by noise and needs help with most daily tasks, a smaller setting may be calmer. Ask what happens when needs change. Can your parent stay with more help, or would they have to move to a nursing home? Our comparison of nursing homes and memory care explains where the line usually falls.

How do I check a memory care residence before we sign?

Look up the license, read the inspection summary, and ask for the two documents New Jersey requires dementia programs to share. That takes less than an afternoon.

  1. Find the license. Search the residence by name in the NJ long-term care facility search. Confirm the license type and that it has not expired.
  2. Read the inspection summary. Each facility page counts routine and complaint inspections and deficiencies cited over five years. Ask the residence about any complaint findings and to show you its most recent survey and plan of correction.
  3. Ask for the activity list. A residence with a dementia program must give anyone seeking placement a written list of its dementia activities, how often they happen, and its safety and security policies.
  4. Ask for staffing records. Dementia programs must keep daily records of direct care staff on each shift and share them with the public on request. Compare day and night.
  5. Visit at a hard time of day. Late afternoon and early evening are when many people with dementia struggle most. Our guide to sundowning explains why.

What should we ask on a memory care tour?

Ask the same questions in every building and write the answers down. Bring a second family member if you can.

  • How many residents live in the memory care area, and how many aides and nurses work there on each shift?
  • What dementia training do staff get, and how often? Who is the program director?
  • How are the doors secured? Can residents walk outside safely in a courtyard or garden?
  • What does a typical day look like? Can we see this week's activity calendar? Our guide to activities for a parent with dementia can help you judge it.
  • How do you handle agitation without medication first? How often do you call families?
  • What is the monthly rate, what does it include, and when does it go up? A residence cannot raise charges for more care unless a registered nurse reassesses your parent and documents the need.
  • Do you offer short respite stays? Brighton Gardens of Saddle River, for example, lists short-term stays.

Will Medicaid pay for memory care in Bergen County?

It can pay for the care, but only at a residence that accepts NJ FamilyCare's MLTSS program. None of the 11 websites we checked said plainly that they accept it, so ask each one.

MLTSS covers assisted living services for people who meet NJ FamilyCare's financial rules and need a nursing home level of care. Your parent pays room and board from their own income. Ask whether the residence accepts MLTSS from move-in or only after a period of private pay, and whether your parent could stay if the money runs out. Our guide to NJ FamilyCare and MLTSS explains the application. This is general information, not legal advice.

Bergen County numbers to keep

Bergen County Division of Senior Services (the county ADRC): 201-336-7400 or 1-877-222-3737. Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline: 1-800-272-3900. Alzheimer's New Jersey Helpline: 1-888-280-6055. Long-Term Care Ombudsman: 1-877-582-6995. NJ Department of Health complaint hotline, 24 hours: 1-800-792-9770.

Where can Bergen County families get dementia help?

Call the Bergen County Division of Senior Services at 201-336-7400 or 1-877-222-3737. It is the county's Aging and Disability Resource Connection and helps older adults and caregivers find long-term care and home services.

  • Dementia Friendly Bergen County. The Division of Senior Services runs this initiative. Ask what programs are running near your parent.
  • Wellness Check Program. If your parent still lives at home, the county places a free automated daily call. If no one answers, it calls the friend or relative you name.
  • Senior centers. For lunch programs and activities close to home, see our Bergen County senior centers guide and the Bergen County page.
  • Breaks for you. Our guide to caregiver respite in New Jersey covers state respite programs, and after a dementia diagnosis lists support groups and memory cafes.

For professionals who can help you plan, see our list of care help in New Jersey. If you have a concern about care after your parent moves in, raise it with the director first, then call the Ombudsman or the Department of Health hotline.

A senior living placement advisor can also help you compare these programs and set up tours. Most are free to families because communities pay them, so ask how they are paid.

faq.q: How do I find memory care for my dad in Bergen County?
faq.a: Start with the licensed programs on this page, confirm each one in the NJ Department of Health facility search, and tour two or three in the late afternoon. The Bergen County Division of Senior Services at 201-336-7400 can talk through options.

faq.q: Which memory care communities are in Paramus, NJ?
faq.a: In November 2026 we confirmed Brightview Paramus, CareOne at The Cupola, Harmony Village at CareOne Paramus and Juniper Village at Paramus. Each holds a NJ Department of Health assisted living license and describes a memory care program on its website.

faq.q: What is a residential dementia care home in New Jersey?
faq.a: It is a separate license type in the NJ Department of Health's licensing database for small homes that serve people with dementia. Fox Trail Memory Care Living at Woodcliff Lake holds this license for 15 residents.

faq.q: Does Medicaid pay for memory care in Bergen County?
faq.a: NJ FamilyCare's MLTSS program can pay for the care at residences that accept it, and your parent pays room and board. None of the Bergen websites we checked said plainly that they accept it, so ask each residence directly.

faq.q: What should I ask a memory care community before my mom moves in?
faq.a: Ask how many staff work each shift, what dementia training they get, how doors are secured, what stages the program serves, and when your mom would have to move. Ask for the written list of dementia activities and the shift staffing records, which state rules let you request.

faq.q: Who do I call with a complaint about memory care in NJ?
faq.a: Talk to the director first. Then call the Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-877-582-6995 or the NJ Department of Health 24-hour complaint hotline at 1-800-792-9770.
