title: Holiday visit: signs your parent needs more help in NJ
dek: Where to look during a holiday visit home, what each sign can mean, which ones can't wait, and what to set up before you leave. Plus the New Jersey numbers to call.
keyFacts: Leftovers keep about 3 to 4 days in a fridge at 40°F or below (FoodSafety.gov)
NIA advises heat at 68°F or higher; 60 to 65°F can lead to hypothermia in older adults
Fewer than half of older adults who fall tell their doctor (CDC)
NJ MVC's Medical Review Unit takes written reports from family about unsafe drivers, not anonymous ones
NJ ADRC for county aging services: 1-877-222-3737
body:
A holiday visit is often the first time in months that you see your mom or dad's daily life up close. The signs that a parent needs more help are usually small and practical: spoiled food in the fridge, unopened bills, pill bottles that do not match the calendar, new dents on the car, bruises nobody mentions, or a house that is suddenly too cold. One sign rarely means much. Several together, or a clear change since your last visit, mean it is time to act.

This guide is a plan for the visit itself. It shows where to look and what each sign can mean, how to check without making your parent feel inspected, which signs cannot wait, what to set up before you drive or fly home, and who to call in New Jersey. Our guide to whether a parent is safe living alone covers assessments and care options in depth, and how to talk with a parent about help covers the conversation itself.

What signs should I look for on a holiday visit?

Look at the places where daily life leaves a trail: the kitchen, the mail, the medicine cabinet, the car and your parent. Stay long enough to see an ordinary day, not just the holiday meal.

Where to lookWhat it can mean
Fridge and pantryTrouble shopping, cooking or remembering meals
Mail and billsMoney confusion, scams, missed payments
Pill bottlesMissed or doubled doses
Car and drivingVision, reaction time or memory changes
Bruises, gaitFalls, or sometimes mistreatment
ThermostatBill worries or not feeling the cold
Clothes, hygieneTrouble bathing, laundry or depression

The kitchen

Open the fridge to grab the milk and look around. FoodSafety.gov says a refrigerator should be at 40°F or below and that cooked leftovers keep about 3 to 4 days. Several weeks of old takeout, moldy food, or almost nothing to eat at all deserve a note. So do scorched pots, a burned dish towel or stove knobs left on. Check whether the kitchen still gets used. A parent who used to cook every night and now lives on toast may be tired, sad, or finding it hard to stand.

The mail

Offer to help sort a stack. Look for late notices, shutoff warnings, letters from the IRS or the state, the same charity asking again and again, sweepstakes letters, and bank statements with unfamiliar charges. Piles of unopened envelopes from a parent who once paid every bill the day it came are a real change. Our scams guide helps you sort genuine mail from the rest.

The medicine cabinet

Compare the bottles with the fill dates. A 30-day bottle filled two months ago that is still nearly full suggests missed doses. One that is empty too soon suggests extra doses. Look for expired pills, the same drug from two pharmacies or two doctors, and a weekly pill box with doses still sitting in past days. The National Institute on Aging (NIA) suggests keeping a written list of every medicine and using one pharmacy so the pharmacist can catch problems. Our guide to managing many medications goes further.

Your parent

Notice whether clothes hang looser, whether your dad is wearing the same shirt each day, how he gets out of a chair, and whether he holds the wall or furniture as he walks. Bruises on the arms or shins, a new limp or a cut on the forehead may point to a fall nobody mentioned. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says fewer than half of older people who fall tell their doctor.

The thermostat

The NIA advises keeping the heat at 68°F or higher in cold weather and says even a mildly cool home, 60 to 65°F, can lead to hypothermia in older adults. A cold house may mean your mom is worried about the gas bill. NJ 211, listed below, can point you to heating bill help.

How do I check without making Mom feel inspected?

Join in rather than audit. Most of the checking above happens naturally if you cook together, run errands, sort the mail and sit with your parent through an ordinary afternoon.

  • Do things side by side. Make breakfast together. Offer to drive to the store, then let your dad drive home.
  • Ask open questions. "What's the hardest part of the week now?" gets more than "Are you okay?"
  • Notice out loud, gently. "I saw a few notices from PSE&G. Want me to look at them with you?"
  • Talk to the people around them. A neighbor, a friend from church or the person who drives your mom to the hairdresser may have seen more than you have.
  • Write it down privately. Note the date, what you saw and what has changed since last time. Patterns are easier to see on paper, and specifics help a doctor.
  • Compare notes with siblings before anyone speaks to your parent about it.

Keep the holiday a holiday. A big family talk at the dinner table rarely goes well. If something needs saying, choose a calm, private moment, or plan a follow-up call. Our conversation guide has words that help.

If your parent has already been diagnosed with dementia, our guide to the holidays with a parent who has dementia covers planning the gathering itself.

What do changes in driving tell you?

A lot, and you only learn it by riding along. Ask to be driven to the store or to church. Notice whether your parent drifts between lanes, misses signs, brakes late, gets lost on a familiar route, or seems tense and tired afterward. Walk around the car in daylight and look for new scrapes and dents.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) suggests families collect information, make a plan and follow through, rather than waiting until driving is dangerous. Decisions should not be based on age alone. Our guide to driving later in life covers the talk and the alternatives.

If you have a serious concern and your parent will not stop, New Jersey's Motor Vehicle Commission (MVC) accepts reports from family members to its Medical Review Unit. You write a letter with the driver's name, address, license number and date of birth if you have it, the medical concern, your full name and address, your relationship to the driver and what you have seen. Mail or fax it to the Medical Review Unit (fax 609-292-7504; New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission, P.O. Box 173, Trenton, NJ 08666-0173). Anonymous reports are not accepted. The MVC may then require your parent to see a doctor and return medical forms within 45 days. Questions go to 609-292-7500, ext. 5032.

Which signs can't wait until after the holidays?

Some changes are a medical issue first. Sudden confusion, a parent who seems very different from your last phone call, a fall with a hit to the head, chest pain, trouble breathing or new weakness on one side need care now. MedlinePlus lists sudden confusion as a reason to go to the ER, and the CDC says an older person who falls and hits their head should see a doctor right away. Our guide to urgent care or the ER lists the signs.

Gradual changes are different. Weight loss, more forgetfulness, sadness or a messier house over months call for a doctor's visit soon, not an emergency room. Ask for an appointment focused on memory, mood, medicines and falls. Medicare's yearly Wellness visit includes a review of current prescriptions and a cognitive assessment to look for signs of dementia.

Signs of mistreatment are their own category. Bruises your parent will not explain, fear of a particular person, a new "friend" handling money, or missing valuables call for a report to Adult Protective Services. In an emergency, call 911. Our elder abuse guide explains what happens next.

Sudden change is a medical question. Slow change is a planning question.

What should I set up before I leave?

The days after a holiday visit are the best time to put a few safety nets in place, while you are still nearby and the details are fresh.

  1. Book the doctor visit. Make the appointment before you leave, and ask your parent to sign the office's form allowing the doctor to talk with you. Send the office a short note with what you saw.
  2. Make a medicine list. Copy it from the bottles, including vitamins and over-the-counter drugs. Keep one on the fridge and one on your phone.
  3. Fill in an emergency sheet. Our free emergency info sheet puts doctors, medicines, allergies and contacts on one page.
  4. Find the key papers. Ask whether there is a power of attorney and an advance directive, and where they are. If they do not exist, putting them in place while your parent can still decide is one of the most useful steps a family can take.
  5. Set up a check-in rhythm. A daily call at the same time, a neighbor with a spare key, or a sibling who visits on a set day.
  6. Fix the easy hazards. Brighter bulbs, a night light on the way to the bathroom, loose rugs gone, working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms.
  7. Agree on one next step with your parent. Even a small one, like a call together to the county office on aging.

Who can I call in New Jersey?

Start with the free county office on aging. You do not need a diagnosis or a crisis to call.

Start here

NJ Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC): 1-877-222-3737. It connects you to the office on aging in your parent's county for screening, meals, rides, home care programs and caregiver help. Give your parent's address, since services depend on the county.

  • If you live out of state, the federal Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116 can also point you to local help.
  • Medicare questions: NJ State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP), 1-800-792-8820, for free, unbiased counseling.
  • Food, utility or housing help: dial 2-1-1 or 1-877-652-1148 for NJ 211.
  • Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation: your parent's county Adult Protective Services office, listed on the state's APS page, or the state line at 1-855-835-5277 (1-855-TELL-APS). The state says a trained social worker meets the adult face to face within 72 business hours of a report.
  • A medicine mix-up: NJ Poison Control, 1-800-222-1222, 24 hours a day.
  • A neutral professional opinion: a private geriatric care manager can visit and write a care plan. Most families pay for this privately. Our Find care help page lists some in New Jersey.

Most families leave a holiday visit with a mix of worry and guilt. You do not have to solve everything this week. Write down what you saw, make the doctor appointment, call the ADRC and plan to check again in a month.

faq.q: What are the signs my mom needs more help at home?
faq.a: Look for a pattern of change: spoiled or missing food, unopened bills and late notices, pill bottles that are too full or too empty for their fill date, new dents on the car, unexplained bruises or a new limp, weight loss, wearing the same clothes, and a house kept unusually cold. One sign alone may mean little. Several, or a clear change since your last visit, mean it is time to act.

faq.q: How do I check on my dad during a holiday visit without upsetting him?
faq.a: Do ordinary things together. Cook, sort the mail, run errands and let him drive you somewhere. Ask open questions about what has gotten harder, talk with neighbors and friends, and write down what you notice privately. Save any serious conversation for a calm, private moment.

faq.q: Can I report my parent's unsafe driving in New Jersey?
faq.a: Yes. The NJ Motor Vehicle Commission's Medical Review Unit accepts referrals from family members. Write a letter with the driver's details, the medical concern, your full name, address and relationship and what you have observed. Anonymous reports are not accepted. Questions: 609-292-7500, ext. 5032.

faq.q: What should I do if my parent is suddenly confused during the visit?
faq.a: Treat sudden confusion as a medical problem. MedlinePlus lists it as a reason to go to the emergency room. It can come from an infection, dehydration, a medicine problem or a stroke. Call 911 if your parent also has weakness, trouble speaking, chest pain or trouble breathing.

faq.q: Who do I call in NJ if I'm worried about my parent after the holidays?
faq.a: Start with the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737, which links you to the county office on aging. For suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, call the county Adult Protective Services office or 1-855-835-5277. For Medicare questions, call NJ SHIP at 1-800-792-8820.

title: When an aging parent refuses help: what NJ families can do
dek: Your mom or dad clearly needs more support and keeps saying no. How to tell a choice from a capacity problem, small steps that work, and when to call APS in New Jersey.
keyFacts: NJ APS cannot force services on an adult with capacity who declines help
APS investigates self-neglect; a social worker visits within 72 business hours
APS statewide line: 1-855-835-5277 (1-855-TELL-APS)
Medicare's yearly Wellness visit includes a cognitive assessment
Family can refer an unsafe driver to the NJ MVC Medical Review Unit by letter
body:
When an aging parent refuses help, the first question is whether they are making a choice or have lost the ability to choose. An older adult who understands the risks has the legal right to say no, even to help their family thinks is obvious. In New Jersey, Adult Protective Services (APS) cannot force services on an adult with capacity who declines them.

That does not leave you stuck. Most refusals soften with smaller offers, a doctor's voice and time. If your mom or dad can no longer understand the risks and is in danger, you can call county APS about self-neglect, and guardianship is the court's last resort. This guide is for the stage after the first talk has happened and the answer was still no. If you have not had that talk yet, start with our guide on how to talk with a parent about getting help at home.

Worried your parent is in danger right now?

Call 911. For self-neglect that is serious but not an emergency, call the APS office in the county where your parent lives, or the state line at 1-855-835-5277 (1-855-TELL-APS).

Why do aging parents refuse help?

Usually because accepting help feels like losing something. Independence, privacy, money or the house itself. The refusal is often about fear, and it helps to find out which fear.

Common reasons families hear, in one form or another:

  • "I don't want a stranger in my house." A worry about privacy, theft or being watched.
  • "It costs too much." Many older adults lived through lean years and guard their savings hard.
  • "If I say yes, you'll put me in a home." Help at home can feel like the first step out the door.
  • "I'm fine." Sometimes denial. Sometimes a memory problem that hides the trouble from the person who has it.
  • "I don't want to be a burden." Saying no can be their way of protecting you.
  • Depression. The National Institute on Aging (NIA) notes that depression in older people is sometimes confused with normal aging. A person who has stopped caring about meals or bills may need treatment more than an aide. Our guide to depression and loneliness in older adults covers where to get help.

Ask the question straight out and then stop talking. "What worries you most about having someone come in?" The answer tells you which offer to make next.

Is it a choice or a capacity problem?

Capacity means your parent can understand the facts, weigh the risks and make a decision. A parent with capacity can make a choice you disagree with. A parent without it may not be able to protect themselves, and that is where outside help comes in.

A diagnosis alone does not settle it. Plenty of people with early memory loss still understand what an aide does and why they would rather not have one. Capacity can also vary by decision. Your dad may be able to decide who visits him and still be unable to follow his own bills.

Some questions that help you think it through, before you raise it with a doctor:

  • Can your parent tell you, in their own words, what the risk is? ("If I fall at night, nobody will know until morning.")
  • Is their reason consistent from week to week, or does it change each time?
  • Do they remember the last conversation, or the fall that started it?
  • Is the refusal new, or have they always been this way?

A doctor or other clinician, not the family, is the right person to assess capacity. The New Jersey APS fact sheet describes the adults APS serves as people who are unable to make, communicate or carry out decisions about their own well-being because of illness or disability. If that description fits your parent, the options below change. If it does not, the work is persuasion, patience and planning.

A parent who understands the risk is allowed to take it. Your job shifts to making the risk smaller.

How can I get my parent to accept a little help?

Start smaller than you think you need to. A trial, a single task or something that helps you rather than them is easier to accept than "care."

  1. Offer one specific thing. NIA suggests pairing your worry with a practical offer. "Would you like me to set up grocery delivery every week?" is easier to accept than "You need help."
  2. Make it a trial. "Let's try a cleaner for one month, then decide." A set end date lowers the stakes.
  3. Frame it around you. "I'd sleep better if you wore a fall alert button" asks for a favor. Many parents will do for a child what they will not do for themselves. Our guide to medical alert systems in NJ covers costs.
  4. Keep them in charge. Let your parent interview the aide, pick the day or choose between two options. Choice keeps dignity.
  5. Start with the task they hate. Many people are glad to give up the heavy cleaning, yard work or snow shoveling while they guard the cooking.
  6. Use a familiar face. A neighbor, a church member or a grandchild who already visits may be accepted where a stranger is not.
  7. Wait for a calm stretch. Bring it up again after a quiet week, never right after an argument.

If cost is the objection, check what your parent may qualify for before you argue about money. The county office on aging, reached through the Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) at 1-877-222-3737, can screen for state programs. Ask about JACC and the Statewide Respite Care Program, which help pay for care at home.

If a stranger in the house is the worry, share how you will check the person. Our guide to vetting someone coming into the home lists the checks. Never hand a new helper the checkbook or bank cards.

Can my parent's doctor help?

Yes. A doctor can test for causes you cannot see and can say things a parent will not hear from a child. Ask for a visit focused on memory, mood, falls and medicines.

Medicare's yearly Wellness visit includes a cognitive assessment, and if the provider suspects a problem, Medicare covers a separate, fuller visit. A sudden change in behavior is always a medical question first, since an infection or a medicine problem can cause confusion.

You do not need your parent's permission to tell the doctor what you have seen. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) says the HIPAA privacy rule does not stop a provider from listening to family members. A short note sent before the visit works well. Stick to facts, such as dates, falls, missed medicines, unpaid bills or the stove left on.

Getting information back is different. HHS says a provider can share information with family who are involved in care if the patient agrees or does not object. Ask your parent to tell the office you may speak with staff, or to sign the office's form.

Some parents also listen to a geriatric care manager, a social worker or nurse who comes to the house as a neutral expert. Our guide to geriatric care managers explains when to call one.

What if refusing help puts my parent in danger?

Then decide which risk you are dealing with. Some risks can be lowered without your parent's cooperation, and some cannot. Driving, fire and wandering are where families most often have to act.

Driving

The New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission (MVC) Medical Review Unit accepts referrals from family members. You write a letter describing the driver's medical condition, with their name, address, license number if you have it and date of birth, plus your name, address, relationship and what you have seen. The MVC does not accept anonymous reports. If the MVC opens a review, it may send your parent medical forms that a doctor must fill out, due back within 45 days. Missing that deadline leads to a license suspension. Our guide to driving later in life covers the conversation and other ways to get around.

The house

You can often make the house safer without much discussion. Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, an automatic shutoff for the stove, night lights, grab bars and clear walkways. Our fall prevention guide has more.

Money

Unpaid bills, sudden withdrawals or a new "friend" handling accounts can mean a scam or exploitation. Ask your parent's bank about adding a trusted contact. Our guide to managing a parent's money explains the tools.

Self-neglect and Adult Protective Services

Each New Jersey county has an APS program for adults 18 and older who live in the community. The state's fact sheet says APS investigates reports of maltreatment and self-neglect. Self-neglect looks like a parent who has stopped eating, bathing, taking needed medicine or keeping the home safe.

APS questionAnswer
Who it servesAdults 18 and older living in the community, who cannot protect themselves
First visitA face-to-face meeting within 72 business hours of a report
Can it force help?No, not on an adult with capacity who declines
Can it remove someone?Not without consent or a court order
Is it confidential?Yes, records are shared only by court order
Statewide line1-855-835-5277

A trained APS social worker meets your parent in private and tries to judge their decision-making ability. Services are voluntary unless a court orders them. Many families find a call to APS worth making anyway. A neutral professional may get further than family, and the report creates a record if things get worse. Our guide on how to report elder abuse or neglect in New Jersey lists every county APS number.

When is guardianship the answer?

Only when your parent can no longer make safe decisions and nothing less restrictive will work. It is a court case, and the judge must look at alternatives first.

If your parent still has capacity, the better move is to ask them to sign a durable power of attorney and an advance directive now. Even a parent who refuses an aide may agree to name you as the person who speaks for them "just in case." Our guides to power of attorney and advance directives in New Jersey explain what each does.

If capacity is already gone and no papers exist, guardianship may be the only legal route, and our guide to guardianship in NJ walks through the court process. This page is general information, not legal advice. Talk with a New Jersey attorney about your parent's situation.

How do I keep going when my parent keeps saying no?

Decide what you can live with. You cannot control every risk an adult takes. You can make sure your parent knows help is there, the doctor knows the facts and the papers are in place.

  • Write down your line. Agree with siblings on what would make you act, such as a second fall, a fire or a missed heart medicine.
  • Set up check-ins. NIA suggests asking, with your parent's permission, neighbors and friends who see them often to call you with concerns.
  • Keep an emergency sheet ready. Write down medicines, doctors and contacts in one place, and keep a copy by the phone.
  • Look after yourself. Worry with no way to act is exhausting. Care2Caregivers, a Rutgers peer support line staffed by former family caregivers, answers at 1-800-424-2494. See also our guide to caregiver burnout.

If your parent ever says they feel hopeless or have no reason to live, call or text the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988. NIA advises seeking help right away.

faq.q: What do I do if my mom refuses help but clearly needs it?
faq.a: Find out what she fears most, then offer one small, specific thing as a trial, such as grocery delivery or a cleaner for a month. Tell her doctor what you have seen. If she can no longer understand the risks and is in danger, call her county Adult Protective Services office or 1-855-835-5277.

faq.q: Can I force my aging parent to accept help in New Jersey?
faq.a: Not if your parent has capacity. New Jersey APS says it cannot force services on adults with capacity who decline help, and it cannot remove anyone from their home without consent or a court order. A court can appoint a guardian only if a judge finds your parent incapacitated.

faq.q: How do I get my dad evaluated if he refuses to see a doctor?
faq.a: Try tying the visit to something he already wants, like a new prescription or his yearly Medicare Wellness visit, which includes a cognitive assessment. Offer to drive and go with him. You can also send the doctor a short note about what you have seen. HHS says HIPAA does not stop a provider from listening to family.

faq.q: Does Adult Protective Services handle self-neglect in NJ?
faq.a: Yes. The state's APS fact sheet says APS investigates reports of maltreatment and self-neglect for adults 18 and older living in the community who cannot protect themselves. A social worker visits within 72 business hours. Services are voluntary unless a court orders them.

faq.q: Can I report my parent's unsafe driving to the NJ MVC?
faq.a: Yes. The MVC Medical Review Unit accepts referrals from family members by letter. Describe the driver's medical condition and include their name, address, license number if known and date of birth, plus your name, relationship and what you have observed. Anonymous reports are not accepted.

faq.q: Is a parent with dementia allowed to refuse help?
faq.a: It depends on capacity for that decision, not the diagnosis alone. Many people with early dementia can still decide some things. A doctor can help judge it. If your parent can still understand them, ask about signing a power of attorney and advance directive now.

title: Wandering in dementia: Silver Alert and Project Lifesaver in NJ
dek: Six in 10 people with dementia wander at least once. What to do in the first 15 minutes, when New Jersey issues a Silver Alert, and how county locator programs work.
keyFacts: Six in 10 people living with dementia will wander at least once (Alzheimer's Association)
Search nearby, then call 911 if not found within 15 minutes
NJ Silver Alert requires a known motor vehicle and a belief the person is in danger
Many NJ county sheriff's offices run Project Lifesaver wristband locators
MedicAlert and Alzheimer's Association Safe and Found: 1-800-432-5378
body:
Wandering in dementia means a person leaves, or tries to leave, a safe place and may get lost. The Alzheimer's Association says six in 10 people living with dementia will wander at least once, and many do it more than once. It can happen at any stage, on foot or by car.

If someone with dementia is missing in New Jersey, search nearby right away and call 911 if you have not found them within 15 minutes. Tell police the person has dementia. New Jersey's Silver Alert is for a missing person with dementia who is driving a known vehicle and is believed to be in danger, so do not wait for an alert if your parent left on foot. Many county sheriff's offices also run Project Lifesaver, a wristband locator. This guide covers the alerts, the county programs, home safety and a plan for the first minutes.

If your parent is missing now

Look in the immediate area for up to 15 minutes, then call 911. Say the person has dementia, give a recent photo and say whether they took a car. If they are enrolled in Project Lifesaver, say so.

What should I do in the first minutes if my parent with dementia is missing?

Start looking immediately and call 911 at 15 minutes. The Alzheimer's Association says many people who wander are found within 1.5 miles of where they went missing.

  1. Check the house and yard first. Closets, the garage, the basement, the car and under porches. People hide or get stuck in small spaces.
  2. Search close by. The Alzheimer's Association suggests checking ponds, tree lines, fence lines and brush, where many people are found.
  3. Follow the dominant hand. The Association notes that wandering often follows the direction of the person's dominant hand.
  4. Try the old places. A former home, an old job, a church, a favorite diner or anywhere they have wandered before.
  5. Call 911 at 15 minutes. File a missing person report and say the person has dementia. Give the photo, what they were wearing and whether the car is gone.
  6. Stay reachable. Keep one person at home in case your parent returns or police call.

A person with dementia may not call out for help and may not answer when someone calls their name. The Monmouth County Sheriff's Office makes this point about the people its program finds. Search with your eyes, not only your voice.

How does Silver Alert work in New Jersey?

Silver Alert is a statewide system to spread word fast about a missing person believed to have dementia or another cognitive impairment. Local police request it. Families cannot activate it themselves.

The system was created by state law, N.J.S.A. 52:17B-194.4, as a voluntary effort between law enforcement and the media. The law has the New Jersey State Police share Silver Alert information on social media, with a description and photo of the missing person. It also says specific health information is not to be made public.

NJ Silver AlertDetails
Who it coversA missing person believed to have Alzheimer's, dementia or other cognitive impairment, any age
VehicleMust be operating a known motor vehicle
DangerBelieved to be in danger of death or serious injury, and police must say why
ReportEntered into the national NCIC database as missing
Who asksThe lead police agency, through the NJ State Police ROIC

The State Police criteria add that driving with dementia is not automatically a Silver Alert. All the conditions above have to be met.

New Jersey also has an MVP Emergency Alert System, under N.J.S.A. 52:17B-194.9, for a missing person believed to have a mental, intellectual or developmental disability who may be in danger of death or serious injury. When a case fits both systems, the lead police agency and the State Police decide which one to use. Either way, your call to 911 starts the process.

Silver Alert is for a parent who drove away. If they walked out the door, call 911 and do not wait for an alert.

What is Project Lifesaver, and which NJ counties offer it?

Project Lifesaver is a locator program run through local law enforcement. The person wears a small wrist or ankle transmitter, and trained officers track its signal when the person goes missing.

The New Jersey Ombudsman for Individuals with Intellectual or Developmental Disabilities says many of the state's 21 county sheriff's offices run the program. Rules, costs and phone numbers differ by county. These are the ones we confirmed on the counties' own sites.

CountyHow to ask
BergenSheriff's Community Policing Unit, 201-336-3540
GloucesterSheriff's Project Lifesaver Program, 856-384-4628
MonmouthAge 60+: Office on Aging, 732-431-7450
MorrisSheriff's Operational Services, 973-285-6681
OceanSheriff's Project Locate, 732-569-1321
SomersetOffice on Aging and Disability Services, 908-704-6346

Some county details worth knowing:

  • Monmouth says there is no charge for the bracelet. People under 60 apply through the Sheriff's Office at 732-431-6400, ext. 1129.
  • Gloucester says the county budgets for the program and pays for the bracelet for qualified applicants.
  • Bergen's brochure lists a one-time equipment fee and a monthly maintenance fee, and income-eligible participants may qualify for a waiver of the equipment fee. Ask for current costs when you call. Participants must live in a private home with a 24-hour live-in caregiver.
  • Morris requires a physician-confirmed diagnosis and a primary caregiver in Morris County.
  • Somerset serves older adults 60 and up who are actively wandering, have a physician's diagnosis of dementia or traumatic brain injury and have a caregiver with them around the clock. Staff do an in-home assessment first.
  • Ocean screens by phone, then does a home visit. The person must have a caregiver around the clock, not drive, not live alone and have a history of wandering. The caregiver buys the wristband.
  • Burlington announced in December 2023 that it was replacing its Project Lifesaver equipment with a GPS tracker system and that it keeps a free Persons at Risk Registry. Call the Sheriff's Office at 609-265-3788.

Notice the pattern. Most programs expect a caregiver who lives with the person. If your parent lives alone, ask the county anyway, then ask what else they suggest. For any county not listed, call the county sheriff's office or the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737.

Is MedicAlert or a GPS tracker worth it?

Some form of ID is worth it for anyone who might wander. A tracker adds a way to find the person, but only if they keep it on and it stays charged.

  • ID first. The National Institute on Aging (NIA) suggests an ID card or medical bracelet with the person's name and address and your phone number. If they might take a bracelet off, label their clothes.
  • MedicAlert with the Alzheimer's Association. NIA names the MedicAlert and Alzheimer's Association Safe and Found service as one safe return program. Call 1-800-432-5378 to learn about it. NIA notes there may be a charge.
  • GPS devices. NIA says many GPS systems can track a person's location and can be used alone or with a medical bracelet. Ask how often it needs charging and whether your parent will wear it. A device left on the dresser does nothing.
  • Medical alert buttons. A fall button is a different tool. Some include GPS. Our guide to medical alert systems in NJ covers costs and contracts.

We do not recommend specific brands. Read the contract, ask about monthly fees and cancellation, and test the device together before you rely on it.

How can I make the house safer so my parent doesn't wander?

Make leaving harder and staying easier. No change guarantees safety, so pair home changes with ID and a plan.

At the doors

  • NIA suggests a keyed deadbolt or an extra lock placed high or low on the door, with the key kept nearby for emergencies.
  • Add a door chime or alarm that sounds when a door opens. A pressure mat by the bed or door can alert you at night.
  • The Alzheimer's Association suggests covering doorknobs with cloth the same color as the door, or painting a door to match the wall.
  • Put STOP or DO NOT ENTER signs on doors, as NIA suggests.
  • Keep coats, shoes, purses, suitcases and car keys out of sight. They can prompt someone to leave.

The Alzheimer's Association says never to lock a person living with dementia in at home, and not to leave them unsupervised in new or changed surroundings.

The car

Wandering is not always on foot. The Alzheimer's Association says to remove access to car keys once the person no longer drives, since they may forget they stopped. See when a parent stops driving in NJ.

The daily routine

  • Learn the time of day they tend to wander. For many people it is late afternoon or early evening. Plan a walk or a task for that hour. Our guide to sundowning covers evening routines.
  • Meet basic needs. Hunger, thirst or needing the bathroom can send someone looking.
  • Reassure them when they say they want to "go home," even when they are home. Arguing rarely helps.
  • Avoid busy, confusing places like large malls. Do not leave the person alone in a car.

Who should know about the wandering risk?

More people than you think. Every person who knows your parent's face is another set of eyes.

  • Neighbors. NIA suggests telling neighbors and the local police that the person tends to wander. Give a trusted neighbor your number.
  • Your local police department. Ask whether they keep a voluntary registry for people at risk. Some counties, like Burlington, do.
  • Regular places. The barber, the pharmacy, the diner and the house of worship.
  • Anyone who gives care. Aides, adult day staff and visiting relatives should know the plan.

Keep a recent close-up photo on your phone and a written description with height, weight, eye color and distinguishing marks. The Alzheimer's Association also suggests a list of places your parent might go and a note of dangerous spots near the home, such as water, busy roads and bus stops. Our printable emergency info sheet is a good place to keep it all.

If wandering is getting frequent, it may be time to talk with the doctor and look at more support. Our guides to help after a dementia diagnosis, adult day care and memory care in New Jersey can help you weigh the next step. The Alzheimer's Association helpline answers around the clock at 1-800-272-3900.

faq.q: What do I do if my mom with dementia is missing?
faq.a: Search the house, yard and nearby area right away. If you have not found her within 15 minutes, call 911, say she has dementia and give a recent photo. Tell police whether she took a car and whether she wears a Project Lifesaver bracelet.

faq.q: Can I ask for a Silver Alert in New Jersey?
faq.a: No. Police request it. NJ State Police criteria say the missing person must be believed to have dementia or another cognitive impairment, be operating a known vehicle, be entered as missing in NCIC and be believed to be in danger. Call 911 and police decide.

faq.q: How do I sign my dad up for Project Lifesaver in NJ?
faq.a: Call your county sheriff's office or county office on aging. Many NJ counties run it, but rules differ. Most require a dementia diagnosis and a caregiver who lives with the person. Some counties charge for the bracelet and some do not.

faq.q: Is Project Lifesaver free in New Jersey?
faq.a: It depends on the county. Monmouth says there is no charge for the bracelet and Gloucester pays for it for qualified applicants. Bergen's brochure lists an equipment fee and monthly fee with a possible equipment fee waiver for income-eligible families, and Ocean asks the caregiver to buy the wristband.

faq.q: Does a Silver Alert go out if someone with dementia walks away?
faq.a: Usually not. New Jersey's Silver Alert criteria require the person to be operating a known motor vehicle. That is why you should call 911 quickly when someone leaves on foot. NJ also has an MVP Emergency Alert System that police may use in some cases.

faq.q: How can I stop my parent with dementia from leaving the house at night?
faq.a: Try a door chime or alarm, a pressure mat by the bed, a lock placed high or low, and night lights. Keep coats, shoes and keys out of sight. Never lock the person in alone, and pair these steps with an ID bracelet and a recent photo.

title: Aggression and agitation in dementia: what helps in NJ
dek: Shouting, grabbing or hitting usually has a cause. How to stay safe, calm the moment, find the trigger, weigh the medicines and get crisis help in New Jersey.
keyFacts: NIA says agitation and aggression usually happen for a reason, such as pain, poor sleep or too much noise
A sudden change in behavior calls for a prompt medical checkup
FDA-approved for Alzheimer's agitation: Rexulti (2023) and Auvelity (2026)
Antipsychotics carry an FDA boxed warning of increased death risk in dementia
Every NJ county has a 24-hour psychiatric screening line
body:
Aggression in dementia, such as shouting, cursing, grabbing or hitting, usually has a cause. Pain, an infection, fear, too much noise or being rushed through a bath are common ones. The Alzheimer's Association says aggressive behavior can be verbal or physical and that the person is not acting this way on purpose.

What helps most is staying calm, keeping yourself safe, finding the trigger and calling the doctor, since a sudden change can be a urinary tract infection or a medicine side effect. Medication is an option when other steps fail, and it carries real risks. If anyone is in danger, call 911 and say the person has dementia. Our guide to sundowning covers late-day restlessness. This page covers the harder moments, any time of day.

When it is an emergency

If you or anyone else is being hurt, step away and call 911. Tell the dispatcher the person has dementia. For a crisis that is not life-threatening, each New Jersey county has a 24-hour psychiatric screening line, listed below. The Alzheimer's Association helpline answers 24 hours a day at 1-800-272-3900.

Why does someone with dementia become aggressive?

Most often because something is wrong that they cannot put into words. The National Institute on Aging (NIA) says agitation and aggression usually happen for a reason, and the first job is to find it.

NIA and the Alzheimer's Association list similar causes:

  • Pain or illness. Arthritis, constipation, a bad tooth or an infection. The Alzheimer's Association notes that urinary tract and other infections are common and that people may express the discomfort through aggression.
  • Tiredness, hunger or thirst.
  • Medicines. Side effects, or two medicines that interact. The risk rises with the number of prescriptions.
  • Too much going on. Noise, clutter, a crowd or unfamiliar people in the house.
  • Being pushed. NIA mentions being pressed to bathe, or to remember people and events, when the disease has made that very hard.
  • Change and loss. A new aide, a move, a rearranged room, or grief over lost freedom, such as driving.
  • Loneliness or depression.
  • Your stress. The Alzheimer's Association asks whether the person is picking up on the caregiver's own irritation.

Keep a simple log for a week or two. Write the time, what happened just before, who was there and what you tried. Bring it to the doctor. Patterns often show up on paper that you cannot see in the moment.

What should I do when my parent with dementia gets angry or violent?

Protect yourself first, then lower the temperature. Do not argue, correct or try to reason. The feeling matters more than the facts right now.

  1. Step back. NIA advises staying at a safe distance until aggressive behavior stops. Stand to the side, out of arm's reach, with a clear path to the door.
  2. Lower your voice. Speak slowly in a soft tone. Use short sentences. Do not show frustration, even if you feel it. NIA suggests deep breaths or counting to 10.
  3. Respond to the feeling. The Alzheimer's Association suggests focusing on feelings, not facts. "You're upset. I'm here." works better than "Nobody stole your wallet."
  4. Check for a cause. Pain, a full bladder, hunger, cold or a noise. Rule out pain early, as the Association advises.
  5. Change the scene. Turn off the TV, ask visitors to step out, offer a snack or drink, play familiar music or suggest a short walk together.
  6. Drop the task. If the fight started over a shower or getting dressed, stop. Try again later, maybe with a different person.
  7. Walk away if it is safe. The Association says that if the person is in a safe place, you can leave the room for a moment to collect yourself.
  8. Get help if it does not settle. Call a family member or neighbor. If anyone is in danger, call 911.
You do not have to win the argument. You only have to get everyone through the next ten minutes safely.

How can we prevent outbursts?

A calmer, predictable day prevents more outbursts than anything you say in the moment. NIA puts routine near the top of its list.

  • Keep a routine. Bathing, dressing and meals at about the same times each day.
  • Plan hard tasks for good hours. The Alzheimer's Association says most people do best at a certain time of day, often morning.
  • Simplify how you ask. One instruction at a time. Offer two choices, not open questions.
  • Reduce noise and clutter. Let in daylight. Keep loved objects and photos around.
  • Give them something to do. NIA suggests folding laundry, a favorite show or music. Feeling useful calms many people.
  • Watch your own tone. People with dementia often mirror the mood around them.
  • Keep checkups and medicines current. Ask about pain at every visit. Our guide to managing many medications covers medicine reviews.

NIA lists being pushed to bathe as one trigger. If bath time keeps turning into a fight, it is fine to stop and try again later, and to ask the doctor or an aide agency for other ideas.

When should I call the doctor?

Call the same day if aggression starts suddenly or gets worse fast. The Alzheimer's Association says anyone with new behavioral symptoms should get a thorough medical checkup, especially when they appear suddenly.

Call quickly if the change comes with fever, new incontinence, a fall, a new medicine or much more confusion than usual. Sudden confusion after surgery or a hospital stay can be delirium, which is a medical problem. See our guide to delirium after a hospital stay.

Bring your log and a full list of medicines. Our sundowning guide lists questions about infections, pain and medicines. For aggression, also ask:

  • What should we try before a new medicine?
  • If you prescribe something, what are the risks, what side effects should we watch for and when will we review it?
  • Would a geriatric psychiatrist or memory specialist help?

What medicines are used for dementia aggression, and what are the risks?

Medicines are used when non-drug steps have not worked and the behavior is causing distress or danger. Two drugs are approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for agitation associated with dementia due to Alzheimer's disease.

DrugWhat the FDA says
Rexulti (brexpiprazole)Approved May 2023. An antipsychotic. Keeps the class boxed warning on increased risk of death
Auvelity (dextromethorphan and bupropion)Approved April 2026. The first approved drug for this use that is not an antipsychotic

Antipsychotic drugs carry an FDA boxed warning, the agency's strongest, that older adults with dementia-related psychosis treated with antipsychotics have an increased risk of death. Doctors sometimes prescribe other antipsychotics off-label for agitation, and the same warning applies to them.

The FDA lists dizziness, upset stomach, headache, diarrhea and drowsiness among Auvelity's common side effects. Auvelity has its own boxed warning, about suicidal thoughts in young people taking antidepressants. It can also cause seizures and raise blood pressure, so the FDA says doctors should check blood pressure first and ask about other medicines that contain bupropion or dextromethorphan.

Any medicine is a decision to make with the doctor, weighed against how much the behavior is hurting your parent's life and safety. Ask for the lowest dose, a clear goal and a date to review whether it is working.

Where can New Jersey families get help in a crisis?

Call 911 for immediate danger. For a mental health crisis that is not life-threatening, New Jersey's Division of Mental Health and Addiction Services lists a designated screening service in every county for psychiatric emergencies and crisis intervention, answered 24 hours a day.

For advice that is not an emergency:

  • Alzheimer's Association helpline, 1-800-272-3900, 24 hours a day.
  • Alzheimer's New Jersey helpline, 1-888-280-6055, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.
  • NIA's ADEAR Center, 1-800-438-4380, for information and referrals.
  • 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, call or text 988, for you or your parent.

If your parent lives in assisted living or memory care, aggressive behavior can affect whether the residence can keep them. Our guide to memory care in New Jersey explains the rules. If you suspect a care worker is mistreating your parent, see how to report elder abuse in NJ.

How do I stay safe as a caregiver?

Your safety counts too. Getting hurt does not help your parent, and it is not a sign you failed.

  • Lock up anything dangerous. NIA says to hide or lock up car keys, guns and kitchen knives.
  • Know your exit. Keep your phone on you and a clear path out of the room.
  • Step back instead of holding on. Grabbing or holding someone down can get you both hurt. Get distance and call for help.
  • Tell the doctor about every incident. Include the ones that scared you, even if no one was hurt.
  • Get breaks. Adult day programs and respite programs give you regular time off. The ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 connects you to your county.
  • Talk to people who get it. Care2Caregivers, a Rutgers peer support line, answers at 1-800-424-2494. See also caregiver support groups and caregiver burnout.

If you feel close to losing your temper, put your parent somewhere safe and leave the room. Then call someone. Needing help with this is normal, and New Jersey has people ready to give it.

faq.q: What do I do when my mom with dementia hits me?
faq.a: Step back out of reach, keep your voice low and do not argue or restrain her. Check for pain, hunger or a full bladder, and remove noise or the task that upset her. If anyone is in danger, call 911 and say she has dementia. Tell her doctor about every incident.

faq.q: Why is my dad with dementia suddenly aggressive?
faq.a: A sudden change is often medical. The Alzheimer's Association notes urinary tract and other infections are common, and pain or a new medicine can also cause it. Call his doctor the same day, and bring a list of every medicine he takes.

faq.q: Is there medication for aggression in dementia?
faq.a: The FDA has approved two drugs for agitation associated with Alzheimer's dementia, Rexulti in 2023 and Auvelity in 2026. Antipsychotics, including Rexulti, carry a boxed warning about increased risk of death in older adults with dementia-related psychosis. Discuss risks and goals with the doctor.

faq.q: Who do I call in NJ if my parent with dementia is out of control?
faq.a: Call 911 if anyone is in danger and say the person has dementia. For a crisis that is not life-threatening, call your county's 24-hour psychiatric screening line. The Alzheimer's Association helpline also answers around the clock at 1-800-272-3900.

faq.q: How can I calm someone with dementia who is agitated?
faq.a: Speak slowly and softly, reassure them they are safe and respond to the feeling, not the facts. Offer a snack, a drink, music or a short walk. Reduce noise and people in the room, and drop any task that started the upset.

faq.q: Can assisted living ask my parent to leave for aggressive behavior?
faq.a: It can happen, so read the admission agreement for the conditions the residence says it will keep a resident through. Our memory care guide explains the New Jersey rules. For help with a discharge notice, call the NJ Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-877-582-6995.

title: Hospital stay checklist for NJ families: what to bring and ask
dek: A printable checklist for when your mom or dad goes into the hospital: what to pack, what to ask the care team, your rights as a designated caregiver under New Jersey law, and what Medicare pays.
keyFacts: NJ hospitals must offer patients the chance to name a family caregiver and, before a discharge home, teach that caregiver the after-care tasks.
A designated caregiver must be told of discharge no later than when the doctor issues the discharge order.
Original Medicare 2026: $1,736 inpatient deductible, then $0 a day through day 60.
Medicare's hospital coverage does not include personal care items like razors or slipper socks.
NJ Department of Health 24-hour complaint hotline for hospitals: 1-800-792-9770.
body:
A hospital stay checklist covers three jobs for the family: what to pack, what to ask the care team while your mom or dad is in the bed, and what to line up before discharge. Pack the medication list, insurance cards, a copy of the advance directive, glasses, hearing aids and a phone charger. Ask every day whether your parent is an inpatient or under observation. Our printable checklist below fits on one page.

Many stays start in the ER with no time to plan. That is fine. The bag can follow later the same day, and the questions matter more than the packing. Once discharge is in sight, our guide to when a parent leaves the hospital takes over.

What should I pack for my parent's hospital stay?

Papers first, then the things that help your parent see, hear and feel like themselves. Leave valuables at home.

Papers

  • The full medication list, with doses and allergies.
  • Photo ID and every insurance card, including Medicare, any Medigap or Medicare Advantage card, the Part D card, and NJ FamilyCare or PAAD cards.
  • A copy of the advance directive and POLST, if your parent has them. Our POLST guide explains that form.
  • Names and phone numbers of the main doctor and specialists.
  • A short list of family contacts, with the main contact marked.

Comfort and safety

  • Glasses, hearing aids with spare batteries, and dentures, each in a case labeled with your parent's name.
  • The walker or cane, also labeled.
  • Nonslip slippers or shoes with backs, a robe and a sweater. Hospital rooms run cold.
  • Toothbrush, comb, razor, lip balm and lotion. Medicare's hospital coverage does not include personal care items like razors or slipper socks, so bring your own.
  • A phone, a long charging cord, and the key phone numbers on paper in case the phone dies.
  • A notebook and pen, a large-print clock or calendar, and a family photo for the tray table.

What to leave at home

Jewelry, cash, credit cards and checkbooks. Bring the medication list in place of the pill bottles unless the hospital asks for them, and ask the nurse what to do with any medicines your parent arrived with.

Label the hearing aid case. Small things vanish into hospital bedding fast.

What should we ask the care team in the first day or two?

Find out who is in charge, what the plan is and how the team will reach you. Write the answers down, with names and the date.

The doctor running the stay may be a hospital doctor, often called a hospitalist, rather than your parent's own doctor. Nurses change with each shift. Your notebook becomes the thread that ties it all together.

  • Who is the attending doctor, and when do they usually make rounds?
  • What is the working diagnosis, and what tests are planned today?
  • Is she admitted as an inpatient, or here under observation?
  • Which of her home medicines are continuing, stopped or changed?
  • Is she wearing her glasses and hearing aids?
  • Who is the case manager or social worker, and how do I reach them?
  • What is the best time and number to call for an update?
  • When might she go home, and to where?

Ask your parent to tell staff, in front of you, that the team may share information with you. Medicare's fact sheet on talking with a family member's doctor says the doctor needs your parent's permission, and once it is given the doctor can talk with you directly. If your parent can't speak for themselves, the health care representative named in the advance directive should hand staff a copy.

Ask about status every day

Some patients spend nights in a hospital bed under observation, which Medicare bills as outpatient care. Medicare.gov says you or your caregiver should ask the hospital or doctor about status each day of the stay. Our discharge guide explains why it matters for rehab coverage and how to appeal a change.

Can I be named my parent's caregiver at the hospital?

Yes. New Jersey's caregiver law, often called the CARE Act, requires hospitals to offer patients the chance to name a family caregiver, to tell that person about the discharge, and to show them how to do the care at home.

Under the state's hospital rules (N.J.A.C. 8:43G-11A.4), the discharge planning team must offer your parent, or the person legally allowed to decide for them, a chance to designate a caregiver after arrival and before discharge. If your parent arrived unconscious with no one legally able to decide for them, the offer can come once they recover. A caregiver can also be named in an advance directive. Your parent can decline, or change the name at any time before discharge. The hospital will also ask your parent for written consent to share medical information with you. Without that consent, the law does not require the hospital to give you the notices below.

Once you are named, the law (N.J.S.A. 26:2H-5.27 and 26:2H-5.28) says the hospital must:

  • Tell you about a discharge or a transfer to another facility as soon as possible, and no later than when the attending doctor issues the discharge order.
  • Before a discharge home, consult with you and issue a discharge plan that describes the after-care tasks your parent will need to stay at home.
  • Teach you those tasks, in person or by video as you prefer, with a demonstration and a chance to ask questions.

You can still say no. Being named does not obligate you to do any after-care (N.J.S.A. 26:2H-5.26), and the hospital rules require the team to tell you and your parent that if you decline the designation, you have no obligation to provide it. Ask to be named on the first or second day, so the hospital has your number when plans move fast. This is general information, not legal advice.

What will a hospital stay cost with Medicare?

Under Original Medicare in 2026, an inpatient pays a $1,736 deductible per benefit period and then nothing more per day through day 60. Longer stays cost more each day.

Inpatient daysYour parent pays (2026)
Days 1 to 60$1,736 deductible, then $0 a day
Days 61 to 90$434 a day
Days 91 to 150$868 a day, from 60 lifetime reserve days
After day 150All costs

Medicare says Part A covers a semi-private room, meals, general nursing, and certain drugs as part of inpatient treatment. It does not cover private-duty nursing, a private room unless medically necessary, or a TV or phone with a separate charge. Medicare Advantage plans may charge copays instead, so call the number on the plan card. A Medigap plan may pick up the deductible. For free help reading a bill, call New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) at 1-800-792-8820.

How can family help with confusion in the hospital?

Keep your parent able to see, hear and tell the time, and tell the nurse right away about any sudden confusion. That can be delirium, a medical problem our guide to delirium after surgery or a hospital stay explains.

What other rights help families during a stay?

Your parent has a right to a free interpreter, to help with hearing or vision problems, and to file a complaint with the state.

  • Language help. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services says medical providers must offer free interpretation, and patients are not required to bring their own interpreter or rely on a child or family member.
  • Hearing and vision. Providers must take steps for people with speech, hearing or vision disabilities, including qualified interpreters, readers, Braille or large print.
  • Complaints. The NJ Department of Health's 24-hour complaint hotline at 1-800-792-9770 takes complaints about hospitals, and the department also takes them online. Try the unit's nurse manager or the hospital's patient advocate first.

Siblings can take shifts at the bedside. Our caregiver log helps everyone record what doctors said and what changed each day. If you are coordinating from another state, see long-distance caregiving.

What should we line up before discharge?

Start asking about the plan early, because discharge can come quickly. Know where your parent will go, who will be home with them, which medicines change and what equipment is needed.

The full day-of checklist, the Medicare notices and how to appeal a discharge that feels too soon are in our guide to when a parent leaves the hospital. If your parent may need rehab, read rehab after a hospital stay before the planner hands you a list of facilities. Next time you are deciding whether to go at all, our guide to urgent care or the ER can help.

Print the checklist below and keep it in the bag, so whoever grabs it next has it too.

Tick each item. Keep this page in the bag or by the bed.

  • Photo ID and every insurance card
  • Copy of advance directive and POLST
  • Doctors' and family phone numbers on paper
  • Glasses, hearing aids, batteries, dentures, labeled
  • Walker or cane, labeled with name
  • Nonslip slippers, robe, sweater
  • Toothbrush, comb, razor, lip balm
  • Phone and a long charging cord
  • Notebook, pen, large-print clock or calendar

Ask the team

  • Who is the attending doctor? When are rounds?
  • Inpatient or observation? (ask every day)
  • Which home medicines continue, stop or change?
  • What tests are planned today?
  • Who is the case manager or social worker?
  • Best time and number for updates?
  • Please record me as the designated caregiver.
  • When might discharge be, and to where?

  • Caregiver training done for care at home
  • Updated medication list in hand
  • Follow-up visit booked, ride arranged
  • Number to call at night

faq.q: What should I pack for my mom's hospital stay?
faq.a: Her medication list with allergies, photo ID and every insurance card, a copy of her advance directive and POLST, doctors' and family phone numbers, labeled glasses, hearing aids and dentures, her walker, nonslip slippers, a robe, toiletries, a phone with a long charger, and a notebook. Leave jewelry, cash and checkbooks at home.

faq.q: How do I become the designated caregiver for my dad in a New Jersey hospital?
faq.a: Ask the nurse or case manager to record you as his designated caregiver under New Jersey's caregiver law. He, or his legal decision maker, makes the designation, and he will be asked to sign consent for the hospital to share his medical information with you. The hospital must then tell you about the discharge, consult with you on the plan and teach you the care tasks, in person or by video.

faq.q: What questions should we ask the hospital team?
faq.a: Who the attending doctor is and when rounds happen, the working diagnosis and today's tests, whether your parent is an inpatient or under observation, which home medicines changed, who the case manager is, the best time to call for updates, and when and where discharge is likely.

faq.q: How much does a hospital stay cost with Medicare in 2026?
faq.a: Under Original Medicare, an inpatient pays a $1,736 deductible per benefit period, then $0 a day for days 1 to 60, $434 a day for days 61 to 90, and $868 a day for up to 60 lifetime reserve days. Medicare Advantage plans set their own copays.

faq.q: Does my parent have a right to an interpreter in the hospital?
faq.a: Yes. Federal guidance from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services says medical providers must offer free interpretation, and patients are not required to bring their own interpreter or rely on a child or family member.

faq.q: Where do I complain about care in a New Jersey hospital?
faq.a: Start with the unit's nurse manager or the hospital's patient advocate. You can also call the NJ Department of Health's 24-hour complaint hotline at 1-800-792-9770 or file a complaint online.

title: Free printable caregiver log for tracking care at home in NJ
dek: A one-week log for tracking your mom or dad's medicines, meals, sleep, mood, falls and visits, so siblings and aides stay on the same page and doctor visits start with facts.
keyFacts: The CDC says more than one in four older people fall each year, and less than half tell their doctor.
Delirium is sudden, severe confusion that comes with illness and is often reversible, according to MedlinePlus.
NIA suggests bringing insurance cards, other doctors' names, a medication list and questions to every appointment.
Medicare Form CMS-10106 lets 1-800-MEDICARE talk with someone your parent chooses about claims.
NJ's ADRC line, 1-877-222-3737, connects families with county aging services.
body:
A caregiver log is a short daily record of how your mom or dad is doing: medicines given, meals, sleep, mood, falls, visits and anything that changed. Whoever is on duty, whether that is you, a sibling or a paid aide, writes a word or two each day. Bring the log to doctor visits so you can answer "how has she been?" with facts. Our free one-week log below prints on one letter page.

A log is most useful when several people share the care. It keeps everyone working from the same story, and it catches slow changes that are easy to miss from one day to the next.

Why keep a caregiver log?

Memory gets fuzzy when you are tired, and doctors decide better with specifics. A log turns "Dad seems worse" into "Dad slept about four hours a night this week and skipped two lunches."

  • Doctor visits. Appointments are short. A week of notes tells the doctor more than a summary from memory.
  • Slow changes. Less appetite, more napping or a shuffling walk build up over weeks. On paper, they are hard to miss.
  • Sudden changes. MedlinePlus describes delirium as sudden, severe confusion that comes with illness and is often temporary and reversible. If the log shows Mom was sharp on Monday and confused on Wednesday, call her doctor that day.
  • Falls. The CDC says more than one in four older people fall each year, and less than half tell their doctor. The log records the fall even if your parent would rather forget it.
  • Medicines. A check for each dose shows whether pills are being missed or doubled.
  • Sharing the load. It shows who covered which days, which can take the heat out of sibling arguments.
"Seems off" is hard for a doctor to act on. "Skipped lunch three days running" is easy.

What should a caregiver log track?

A few things every day, plus anything unusual. A word, a number or a check mark is enough for most entries.

TrackWhat to write
Meds givenA check per dose, or "missed" and why
MealsAte well, half, or skipped, and drinks
SleepRough hours, nights up, long naps
MoodOne word, like calm, low or upset
FallsWhen, where, and any injury
ChangesNew pain, cough, swelling, confusion
VisitsDoctor, nurse, aide, therapist, friend

Stick to what you saw and heard. "Refused lunch, said her stomach hurt" helps a doctor more than "difficult day." Note near falls too, like a stumble on the stairs or a grab for the counter.

Write down what helped as well. If a short walk after lunch made the afternoon calmer, the next person on duty should know. If the evenings are always harder than the mornings, that pattern is worth a line every day, since it helps the doctor see what is going on.

The log records doses given. The medication list records what the doses should be. Keep the two together on the same clipboard.

How do we share the log with siblings and aides?

Use one log, keep it in one place, agree who writes in it, and review it on a set day each week. A clipboard by the kitchen phone works. So does a photo of the page sent to a family group text.

  1. Give it a home. Next to the pill organizer on the kitchen counter is easy for everyone to find.
  2. Agree who writes. Whoever is with your parent that day, including paid aides. If an agency sends the aide, ask whether its staff keep their own visit notes and whether the family can see them.
  3. Send a photo at the end of the week. Siblings who live away can spot patterns the person on duty is too close to see.
  4. Hold a ten-minute weekly call. What changed, what the doctor needs to hear and who covers next week. The National Institute on Aging's caregiver worksheets include one for dividing tasks among family and friends.
  5. Keep the old pages. File them by month. A doctor may ask when a problem started.

Talk with your parent about the log before you start. Most people accept it more easily when it is framed as a way to make doctor visits go better. Keep it to care facts, and leave bank details and passwords out of it.

A log can also flag trouble with paid help. If entries show bruises nobody can explain, missing money or a parent who seems afraid of a helper, read our guide to reporting elder abuse in New Jersey. Before anyone new starts, our hiring checklist has the questions to ask. If you are the sibling far away, see long-distance caregiving.

What should we bring to doctor appointments?

The log pages since the last visit, the medication list, insurance cards and a short list of questions with the most important first.

The National Institute on Aging's tips for caregivers suggest bringing insurance cards, the names and phone numbers of other doctors, a current medication list and a list of questions, starting with the most important. Make sure your parent has their glasses and a working hearing aid, so they can take part.

  • Circle the two or three entries that matter most before you go.
  • Let your parent answer the doctor's questions when they can, and use the log to fill gaps gently.
  • Take notes on what the doctor says. NIA says writing things down helps you both remember what the doctor said.
  • Ask for written instructions to take home, and add any changes to the log and the medication list that day.

Doctors need your parent's permission to talk with you. NIA says most offices use a consent form, sometimes called a HIPAA release, and suggests asking your parent to add your name at each provider's office. To talk with 1-800-MEDICARE about claims, your parent can sign Medicare's Authorization to Disclose Personal Health Information (Form CMS-10106).

When does the log show it's time for more help?

When the same problems keep showing up, or when the log shows the person doing the care is running on empty. A few patterns to act on:

  • Missed doses several times a week. Ask the pharmacist about blister packs, and see our guide to managing many medications.
  • Skipped meals week after week. Tell the doctor, and look into Meals on Wheels in your parent's county.
  • Any fall. Tell the doctor at the next visit, or sooner if there was an injury, and read our guide to preventing falls at home.
  • Low or flat mood most days. Show the doctor the mood column and ask whether depression could be part of it. Bring the sleep and meals columns too.
  • The same name in every box. If one person is covering every day, it is time to share the load. Our guide to caregiver burnout covers respite and where to find a break.
Need help near your parent?

New Jersey's Aging and Disability Resource Connection (ADRC) line connects families with the county office on aging for home care, meals, respite and caregiver support. Call 1-877-222-3737.

Print a fresh sheet each Monday and clip it next to the pill organizer. Ask everyone who visits to add a line, even if it is only "fine today, ate well." A quiet week on paper is worth having too. It gives the doctor a baseline to compare against when something does change.

faq.q: How do I keep track of my mom's care when my siblings and I take turns?
faq.a: Keep one paper log in one place, such as a clipboard by the pill organizer. Whoever is with her writes a word or two each day about medicines, meals, sleep, mood, falls and visits. Send a photo of the page to the family at the end of each week and hold a short weekly call.

faq.q: What should a caregiver write in a daily log?
faq.a: Medicines given or missed, how much was eaten and drunk, sleep, mood in one word, falls or near falls, new symptoms like pain, swelling or confusion, and who visited. Write what you saw and heard rather than general impressions.

faq.q: Should I tell my dad's doctor about a fall even if he wasn't hurt?
faq.a: Yes. The CDC says more than one in four older people fall each year and less than half tell their doctor. A fall can point to a medicine problem, weakness or a vision issue the doctor can address. Write it in the log with the date and what happened.

faq.q: Can a paid aide write in our family's caregiver log?
faq.a: Yes, if you ask. Many families have whoever is on duty, including aides, add a line each day. If an agency sends the aide, ask whether its staff also keep their own visit notes and whether the family can see them.

faq.q: What do I need so my parent's doctor will talk to me?
faq.a: Your parent's permission. Most offices use a consent form, sometimes called a HIPAA release, that lists who may receive information. Ask your parent to add your name at each office. For 1-800-MEDICARE, your parent can sign Form CMS-10106.

faq.q: When does sudden confusion need a call to the doctor?
faq.a: Right away. Sudden, severe confusion can be delirium, which comes with illness and is often reversible. If your parent is confused and also very drowsy, has trouble breathing or shows stroke signs, call 911.
